10012-the-mountains-of-california:
John Muir's book on the mountains of California opens with the Sierra Nevada itself, then moves through glaciers, snow, a near view of the high Sierra, and the passes. Glacier lakes and meadows follow, with forests, the Douglas squirrel, and a wind-storm in the trees.

Muir writes as a naturalist who walked the range, slept under its pines, and studied how ice carved its valleys. His prose joins science with wonder, and helped Americans see the Sierra as a treasure to protect. Readers get the classic Muir: vivid, exact, and full of joy in wild places.
10899-olivia-in-india:
O. Douglas wrote Olivia in India as a happy book in letter form, praised by James Douglas in the Star as a book one must tell friends about. Douglas writes that Olivia can write the most fascinating letters ever read, and the Glasgow Herald calls the author an extremely likable personality. The novel follows Olivia's life and letters in India, with humor and warmth.

The book's charm lies in its voice: cheerful, observant, and fond of people. Readers meet Anglo-Indian society through a young woman's eyes, without bitterness or gloom. Those who like light, likable novels of travel and friendship will find Olivia good company.
10972-with-the-die-hards-in-siberia:
Colonel John Ward commanded Middlesex Regiment battalions sent to Siberia after the First World War, and he wrote this 1920 account for his sons, in case he did not return. Ward refuses to rewrite his judgments with hindsight, recording events and motives as they seemed at the time. He argues that Admiral Kolchak took up the Omsk government only after Allied urging and promises of support.

Ward describes Vladivostok, plots against prisoners, and the tangled politics of Russian factions, with letters and reports quoted in full. The narrative honours his men, the Die-Hards, while admitting that Allied policy often misread Russian affairs. It remains a firsthand source for the British intervention in Siberia and for the hopes placed in a constituent assembly at Moscow.
11212-modern-india:
William Eleroy Curtis published this 1905 volume, Modern India, a series of letters written for the Chicago Record-Herald during the winter of 1903–04, dedicated to Lady Curzon. Curtis covers Bombay, servants, hotels, and cave temples, the empire of India, two Hindu weddings, the religions of India, how India is governed, and its railways.

Later letters visit Ahmedabad, Jeypore and its Maharaja, snakes and tigers, the Rajputs, the Mogul empire and architecture, Delhi's temples and tombs, thugs, fakirs, and nautch dancers, Simla, famines, the frontier. At Agra, Curtis describes marble mosaics of flowers, birds, and beasts in precious stones, designed by Austin de Bordeaux, a Frenchman who defrauded European princes with false gems. The book gives American readers a reporter's India.
11869-venetia:
Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield, first published Venetia in 1837, and this edition carries his dedication to Lord Lyndhurst. The novel opens some ten years before the American revolt at Cherbury, an ivy-covered hall in the English midlands belonging to the Herbert family.

Venetia, the heroine, grows up sheltered and largely cut off from her father's family, whose members remain distant names rather than living relations. Through her friendship with the young poet Lord Cadurcis, Disraeli shadows forth two renowned spirits of his own age. The novel blends romance with a portrait of genius, fame, and disappointment.
12270-the-doomswoman-an-historical-roman:
Gertrude Atherton published The Doomswoman in 1900, an historical romance of old California under Mexican rule. Atherton, a Californian writer, sets the story in Monterey at Governor Alvarado house.

Chonita, an Iturbi y Moncada, comes to stand godmother to Alvarado child with her friend Dona Martina, and first hears of Diego Estenega, a man her family will not name. Love, family honor, and tradition pull against each other: traditions are fivefold, she reflects, and multiplied by duty, while love is sweet but single. Atherton writes with local knowledge and romantic sweep. The novel captures Californio society just before American conquest changed it.
12342-the-nuttall-encyclop-dia:
The Reverend James Wood edited The Nuttall Encyclopaedia in 1907, the sixty-first thousand, as a concise and comprehensive dictionary of general knowledge. The volume holds over sixteen thousand terse and original articles on nearly all subjects in larger encyclopaedias.

Entries cover history, biography, geography, literature, philosophy, religion, science, and art, with special strength in concise lives and places. A mid-book entry treats Sebastian Brant, whose writings are numerous but rare, including the Narrenschiff, or Ship of Fools. Wood, editor of Nuttall Standard Dictionary, aimed at busy readers who wanted facts without bulk. The encyclopaedia remains a handy Edwardian reference, dated in places but admirably compact.
1265-queen-victoria:
Lytton Strachey was the debunker of Eminent Victorians, and he turns to the queen herself in this biography. His subject is the sheltered girl who took the throne at eighteen. She became the wife who leaned on Albert, the widow who ruled an empire in black, and the old woman who outlived her age.

Strachey writes with wit and a novelist's eye, mixing state papers with private letters and sharp portraits of ministers. His Victoria is human, stubborn, and often comic. The book reshaped royal biography, and it still reads as the liveliest short life of the queen.
12697-the-splendid-idle-forties-stories-:
Gertrude Atherton's 1902 stories, revised from her earlier Before the Gringo Came, picture old California before American rule. Monterey race days, proud dons, flirtatious señoritas, padres, and vaqueros fill a world of leisure, honour, and sudden violence. Pearls, bells, and lost loves recur through the tales.

Atherton writes with fondness for the Spanish past, even as American officers and settlers press into the scene. Her heroines bargain with charm and pride, while her men duel, feast, and lose. The book remains a rich, romantic portrait of a California that vanished within a generation.
12820-the-case-for-india:
Annie Besant delivered The Case for India as her presidential address to the thirty-second Indian National Congress at Calcutta on December 26, 1917. Chosen while interned as a person dangerous to public safety, she thanks delegates who crowned her with honour while she was silenced and slandered. Her debt to them, she says, exceeds that of any predecessor.

Besant argues that the war quickened Asia's awakening, and that English education, democratic ideals, and Japan's victory over Russia stirred new hopes in India. She calls for a larger share in rule to meet those hopes. The address stands as a landmark of the Indian self-rule movement.
12878-the-radio-boys-in-the-thousand-isl:
J. W. Duffield's 1922 Radio Boys adventure sends Cub Perry, Hal, and Bud to the Thousand Islands for a summer holiday. Vacation plans turn to mystery when radio signals, a deserted camp, and a diary left by a castaway figure point to a hidden prisoner. Chapters on catwhiskers, diagrams, and shore hook-ups mix radio craft with detection.

Hal's worry that the prisoner may be his cousin gives the chase its heart, as the boys follow enemies to Friday Island and face hostages and a radio eavesdropper. A hazing prank closes the fun. The book charms as an early wireless tale for boys who loved gadgets and islands.
12992-the-naval-pioneers-of-australia:
Louis Becke and Walter Jeffery wrote The Naval Pioneers of Australia in 1899. It traces sea discovery from Portuguese, Spanish, and Dutch voyagers through Dampier, Cook, Phillip, Hunter, King, Bass and Flinders, and Bligh. Chapters cover the First Fleet, the New South Wales Corps, Flinders's captivity, and the Bounty mutiny, with views of Botany Bay and Sydney Cove.

A letter from an old governor, indignant at an anonymous assassin who accused him of conniving at trade, shows the personal heat of colonial rule. Becke and Jeffery write with sailorly enthusiasm. The book remains a popular, illustrated history of Australia's naval founding.
13232-stories-of-california:
Ella M. Sexton's 1903 Stories of California, published by Macmillan, tells the state's history for young readers in short chapters. Contents run from California's name and early history to the missions and Father Serra, the Bear Flag Republic, the days of gold, and the building of the overland railroad. Later chapters cover wheat, orchards, oranges, big trees, birds, and wild animals.

Sexton notes gold dust left untouched in open tents. Plenty more lay for the picking. Sand bars on the Yuba were so rich that men picked a tin cupful a day for weeks. She also describes eagles, owls, and the road-runner, said to ring a sleeping rattlesnake with cactus thorns. The book is a friendly, old-fashioned introduction to a young state.
1326-the-crisis-in-russia:
Arthur Ransome, the English journalist who knew Russia firsthand, reports on the Bolshevik revolution and the civil war that followed. Writing in 1919, he describes the soviets, the food crisis, and the Allied intervention, and he argues that the new regime, for all its faults, had come to stay.

Ransome writes as a witness, not a theorist, and his dispatches carry the noise of Petrograd and the provinces. The book stirred fierce debate in Britain. It stands as a firsthand report from a turning point, and it still informs readers on revolution seen up close.
13291-the-world-s-great-men-of-music-sto:
Harriette Brower's 1922 World's Great Men of Music, also titled Story-Lives of Master Musicians, gives short lives of composers for young readers. Chapters run from Palestrina and Bach through Handel, Gluck, Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, Weber, Schubert, and Mendelssohn to Schumann, Chopin, Berlioz, Liszt, Verdi, Wagner, and Debussy. Brower, author of piano study books, writes with warmth.

Young Beethoven studies Latin, French, Italian, logic, and organ, while his mother tours Holland with him to earn money from wealthy homes. The boy calls the Dutch stingy and vows not to trouble them again. Later, Liszt nearly ruins himself paying for a festival, then makes Weimar a musical capital and champions Wagner. The book is a friendly first gallery of great composers.
13340-mr-isaacs-a-tale-of-modern-india:
F. Marion Crawford's 1882 novel of modern India opens on adventurers who rise or fall by will and servility where freedom shades into licence. At its centre stands Mr. Isaacs, a commanding figure whose wealth, charm, and hidden past draw the narrator into a world of maharajahs, debts, and British rule.

Isaacs presses the Maharajah of Baithopoor over repudiated debts and traitors harboured in his palace, threatening to print the charge across the Raj. Music, love songs, and evening talk soften the intrigue, with Lord Steepleton Kildare among the company. Crawford mixes romance, money, and empire into a tale of a man who seems able to bend India to his purpose.
13405-the-travels-and-adventures-of-mons:
Captain Marryat tells the travels of Monsieur Violet through California, Sonora, and western Texas. Violet was ruined with many old French families by the Revolution of 1830 that drove Charles the Tenth from his throne. He crosses a border country of settlers, soldiers, and adventurers in search of a new life.

The road runs through ruined towns held by tipsy sailors and pirates, parties of Shoshones and Mexicans, and prairie fires that race like a sea of flame before horses driven by fear. Violet watches great animals through an opera glass and rides with buffalo herds to escape the blaze. Marryat mixes romance, frontier hardship, and a French exile's eye for a wild, unsettled West.
1349-russia:
Donald Mackenzie Wallace was a Scots scholar who lived years in Russia. He writes this classic account of the empire under Alexander II: its peasants, nobles, priests, officials, and revolutionaries, drawn from travel and talk across the land. The book covers village communes, courts, and the press.

Wallace writes with a traveler's eye and a historian's care, and his Russia, though dated by revolution, remains a mine of detail. The work shaped British views of Russia for a generation. It draws readers who want the old empire seen from inside.
13854-the-old-franciscan-missions-of-cal:
George Wharton James wrote this 1913 history of California's old Franciscan missions, with photographs. Mission San Luis Rey, partly restored, fronts the volume. James dedicates the book to good men and women of all creeds whose lives show unselfish humanity. Chapters follow mission founding, growth, and decline.

James asks whether early explorers found cities and wealth like those of Cortés and Pizarro. He describes mission churches, gardens, and Native labour with sympathy. The book praises Franciscan zeal while noting hardship. Photographs help readers picture arches, courtyards, and chapels. It suits travellers and students of California history alike.
13895-patricia:
Emilia Elliott wrote Patricia in 1910, a children's novel published after her death. Publishers regret she did not live to see it in print. Patricia sits on a back fence under an old apple tree, talking gravely to a small black dog. Chapters follow a fatiguing day, a gingham apron party, and the way of a grandmother. A Christmas family closes the book.

Patricia seeks a home for her dog, trying Miss Jane, who keeps a very intelligent cat instead. Her talk is earnest, funny, and kind. Elliott writes for young readers with warmth and humour. The novel suits children who love animals and family stories. It remains a sweet, little-known Edwardian children's book.
13974-the-last-west-and-paolo-s-virginia:
G. B. Warren published this Canadian poetry volume in 1919, pairing The Last West with Paolo's Virginia, a spring fantasy. Poems picture Boundary Bay at daybreak, the Great Divide, and winter sunset in the Cascades. Baker's cone shadows the world below in bold, cold snow. Wildfowl, coasts, and seal rookeries fill later pieces.

Jansen's curse, a survey cook, and a raid on seal rookeries add narrative colour. Vancouver and Victoria, British Columbia, get their own poems. Paolo's Virginia turns to spring fantasy after northern scenes. Warren's verse is earnest and scenic. The volume suits readers of Canadian regional poetry.
14174-the-mating-of-lydia:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's 1913 novel The Mating of Lydia opens in damp Cumbrian weather, with Dixon feeding a fire that has no heart for burning. Mrs. Dixon frets that guests may not cross flooded roads by Grier's mill, with dinner spoiling and fires wasting. Lydia herself soon takes charge, straightening her sister Susan's collar and hair, patting her cheek, and prescribing walks over poetry after lunch.

Inheritance drives the plot. Lady Tatham denounces a stranger, Mr. Faversham, for worming into an old man's confidence and carrying off Melrose estates from helpless women, while aiding a tyrant's oppressions. Lydia protests, insisting short acquaintance cannot prove such villainy. Ward writes northern speech with care and social judgment with force, tracing how a young woman's marriage choices tangle with money, family duty, and reputation in a changing England.
14356-the-emperor-of-portugallia:
Selma Lagerlöf's Swedish novel, translated here by Velma Swanston Howard, follows Jan, a poor farmer in Värmland, and his daughter Klara, called Glory Goldie. When Klara leaves home to earn money in the city, Jan's grief unhinges his mind.

He comes to believe he is an emperor, with his daughter as empress, and the village humors and tests his delusion. Lagerlöf weaves farm work, church life, and folk belief into a story of parental love pushed past reason. The novel ends in sorrow and reconciliation, and it remains one of her most tender studies of devotion.
1436-a-voyage-to-abyssinia:
Father Jerome Lobo, a Portuguese Jesuit born in Lisbon in 1593, tells of his mission to Abyssinia, now Ethiopia, in the seventeenth century. Translated from the French by Samuel Johnson, the account follows Lobo's sea voyage, his overland journey, and his years among Abyssinian Christians.

Lobo describes courts, churches, customs, and the source of the Nile region with a missionary's eye and a traveller's detail. Johnson's introduction frames the tale for English readers. The book is a classic early account of Ethiopia, valued for its firsthand scenes of a little-known kingdom.
14426-london-to-ladysmith-via-pretoria:
Winston Churchill, then a young war correspondent, collected his newspaper letters from the first five months of the Boer War into this 1900 volume. The letters trace his journey from London to Natal, his capture by Boer forces, and his escape from Pretoria.

Churchill describes railway journeys, camp life, skirmishes, and the British effort under Sir Redvers Buller to relieve the besieged town of Ladysmith. He also records talks with Boer prisoners and officers. The book is vivid firsthand reporting, and it shows the future prime minister already shaping events into a personal story.
14657-philo-jud-us-of-alexandria:
Norman Bentwich, sometime scholar of Trinity College, Cambridge, wrote this 1910 life of Philo-Judaeus of Alexandria for the Jewish Publication Society of America. Bentwich dedicated it to his mother.

Chapters cover the Jewish community at Alexandria, Philo's life and times, his works and method, his reading of the Torah, his theology, and his influence. Bentwich argues that Alexandrian Jews, meeting Greek ethics, learned to interpret scripture allegorically. The book is a clear, scholarly introduction to a thinker who bridged Judaism and Greek philosophy. Bentwich later worked as a lawyer in Mandate Palestine.
14698-ranching-for-sylvia:
Harold Bindloss published this 1913 prairie novel in England as The Trustee. George Lansing takes on a ranch out of duty, after a strong appeal. Friends debate whether he is fit for the tangled affairs that come with it.

Work on the prairie follows: a cattle drive, liquor runners, a constable's suspicions and a blizzard test George's nerve. Sylvia seeks amusement, Herbert presses a claim, and Bland is drawn into sacrifice and disorder. Through diplomacy, disaster and a final revelation, George must decide what he owes Sylvia and what he owes himself. It is ranch fiction built on duty, friendship and hard weather.
14881-the-log-school-house-on-the-columb:
Hezekiah Butterworth's tale of pioneers of the great Northwest centres on a log schoolhouse on the Columbia River. Gretchen's violin, the chief of the Cascades, Boston Tilicum and Mrs. Woods's tame bear, Little Roll Over, open a story of settlement, school and frontier friendship.

A nest of the fishing eagle, a mountain lion, smoke talk, the black eagle's nest at the falls of the Missouri and Gretchen's visit to the old chief follow. Old Joe Meek, Mr. Spaulding, a warning, a potlatch and a silent tribe widen the picture. Butterworth writes for young readers, mixing adventure with respect for Native peoples and for the teachers who built schools on the edge of the map.
15159-heart-s-desire-the-story-of-a-cont:
Emerson Hough's 1905 novel tells of Heart's Desire, a contented Western town, its peculiar citizens, and two fortunate lovers. The opening chapter, on the land of heart's desire, begins in part with Curly and a can of oysters, a sign of the book's comic, anecdotal style. A frontispiece shows a lover at a door.

Through town talk, mining days, and courtship, Hough builds a portrait of a place where people know each other well and trouble stays small. The novel blends humor, romance, and frontier color without heavy drama. Fans of Western town tales will enjoy its easy pace and its affection for its people.
15190-with-the-harmony-to-labrador-notes:
B. La Trobe's notes record a voyage with the Harmony to Moravian mission stations on Labrador's northeast coast, printed in London at threepence. The ship's 119th voyage calls at Hopedale, the southern station, then Zoar and Nain, between islands and over cold seas. A climb to Ship Hill at Zoar adds a walker's view.

La Trobe describes marriages and funerals, native helpers, communion Sundays, and strolls to the heathen, with warmth for mission work. The notes are short, plain, and firsthand. Readers interested in Labrador, Moravian missions, or Arctic coast travel will find the booklet vivid and humane.
15526-john-l-stoddard-s-lectures-vol-10-:
John L. Stoddard's tenth and final lecture volume, published in Boston in 1900, gathers three illustrated discourses from eighteen years of lecturing. They are Southern California, the Grand Canyon of the Colorado River, and Yellowstone National Park. Views of famous places and people embellish the text, as in the earlier volumes.

Southern California opens with nature guarding the region: ocean to the west, dreary deserts to the east, and a long, hard crossing past Flagstaff before the land softens. Later passages describe Pueblo life, where women build dwellings, trace descent through the mother, and may evict a husband who ill-treats them. Stoddard writes as a genial lecturer, mixing scenery, history, and custom for audiences who traveled by book when they could not travel by rail.
15921-the-haskalah-movement-in-russia:
A history of the Jewish enlightenment in Russia by Jacob S. Raisin, issued by the Jewish Publication Society of America in Philadelphia in 1913. Raisin, author of Sect, Creed and Custom in Judaism, takes the Maskilim, the enlighteners, as his subject. His epigraph from Daniel promises that the Maskilim shall shine as the brightness of the firmament.

Raisin traces how Russian Jews met modern learning, Russian letters, and new hopes for civic life. Schools, writers, and reformers carry the movement through repression and hope. Tradition and change clash in every chapter. The book still serves students of Jewish history: a clear, sympathetic account of enlightenment under an empire.
16050-the-gold-hunters-adventures-or-lif:
A gold-rush narrative by William H. Thomes, a returned Australian, illustrated by Champney. Lee and Shepard issued it in Boston, with Charles T. Dillingham in New York. Thomes writes from his own Australian years, for readers hungry for gold-field tales. First thoughts of going to Australia open the book.

Departure from California, life on board ship, and arrival in Australia follow in turn. Diggings, mates, bushrangers, and colonial towns fill the long narrative. Thomes keeps the detail practical: how men lived, worked, and sometimes struck it rich. The book stands as a firsthand gold-field record: Australia seen by a man who dug there.
16303-guy-rivers-a-tale-of-georgia:
W. Gilmore Simms's Guy Rivers, in a new and revised Chicago edition of 1890, sets its scene in upper Georgia, then fruitful of dispute within Cherokee territory. The opening chapter, The Sterile Prospect and the Lonely Traveller, places the route between the Chattahoochee and its branch the Chestatee, after a people once settled there. Simms, author of The Yemassee and The Partisan, knew the Southern frontier well.

From that lonely road grows a tale of Georgia settlers, Indians, outlaws, and disputed land, told with Simms's romantic vigor. The novel belongs to his long series on Southern history and legend. Readers of frontier romance will enjoy its local color and its stirring frontier plot.
16344-the-waif-of-the-cynthia:
Jules Verne and Andre Laurie tell a sea adventure that opens with the famed Stockholm doctor Schwaryencrona, whose face graces millions of cod liver oil bottles. A foundling tied to the ship Cynthia sets the plot in motion, and the tale follows the boy's strange fortunes across the seas. The Seaside Library issued it as a cheap pocket edition in the 1880s.

Verne's love of ships, science, and odd facts runs through the story, while Laurie adds a warm human thread. The pace is brisk, the scenes shift from port to open sea, and the mystery of the waif's birth drives the action. Young readers of adventure fiction will find it a lively, old-style yarn.
16382-in-clive-s-command-a-story-of-the-:
Herbert Strang's In Clive's Command, a story of the fight for India, opens on a fine autumn evening in 1754. A country cart jogs into Market Drayton behind a thick-set, broken-winded cob. Its worn tilt sways over two men on the front seat, dark figures against a crimson sky, while the town hums like innumerable bees. Through Shropshire Street and the High Street the cart stops, where the Court Leet entertains Colonel Robert Clive.

From that Shropshire meeting, the hero follows Clive to India, war, and fortune in the struggle for empire. Strang writes brisk boys' adventure with history woven through it. Young readers who like military tales will enjoy this rousing story of Clive's India.
16460-from-aldershot-to-pretoria:
W. E. Sellers tells of Christian work among British troops in South Africa in this book, with an introduction by R. W. Allen and fifteen pictures. The route runs from Aldershot and the sea voyage to the front, Magersfontein, Kimberley, Bloemfontein, and on to Pretoria, with chapters on Lord Methuen, Lord Roberts, and Sir Redvers Buller.

Sellers writes as a worker among soldiers, noting parade services, veldt life, and the last letters of men who fell. The frontispiece, His Last Letter, sets the sober tone. The book gives a humane, ground-level view of the Boer War through chaplains' and workers' eyes.
16544-the-boy-scouts-in-russia:
Captain John Blaine sends the Boy Scouts into Russia in this 1916 Saalfield adventure. A train stops at Virballen, where half the platform lies in Russia and half in East Prussia. Border arrest, a strange meeting, cousins, Germans, a tunnel, and a daring ruse follow, with Cossacks, a trick, and an escape through the night.

Blaine writes brisk wartime adventure for boys, with scouts using pluck and craft behind enemy lines. The Great White Czar chapter closes the tale. Young readers of series fiction will find a fast, patriotic yarn from the First World War years.
16653-myths-of-babylonia-and-assyria:
Donald A. Mackenzie retells the myths of Babylonia and Assyria in this volume, closing with the last days of Assyria and Babylonia. Merodach's cunning plan opens the quoted passage: he splits the dragon Tiamat like a flat fish, forms heaven from one half and earth from the other, and sets the universe in order. His power as maker comes from the fierce Great Mother herself.

Mackenzie draws on King's Seven Tablets of Creation and other scholarship, weighing words like Ku-pu. The book mixes myth retelling with learned notes. Readers of ancient myth will find a rich, old-style survey of Mesopotamia's gods, dragons, and creation tales.
16664-town-life-in-australia:
R. E. N. Twopeny wrote this 1883 account of town life in Australia, issued by Elliot Stock in London. It began as a set of letters, kept only in part in letter form, and it walks through Melbourne, Sydney, and Adelaide. Chapters take up houses, food, dress, servants, schools, politics, shops, amusements, papers, and books.

Twopeny writes for English readers who knew Australian towns were large but could not picture them. He notes how folk lived, worked, worshipped, and played, with an eye for small daily facts. The book gives a vivid, first-hand view of colonial city life in the 1880s, useful for history readers and for anyone keen on old Australia.
16891-peter-parley-s-tales-about-america:
Peter Parley wrote these tales about America and Australia, new edition brought down to the present time and revised by the Rev. T. Wilson, with pictures by S. Williams, issued in London by Darton. The book gives young readers short, plain tales of two new worlds, in the kindly, teaching voice that made Parley famous with children.

Parley mixes geography, history, and anecdote, so a child learns lands and peoples through stories, not dry lists. The tales reflect 1800s views of America and Australia, which modern readers will weigh with care. As a period children's book, it offers a clear window on how the young were once taught about far lands.
16930-a-short-history-of-russia:
Mary Platt Parmele wrote this short history of Russia, illustrated, issued by Scribner's in New York in 1907, with copyrights in 1899, 1904, and 1906. Her preface warns that the book tells the history of a power, not of a people, since the Russian folk, in her view, had no history yet. Only a vast governing system evolved, she says, while the mass of folk had no part in it.

Parmele follows natural barriers, ethnic tangles, Russia's entry among great nations, and the recent disastrous conflict and its changed conditions. Her view reflects early 1900s Western ideas about Russia, which modern readers will weigh with care. The book gives a brisk, old-style survey, useful as a period history and as a record of how America then saw Russia.
16965-queen-victoria:
E. Gordon Browne's 1915 life of Queen Victoria follows her from childhood at Kensington to the head of a world empire. Chapters trace her early years, her marriage to Albert, family life, court friends, and the strain of long rule. Balmoral, the Great Exhibition, and the work of Peel, Melbourne, and Disraeli mark the reign's public turns.

Twelve full-page pictures add palaces, councils, and memorials to the plain text. Browne writes for young readers, with short chapters and a warm, loyal tone. The book gives a clear first life of a queen whose reign shaped Britain, and it shows why Victorians called her age their own.
1739-the-black-death-and-the-dancing-man:
Two medieval horrors share this volume: the Black Death crossing Europe, and crowds dancing for days in a frenzy no priest or doctor could stop. The first follows the Black Death across Europe, where fear itself killed many before the plague reached them, and where whole towns watched order break down. The second follows the dancing mania, in which whole crowds danced uncontrollably for days, beyond any priest's or doctor's power to halt.

Hecker, a professor of medicine, writes as a historian of disease rather than a moralist, and his accounts rest on chronicles and town records. Readers get a vivid picture of how past ages met disaster they could not explain, and of the strange forms that terror took when medicine had few answers.
17404-kinship-organisations-and-group-ma:
Northcote W. Thomas, a Cambridge scholar and corresponding member of the Paris Society of Anthropology, published this study with Cambridge University Press in 1906. He dedicates it to Miss C. S. Burne, who first guided his steps into anthropology. His preface argues that anthropology needs minute discussion of special themes and detailed study of limited areas, not ranging talk over all peoples.

Thomas takes Australia as his limited area, surveying what was then known of Australian kinship organisations in the hope of spurring further research on the spot. Readers get an early, careful work of social anthropology, with tables and a scholarly apparatus that the text format notes with care. It remains a reference for the history of kinship studies.
17894-franco-gallia:
Francis Hotman, a French lawyer of the 1500s, wrote Franco-Gallia in Latin in 1574. He argued that France had once been a free state, ruled with its people, not by one man's whim. The English version here, printed in London in 1721, was made by the author of the Account of Denmark, with a new preface.

Hotman traces old Frankish kings, councils, and laws to show that kings once shared power with the realm's great men. His case spoke to English readers too, who prized their own old rights. The book still counts as a landmark in the history of free rule, and a bold early claim that a people's assent sets bounds on kings.
18007-more-songs-from-vagabondia:
Bliss Carman and Richard Hovey wrote More Songs from Vagabondia, printed in Boston in 1896 by Copeland and Day, with designs by Tom B. Meteyard. The book is dedicated to M. G. M., who lightened the boys' cares, and it follows their first Vagabondia songs.

Songs run from jongleurs and earth's lyric to a faun's song, the mocking-bird, Barney McGee, the sea gypsy, and the first julep. Carman and Hovey sing of roads, woods, and fellowship with a light, roving joy. It is a charming book of vagabond verse, best for readers who love the open road and a song by the fire.
1812-a-prince-of-bohemia:
Paris in the 1830s had a whole underworld of writers, hangers-on, and patrons trading wit for dinner, and this tale follows one of its princes through the salons. The story follows a prince of Bohemia, a charming, rootless man of letters, through Paris salons, where a lady, cool to a persecutor on her stairs, must decide whom to trust.

Balzac uses the Bohemian prince to sketch that Paris literary underworld, where writers, hangers-on, and patrons trade wit for dinner. The tale is short and glittering, and its point is social: in Bohemia, talent and debt live side by side. A man's reputation is the only coin he cannot borrow.
18210-the-heptalogia:
Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote The Heptalogia, taken from volume five of his collected poetical works, printed in London in 1917 by William Heinemann. The book was first printed by Chatto in 1904, and reprinted through 1912.

Pieces run from The Higher Pantheism in a Nutshell and John Jones's Wife to The Poet and the Woodlouse, The Person of the House, and Last Words of a Seventh-Rate Poet. Swinburne parodies his own age's verse with brilliant, biting wit. It is a sharp, learned jest book, best for readers who love parody, wit, and high Victorian verse at its most playful.
18237-a-bird-calendar-for-northern-india:
Douglas Dewar, author of Indian Birds and Birds of the Indian Hills, published this bird calendar for northern India in 1916. Dewar republished sketches first printed in The Pioneer, with help from A. J. Currie's unpublished notes on the birds of the Punjab. Full accounts of the birds appear in the Fauna of British India, while Dewar's own Indian Birds gives popular accounts of most of them.

The calendar runs month by month, from January to December, with a glossary and index. January, Dewar says, mixes sunny English May days, still March nights, and a few rainy mornings into a typical Indian winter month. Readers get a year of bird life in northern India: arrivals, song, nesting, and departure, noted in the field and set down for watchers and travelers.
18238-songs-from-vagabondia:
Bliss Carman and Richard Hovey wrote Songs from Vagabondia, printed in Boston in 1894 by Copeland and Day, with designs by Tom B. Meteyard. The book is dedicated to H. F. W., for debts of love unpaid, and it is the boys' first vagabond songbook.

Songs run from Vagabondia and the joys of the road to evening on the Potomac, a spring song, a rover's song, down the Songo, and a song by the shore. Carman and Hovey sing of roads, rivers, and fellowship with light, roving joy. It is a charming book of vagabond verse, and the start of a beloved American song series.
18259-gentle-julia:
Booth Tarkington wrote Gentle Julia, issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, copyright 1922 by Doubleday, Page, with pictures by C. Allan Gilbert and Worth Brehm. Tarkington, author of Penrod and The Turmoil, dedicates the book to M. L. K.

The tale opens with Florence Atwater, whose mother warns that a proud, thrust-out lip may stay that way for life, like the King of Spain. Florence, dreamy and willful, decides to misunderstand her mother. Tarkington writes with his usual comic warmth for small-town youth. It is a gentle, funny novel of a girl growing up, full of charm and sly wit.
18423-old-kaskaskia:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood, author of The Lady of Fort St. John and The Romance of Dollard, wrote this historical novel, published by Houghton, Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1893. Old Kaskaskia is built in four parts: The Bonfire of St. John, A Field Day, The Rising, and The Flood.

Part one opens on a summer evening early in the century, as Jean Lozier stands on a bluff looking at Kaskaskia. Jean loves the town with the homesick longing of one born for towns and condemned to the fields, old in feeling though not yet out of his teens. Below him lies the long peninsula between the Okaw and the Mississippi in sunset glory. Readers get a French Illinois romance: a town, a lad who aspires, and the river that made and unmade them both.
18567-tintinnalogia:
A lover of the art of ringing wrote this treatise in 1671, printed in London for F. S. and sold by Tho. Archer under the dial of St. Dunstan's Church in Fleet Street. The book sets down plain and easy rules for ringing all sorts of plain changes, with directions for pricking and ringing cross peals.

It also gives a full discovery of the mystery and grounds of each peal, with instructions for hanging bells and all things belonging to them. Dedicated to the noble society of College Youths, it stands as the first English manual of change ringing, written for ringers who wanted rules they could follow in the tower.
18660-the-beautiful-eyes-of-ysidria:
Charles A. Gunnison published this short California tale at San Francisco in 1894, dedicating it to Madame Emma Baudouin of Lubeck. Its narrator looks back to his youth in California before gold fever changed the land, with old Padre Andreas at San Anselmo and simple feasts and fasts. His son Quito, who lives under the shadow of Mount Tamalpais yet cannot see it, treats the mountain as his god and giver of good.

A homely bewitchment scare drives one episode, when housekeeper Catalina kills a hen and ducks she believes Madre Moreno bewitched. Walks, talks, and old customs fill the rest. The tale is a fond, wistful sketch of early Californian life.
18841-elizabethan-sonnet-cycles-phillis-:
Martha Foote Crow edited this volume in 1896, pairing two Elizabethan sonnet cycles: Phillis by Thomas Lodge and Licia by Giles Fletcher. Lodge's Phillis, first published in 1595, mixes pastoral sonnets with elegies and amorous delights. Crow's introduction places Lodge among the busy literary circle of late sixteenth-century London, a writer admired by friends but slow to win lasting fame.

Fletcher's Licia offers a second, contrasting sequence in the same fashion. Together the two cycles show how English poets borrowed the sonnet sequence from Italy and shaped it to praise, woo, and lament. Readers get both the poems and a scholarly frame, helpful for anyone studying how the English sonnet grew in Shakespeare's generation.
19391-a-truthful-woman-in-southern-calif:
Kate Sanborn wrote this travel account of Southern California, first published in the early eighteen nineties. She gives hints for the journey, then visits Coronado Beach, San Diego, Los Angeles, Pasadena, and Santa Barbara, with a camping trip on Mount Wilson and a ride on the kite-shaped track.

Sanborn notes Native basket makers, their coiled trays and dice of acorn shell, as well as hotels, gardens, and rail lines. The title promises truth over booster talk, and the book keeps that promise with a sharp, funny eye for a region then selling itself to winter visitors.
19562-napoleon-and-the-queen-of-prussia:
L. Muhlbach wrote this historical novel of Napoleon and the Queen of Prussia, translated from German by F. Jordan and appearing from a New York press in the early nineteen hundreds. It opens with Ferdinand von Schill and a German song, then follows the queen's flight, Napoleon's entry into Berlin, and his stay at Sans-Souci.

In a small, poor room at a mill, Frederick William and Louisa sit hand in hand, lovers more than royals, thanking God for reunion. The novel blends court scenes with patriotic feeling, and it remains a popular Victorian view of Prussia's darkest years.
19695-forty-one-thieves-a-tale-of-califo:
Forty-One Thieves, published in 1919, calls itself a tale of California. Its scenes open on rough mountain country rich in fish and game. Settlers have come to farm a valley twelve miles wide between mountain walls. The Native people of the place begrudge them the fish and game. That clash of claims drives the story's tension.

California tales of this era mixed settlement pride with frontier conflict. Land, water, and game were the stakes on every page. The title promises a band of thieves numbering forty-one. Numbers that odd tend to come from local legend. The book preserves a piece of California folk storytelling. It also shows the settler viewpoint of its time.
19810-my-a-ntonia:
Willa Cather published My Ántonia in 1918, her great novel of Nebraska settlement. Narrator Jim Burden recalls arriving in Nebraska as a boy. A friendly passenger conductor shepherded the children west. He knew the country they were bound for and advised them freely. He seemed to young Jim an experienced, worldly man. That train ride opens one of America's finest novels.

Ántonia Shimerda, a Bohemian immigrant girl, stands at the book's heart. Cather draws prairie life through work, weather, and memory. Jim's telling turns pioneer hardship into elegy. The novel honors immigrant women who built new lives from sod and debt. It is now a fixed star of American literature. New readers still meet Nebraska through Ántonia.
19986-martyred-armenia:
Faiz El-Ghusein wrote Martyred Armenia as an eyewitness account of the Armenian massacres. He lists the vilayets where Armenians lived: Diarbekir, Van, Bitlis, and Erzerum among them. Mamouret-el-Aziz, Sivas, Adana, Aleppo, and Trebizond follow. Broussa and Constantinople complete his geography of a doomed population. El-Ghusein was a Bedouin sheik and Ottoman official. He saw the forced marches from inside the state offices.

His account carries weight just because he was no Armenian partisan. He records what he saw of the 1915 killings. The book appeared in English during the war itself. Few insider accounts reached print so early. It remains a primary document of the Armenian genocide. Its lists of places mark towns about to be wiped out.
20031-a-final-reckoning-a-tale-of-bush-l:
G. A. Henty wrote tales of adventure for boys, and A Final Reckoning sets its story in the Australian bush. The title calls it a tale of bush life in Australia. Henty was known for mixing brave young heroes with real places and hard travel. His books sold widely in Britain and beyond.

Inside, the action turns on risk, pursuit, and life far from settled towns. The sample shows talk of bold schemes and sudden arrest. Readers who like Henty will find his usual mix of danger, duty, and pluck. The bush itself acts as a harsh, testing ground.
2069-the-religion-of-babylonia-and-assyr:
Theophilus G. Pinches, lecturer in Assyrian at University College London, sets out the gods, myths, and rites of ancient Babylonia and Assyria in this 1906 study. He draws on cuneiform records to explain temples, priests, and the place of kings. Pinches worked at the British Museum's cuneiform collections, so his book rests on tablets, not guesswork.

Pinches also shows how these beliefs touch the Old Testament, comparing stories and ideas without forcing them to match. The book suits readers of ancient history who want a clear, scholarly guide to Mesopotamian religion. His comparison with Hebrew texts helped readers see the Bible's world in a wider ancient setting.
20758-the-religion-of-babylonia-and-assy:
Morris Jastrow Jr. set out to gather what scholars knew of Babylonian and Assyrian faith. Their findings lay scattered in journals and small studies, hard to reach. Jastrow aimed to sort the sure from the unsure, and the unsure from the false.

Gods, prayers, omens, and rites of the Tigris and Euphrates lands fill the book. Clay tablets had just begun to speak to modern scholars then. Jastrow, a noted Semitic scholar, made that new field clear to plain readers. His survey still shows how the study of ancient faiths grew from fresh digs and fresh texts.
20880-the-story-of-russia:
Size alone earns Russia no pride, argues The Story of Russia in its opening turn. The writer grants the land's vast extent, then sets it beside a proud young America. The United States, near Europe's size, fronts two great trade oceans at once.

R. Van Bergen tells Russia's tale for young American readers of 1905. Tsars, invasions, serfs, and reforms crowd a story of a vast, stern land. He writes to breed fair knowledge, not fear, of a rising power. The book shows how Russia looked to American schools on the eve of its war with Japan and first revolt at home.
20892-manasseh-a-romance-of-transylvania:
Half a century back, in the stirring days of 1848, Manasseh sets its tale of Transylvania. Revolts against harsh rule swept Europe that year, the intro notes. Nowhere did heroism shine higher, it says, than in Hungary's bold stand.

Mor Jokai, Hungary's great novelist, wrote this romance of love and revolt. Percy Favor Bicknell turned it into English for new readers in 1901. Barons' sons, war, and faith under fire drive the plot. The book carries Jokai's warm, sweeping style into a land of castles, mountains, and peoples caught between empires old and new.
2127-paul-and-virginia:
Bernardin de Saint Pierre's famous tale, in a full edition that restores passages cut from earlier printings, follows Paul and Virginia, two children raised together on Mauritius in simple, natural life. Their love grows with them. Saint Pierre wrote Paul and Virginia in 1788, as part of a larger work on nature.

Publishers praise the book as a philosophical tale, not a mere children's story, written in language simple and true. Its fame rests on its feeling for nature, innocence, and loss, and it has moved readers for more than two centuries. The Mauritius setting, lush and remote, made the tale a favourite of Romantic readers across Europe.
21383-adventures-in-australia:
Two young Englishmen sail to Australia in W. H. G. Kingston's short adventure novel Adventures in Australia. They plan to stay a while with the uncle of one of them, who runs a station there. The road up country brings them face to face with a new and strange land.

Along the way they meet the wild life of the bush, from kangaroos and wallabies to the wombat and the laughing kookaburra. They also meet the Aboriginal people who first held the land. The pair like the life so much that, with the uncle's help, they buy land and start a station of their own.
21482-the-settlers-a-tale-of-virginia:
Captain Amyas Layton's house looks over Plymouth Sound at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's The Settlers. Brass cannon taken from the Spaniards guard the low wall by the moat. Ships of many rigs crowd the harbour below, bound for far-off lands.

The tale moves to Jacobean Virginia, where settlers meet Pocahontas and other famed figures. Kingston packs the book with activity across its moderate length. Planting a colony among wary peoples brings talks, trades, and fights. Readers get a lively, old-style view of England's first lasting foothold in America, told through Layton's kin.
21512-modern-persia:
Rabbi Mooshie G. Daniel, once a teacher of ancient Syriac at Oroomiah College, wrote Modern Persia in 1897. He spent four years in America and kept meeting the same questions about his homeland. Folk asked if Persia was part of Turkey, or as large as Michigan.

Daniel answers such points in order: the shah's power, the old laws, and what traces of past glory remain. He also reports the moral state of the land since mission work began. The book, issued by Wheaton College Press, speaks to church readers as much as to students of the East.
2155-phyllis-of-philistia:
Frank Frankfort Moore opens a novel of marriage and manners with Mr. Ayrton asking his daughter Phyllis what marriage means, and answering himself that it puts all your eggs in one basket. Phyllis, grieving, is not comforted by phrases. Moore wrote popular novels of love and society, and Phyllis shows his light touch.

Her father, a collector of fine phrases, flutters them before her while she weighs love, duty, and choice. Moore writes a light, talkative romance of its period, with dialogue that carries both comedy and feeling. Mr. Ayrton's phrase-collecting gives the opening its comedy, since he loves words more than sense.
21569-southern-arabia:
Theodore Bent and his wife Mabel record hard travel in Southern Arabia, published in 1900. Theodore Bent had written on the ruined cities of Mashonaland and the sacred city of the Ethiopians. Maps, a portrait, and many pictures back their account.

The route runs from Bahrain's mounds through Muscat and Oman into the Hadhramaut. Chapters treat Makalla, the climb of the Akaba, and the city of Shibam. The pair bid farewell to Shibam's sultan, suffer at their guides' hands, and see debts repaid. Old writers from Pliny to Marco Polo crowd the bibliography of this stark, learned travel book.
21727-digging-for-gold-adventures-in-cal:
Frank Allfrey wants to be a painter, but his grim uncle has other plans in this Ballantyne tale of the California goldfields. Frank is an orphan of eighteen, quick, good-tempered, and fond of hard work more than books. His school-books are covered with drawings of dogs, horses, and his schoolmates. His uncle calls him a goose for dreaming of art.

Fate sends Frank west instead, to dig for gold among strangers in a rough new land. Ballantyne sets a young man's thwarted gift against the raw pull of the gold rush. The tale follows Frank's work, luck, and growth in the diggings. It asks what a man makes of himself when his first dream is taken away.
21886-prisoners-of-hope-a-tale-of-coloni:
Colonial Virginia is the stage of Mary Johnston's Prisoners of Hope, first published in 1898 and reprinted past the hundred-thousand mark. A sloop comes in with its cargo, and a colonial dinner party sets the world of planters and servants turning. The surveyor-general's library, the tobacco house, and the waters of Chesapeake all take their turns as scenes.

Landless, the tale's restless hero, becomes a conspirator, pays the piper, and smokes the peace pipe before the tale ends. A duel, a capture, and a midnight expedition keep the plot hot. Johnston went on to fame with To Have and To Hold. Her Virginia is lush and dangerous, and her love story moves inside real colonial tensions.
22257-bulgaria:
Noel Buxton, a British member of Parliament who knew the Balkans well, travelled with the Bulgarian army in 1912. His book Bulgaria reports the First Balkan War as an eyewitness. Buxton was instructed in the autumn of 1912 to join the Bulgarians as war correspondent for the London Morning Post. He prepared for a country he expected to be cut-throat, where massacre seemed the national sport.

What he found changed many of his judgements. The book follows mobilisation, the advance on Adrianople, and the politics behind the guns. Buxton became a lifelong advocate for Balkan peoples. His wartime report remains a sharp British witness to Bulgaria's brief moment of triumph.
22297-the-coast-of-bohemia:
William Dean Howells published The Coast of Bohemia in 1893, a novel of art and ambition. Howells recalled its germ in a thought. What a good thing, he mused, to send a nice village girl to study art in New York. She should have a real but limited gift — and she should be married! From that inchoate idea Cornelia and her mother stepped out, and Ludlow advanced from another quarter of chaos.

Cornelia Saunders leaves her village to study painting among New York's Bohemians. Howells watches her talent, her suitors, and the art world's humbug with amused realism. The coast of Bohemia is not on any map; it is where young artists live. The novel is minor Howells, which means shrewd, kind, and well observed.
22370-a-little-maid-of-old-philadelphia:
Alice Turner Curtis wrote A Little Maid of Old Philadelphia, published in 1919. Young Ruth Pernell is its worried heroine at the start. Her dog Hero has vanished from house, shed, and garden.

Ruth stands in the kitchen doorway, near tears, asking Aunt Deborah. Aunt Deborah works on as Ruth pleads her question. A lost dog opens a story set in old Philadelphia. Curtis wrote many such tales of girls in early America. Her books mixed daily life with the nation's founding years. Young readers got history through a girl's eyes. This volume offers that blend in a household touched by revolutionary times.
22594-colonial-records-of-virginia:
Colonial Records of Virginia is a documentary collection of early Virginia papers copied from the Public Record Office in Britain. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. The papers were gathered for a practical legal fight: the boundary dispute between Maryland and Virginia that reached the Virginia legislature in 1860.

Virginia sent Colonel Angus W. McDonald across the Atlantic to fetch the records its case required. The volume prints what he brought back, giving readers the raw material of colonial government rather than a retelling. Deeds, orders, and official letters of this sort let historians test later accounts against the sources. The book remains a working tool for anyone studying colonial Virginia or the long boundary quarrel.
22669-the-young-miner-or-tom-nelson-in-c:
The Young Miner, or Tom Nelson in California, is a boys' novel of the gold country, second volume of the Pacific Series. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. A publisher's note explains the plan. The first volume, The Young Adventurer, had promised a sequel called The Young Pioneer. The title changed to avoid confusion with a similar book.

Tom Nelson's adventures take him to California, where a boy's honesty and pluck meet the rough chances of mining life. Series fiction of this kind taught that hard work and clean conduct beat luck in the end. The note about the changed title is itself a small window into the trade in boys' books. Readers meet both a gold-rush tale and the machinery that sold it.
22837-the-lost-dahlia:
Small losses fill Mary Russell Mitford's sketch The Lost Dahlia. The narrator counts her mishaps with comic despair. A prized pin, her dear friend's first present to her, slipped from her shawl somewhere along the main road. Of shawls themselves, she sighs, there is simply no end to the loss.

A prized flower gives the piece its title and its gentle stakes. Village gardening, friendly rivalry, and the hunt for what has gone missing carry the pages. Mitford turns trivia into portrait, showing how much feeling country neighbors invest in small things. Nothing grand happens, and that is the design. The sketch preserves the texture of village days, one dropped pin and one vanished bloom at a time.
2288-through-russia:
Maxim Gorky writes of Russia as he walked it, in stories and sketches drawn from tramps, peasants, and wanderers. Through Russia collects pieces from his years on the road, when the future novelist lived among the poor and listened to their tales. The Russia here is harsh, funny, and full of talk: pilgrims, thieves, and dreamers argue about God and justice.

Gorky's eye for the downtrodden gives the book its moral force, and his prose carries the rhythms of spoken Russian life. The volume shows the writer before fame, learning his craft from the road itself. It offers a vivid portrait of a vanished empire's underside.
23163-the-eyes-of-asia:
Rudyard Kipling writes a soldier's letter home in The Eyes of Asia, published in 1917. Five months of war, the sepoy reports, left him feverish and ruptured, and the doctor ordered him out of the fighting for good. Surgeons cut his wounded leg as well. It has healed, he writes, but its strength is gone, and the leg fears the ground now.

Kipling built these pieces from the letters of Indian soldiers on the Western Front, rendered in their own imagined voices. Wounds, weather, French villages, and family news from Punjab villages fill the pages. The result is among his finest wartime work, ventriloquism in the service of attention. Asia's eyes, turned on Europe's war, see things Europe had stopped noticing.
2331-history-of-phoenicia:
George Rawlinson, the Victorian historian of the ancient world, reconstructs the Phoenicians: sailors, traders, and alphabet-bearers of the Levant. History of Phoenicia follows Tyre and Sidon from their early cities through their Mediterranean colonies, including Carthage, to their fall under Persia and Rome. Rawlinson draws on classical writers and the archaeology of his day.

The book's strength is its synthesis of scattered sources into a readable narrative. Later discoveries have revised many details, but the outline endures. Ancient history readers will find a solid Victorian survey. Rawlinson also wrote histories of Egypt, Parthia, and the ancient Near East.
2352-eurasia:
Christopher Evans's Eurasia is a work of speculative geography and history, imagining the great landmass of Europe and Asia as a single theater of peoples, empires, and migrations. The book ranges across steppe and sea, tracing how trade, conquest, and ideas crossed a continent without natural borders. Evans writes for readers curious about the deep patterns of history.

The volume's breadth is its appeal: nomads, merchants, and empires all share the stage. Its generalizations invite debate, as such syntheses must. Readers of big-picture history will find a stimulating overview.
23546-wealth-of-the-world-s-waste-places:
Jewett C. Gilson, former superintendent of schools in Oakland, California, wrote this nineteen thirteen geography reader on the wealth of the world's waste places and Oceania, for Redway's Geographical Readers. A National Geographic picture of the great Rainbow Bridge of southern Utah fronts the book.

Part one tours arid lands. It covers the wealth of the arid south west, the Grand Canyon, Yellowstone Park, and prehistoric cemeteries of giant reptiles and giant trees. Death Valley, the mineral wealth of the Andes, and the czar's greater domain follow. Oceania follows, with islands, peoples, and products. Gilson writes for school readers, plain and keen, turning deserts and seas into lessons on resources. Young geographers will enjoy the pictures and the plain talk of how waste places yield wealth.
24102-owen-clancy-s-happy-trail-or-the-m:
Burt L. Standish wrote this boys' adventure tale of early motoring in California, with Owen Clancy, the motor wizard of the title, at its center. It opens in Los Angeles on a festival morning, when a Chinese dragon parade a block long winds down Sixth Street and throws four street corners into confusion. Among the crowd is Hiram Hill, a tow-headed youth hunting for his missing father.

Hill spots the man he seeks riding in an automobile held up by the parade, and the chance sighting sets off the chain of mishaps that drives the story. Clancy's skill with cars, Hill's search for his father, and the bustle of Los Angeles streets give the book its pace. Readers get a fast, light tale of cars, luck, and new roads in early California.
2427-the-patagonia:
Henry James's tale The Patagonia takes its name from a ship crossing the Atlantic, aboard which an American narrator observes a marriage in crisis. The story follows a couple whose union is quietly coming apart, watched by fellow passengers who guess more than they say. James's late manner turns a sea voyage into a study of consciousness.

The tale is subtle, melancholy, and beautifully written, with the ship's motion mirroring emotional drift. Readers of James's shorter fiction will find a fine, if lesser-known, piece. James grouped this tale with Pandora and other stories of Americans abroad.
24654-chaldea-from-the-earliest-times-to:
Zenaide A. Ragozin wrote this history of Chaldea from the earliest times to the rise of Assyria, treated as a general introduction to ancient history. Ragozin, a member of the Societe Ethnologique of Paris and the American Oriental Society, also wrote histories of Assyria and Media. Her book went through several editions.

She follows the peoples of southern Mesopotamia from their first cities through kings, temples, and trade, to the coming of Assyrian power. Ragozin quotes Emerson on Carlyle: history, well told, reads like poetry. Her narrative aims at that standard. Readers of ancient history will find it a clear, old-fashioned survey.
24728-stories-of-georgia:
Joel Chandler Harris wrote these stories in 1896 to give young Georgians a lively first history of their state. He retells episodes from the first Spanish marches through the Revolution and into the early republic, linking them into one chain. De Soto, Oglethorpe, and the fighters of the southern campaigns all take their turn.

Harris aimed at readers who found dry school histories dull, so he tells each tale as a story, with people and motives in the foreground. Later chapters take up tangled affairs like the Yazoo land fraud and the French envoy Genet. The book works both as a set of tales and as a stepping stone into fuller histories of Georgia.
24893-in-mesopotamia:
Martin Swayne published In Mesopotamia in London in 1917, with pictures drawn by himself. The book follows the British campaign up the Tigris in the First World War. It runs from the gateway of the Garden of Eden at Kurna through Basra, Amara, and the Narrows to the battle of the Bund.

Swayne writes of sick and wounded men, heat-stroke, and mirage, and of hospitals strained after the fall of Kut. Day temperatures passed a hundred degrees by the river, and thermometers cracked in the airless palm groves. The book gives a close, human account of war in a land of dust, rivers, and fierce heat.
24897-the-great-white-tribe-in-filipinia:
Paul T. Gilbert published The Great White Tribe in Filipinia in 1903, a year after the Philippine-American War's close. The book surveys American life in the islands: old Manila, town life, the provinces, summer seas, and the pagan tribes, with chapters on Visayan villages, Moro country, and the constabulary.

Gilbert writes of Moro warriors with shield and bolo, agile in hand-to-hand fights, and of friars, officers, and soldiers in camp and barracks. His view is that of an American of his day, proud of the new regime and curious about Filipino ways. The book now serves as a period portrait of the Philippines under early American rule.
2490-lamia:
John Keats's Lamia tells of a serpent-woman who takes human form to love the young Lycius, and of the philosopher Apollonius who exposes her at their wedding feast. The poem's lush verse and tragic ending make it one of Keats's great romances, full of color, music, and doomed desire. Lamia herself is sympathetic, not monstrous.

The poem asks whether truth should always break enchantment, and leaves the answer aching. Keats's imagery glows on every line. Poetry readers will find a masterpiece of the Romantic age. Keats wrote Lamia in 1819, the year of his great odes.
24994-wheat-growing-in-australia:
This 1915 Commonwealth handbook, issued under the authority of Australia's Minister of State for External Affairs and printed in Melbourne, promotes wheat growing to prospective settlers. Chapters cover the wheat area, the factors governing the crop, securing a farm, the plant required, working the farm, cost of production, share farming, settler assistance, and social life. Information offices listed range from the Australian Pavilion at San Francisco's Panama Pacific Exposition to the High Commissioner in London.

Practical detail dominates. The settler fences his holding into paddocks, with posts nine or eleven feet apart carrying six or seven wires, and wire netting on boundary fences where rabbits menace the crop. Timber posts come from the farm itself, split to length, with droppers between wider-spaced posts. The booklet reads as both guide and advertisement for a new agricultural life.
25358-bert-lloyd-s-boyhood-a-story-from-:
J. Macdonald Oxley's Bert Lloyd's Boyhood, published in London in 1892, pictures boy life in Nova Scotia a generation earlier. Oxley, drawing on his own school days, says he departed as slightly as possible from personal experience.

Bert, whose full name is Cuthbert Lloyd, and his inseparable friend Frank Bowser meet a classics-loving doctor at school, who calls them Damon and Pythias. A frontispiece shows a crowd pummeling a boy on page 165. The book offers Canadian readers a story of their own boyhood, told with humor and affection. The story honors school friendship and the Nova Scotia coast alike.
25976-peeps-at-many-lands-australia:
Frank Fox gives young readers a peep at Australia in this 1911 book from Black, with twelve color plates by Percy F. S. Spence. Chapters run from Australia's beginning and Australia of today to the natives, the animals and birds, the bush, and the Australian child. Plates show kangaroo hunting, snowy mountains near the federal capital site, the barrier of the Blue Mountains, and garden streets of Adelaide.

Town views take in Collins Street, Melbourne, and Sydney's town hall, while bush scenes show a sheep drover, a hut, surf bathing, and children riding to school. A cover picture shows the nomad of the interior. Fox writes for children curious about a far land, mixing towns, farms, wild life, and native life in short, bright chapters.
26048-some-reminiscences-of-old-victoria:
Edgar Fawcett recalls old Victoria and its pioneers in Some Reminiscences of Old Victoria, printed at Toronto in 1912 and dedicated to Premier Richard McBride. Fawcett says typhoid laid him aside eight years before, and convalescence at the seaside set him writing. On the beach with a pad he began a British boy's experiences in San Francisco in the early fifties, and kept at it for eight years with pioneers' encouragement.

A frontispiece shows Fort Victoria in 1859. One church tale tells of a barrel organ fitted with a keyboard for Sunday mornings, played by Mrs. Atwood, while barrels turned by handle gave evening music. Fawcett, forgetting hymn verses one night, stopped, restarted two notes behind, and made confusion worse confounded. The book is a warm, anecdotal pioneer memoir.
26090-condemned-as-a-nihilist-a-story-of:
G. A. Henty's tale sends Godfrey into Siberian exile after his capture by the Russian police. Condemned as a nihilist, he works under the name Ivan Holstoff, first in an office and then, at his own request, back at the mine, where confinement had harmed his health. Mikail and other prisoners help him plan.

Chapters build toward flight, with preparations, a long winter's wait for the thaw, and a Samoyede encampment on the road out. Walter Paget's illustrations mark the capture and the escape stages. The story pairs adventure with a plain picture of exile life: forced labor, fear of the dreaded Kobylin, and the slow work of getting free.
26316-virginia:
Ellen Glasgow's Virginia, issued by Doubleday, Page in 1913 and dedicated to her sister Cary, follows one woman's life in three books: The Dream, The Reality, and The Adjustment. It opens in May 1884 at the Dinwiddie Academy for Young Ladies, where Miss Priscilla Batte, a majestic woman of fifty, feeds her canary after learning her geography lesson by heart.

Virginia's dream covers her inheritance, first love, the Treadwells, and Oliver the romantic, ending with Oliver's surrender. Reality brings children, failure, shadow, and the pang of motherhood, with the problem of the South woven through. Adjustment faces middle age, the price of comfort, and life's cruelties. The novel tracks a southern woman's hopes against a changing order.
26601-gambia:
Fred J. Melville, president of the Junior Philatelic Society, published this stamp handbook in London in 1909 as one of the Melville Stamp Books. It covers the stamps of Gambia, the British West African colony on a narrow strip along the Gambia River, with Bathurst as its capital. An opening chapter sketches the colony and its posts from Portuguese discovery in 1447 onward.

Later chapters take each issue in turn, from the embossed Cameo issue of 1869 through issues of 1874, 1880, and 1886-87. They continue to the Queen's Head series of 1898 and the King's Head series of 1902-1906. Melville warns collectors to guard Cameo embossing with sunk mounts and tissue paper. A bibliography, check list, and notes on postmarks by Douglas Ellis close the book.
26632-the-bounty-of-the-chesapeake-fishi:
James Wharton wrote this short history as number thirteen in the Jamestown 350th Anniversary Historical Booklets, published by the University Press of Virginia. Copyrighted in 1957 for the Virginia 350th Anniversary Celebration Corporation, it surveys fishing in colonial Virginia from the first settlements onward. The Chesapeake's bounty, the title argues, fed a colony that might otherwise have starved.

Wharton draws on Virginia Company records and settlers' letters, including a 1623 note that oysters were the most evident hope against starving. John Smith had warned emigrants to bring nets, hooks, and lines, and the booklet follows how colonists caught, kept, and traded fish. It is a compact, source-based introduction to an everyday industry of early Virginia.
26705-the-caravan-route-between-egypt-an:
His Imperial Highness the Archduke Ludwig Salvator of Austria wrote this travel book, translated from the German. Chatto and Windus published it at London in 1881, with twenty-three full-page illustrations by the author. Chevalier de Hesse-Wartegg's preface to the translation notes the Archduke's election as an honorary member of the Royal Geographical Society, one of only nine among some thirty-five hundred fellows.

The Archduke, wintering in Egypt, turned from harbour and railway schemes at Jaffa, the Jordan valley, and Beyrout. He turned instead to the old overland route between Syria and Egypt. He resolved to examine personally the caravan route over Wadi el Harish, the ancient Torrens Egyptii, as a possible railway line round the coast. Stages run from El Kantara through Katya and El Harish to Sheik el Zvoyed, Khanyunis, and Gaza, past telegraph posts, sandy El Brej, and Bedouins begging water.
26733-more-trivia:
Logan Pearsall Smith, author of Trivia, published this sequel with Harcourt, Brace and Company at New York in 1921, printed by Quinn and Boden at Rahway, New Jersey. It is a long run of short pieces, each only a page or two. They cover London streets, clubs, gardens, and the inner life. Titles run from Reassurance and The Great Adventure to The Welsh Harp and The Argument.

Smith greets Posterity across the void of time. He laughs at readers' funny clothes and hats and horrid sex-theories. He urges the unborn to hurry up and get born to read him. Later pieces muse on matter as mere idea inside an immense thought-bubble. Others muse on loneliness, where no friend hates Ibsen, problem plays, the supernatural, Switzerland, and adultery as much as he does. It is witty, detached, and deliberately slight.
268-the-octopus-a-story-of-california:
Presley, a young poet on a California ranch, hears a railroad whistle and forgets his watch. Frank Norris's Octopus opens on the county road between the Broderson and Los Muertos ranches, near Bonneville. The railroad, its shops, and its land hunger coil around the valley.

Ranchers, led by the Derricks, fight the octopus of rates, freight, and courts. Presley watches, writes, and fails to act as wheat, drought, and violence decide fates. Norris's naturalism makes the railroad a force beyond any one villain. The novel stands as the great California epic.
27293-a-sketch-of-the-life-and-services-:
Osmond Tiffany read this short life of Gen. Otho Holland Williams before the Maryland Historical Society on 6 March 1851, and it was printed in Baltimore the same year. Tiffany presents Williams as a patient, disinterested, and zealous Maryland officer of the American Revolution, whose deeds and character still spoke to readers a lifetime later.

Williams was born in Prince George's County in March 1749, of Welsh ancestors settled in Maryland a generation before, and spent his boyhood near the mouth of Conococheague Creek in Frederick County. The sketch follows him from that quiet youth into the trials of camp and war. It serves as a compact portrait of a Revolutionary officer from his home state.
27382-the-sequel-what-the-great-war-will:
George A. Taylor of Sydney published this wartime narrative in June 1915, with a second edition the next month, as the story of Lieutenant Jefson, aviator. Taylor had already written on the air age and its military significance, and here he asks what the Great War will mean to Australia, told through a flying officer's eyes.

Jefson complains that commanders do not know what to do with aviators. Though men have flown for eight years, their own batteries still fire on them overhead, mistaking a Bleriot for an enemy Taube. The book mixes aviation detail with speculation about a new arm of war. It captures Australian wartime hopes and worries while the war was still young.
27517-equal-suffrage-in-australia:
The National American Woman Suffrage Association published this short pamphlet as number six in its Political Equality Series, issued monthly from headquarters at Warren, Ohio, at ten cents a year. Its article, by Lady Holder, first appeared in the New York Independent of 9 June 1904.

Lady Holder, wife of Sir Frederick W. Holder, Speaker of the House of Representatives of Federated Australia, and a leader in philanthropic work in South Australia, reports that women there had political equality with men for several years. The change, she says, produced no marked effect on female character or domestic life, while women grew more interested in public affairs. American suffragists used Australia as a working example.
27811-macaria:
Augusta J. Evans Wilson, author of Beulah and St. Elmo, wrote Macaria, published in London and Melbourne by Ward, Lock and Company in 1921. The novel follows Irene and her friends through thirty-five chapters, from Russell Aubrey and Irene's friendship to civil war and hospital work.

The story opens at midnight with a young accountant bent over a ledger, and it moves through a missing watch, a sacrifice, a fever, and a blockade runner. Wilson's Southern romance mixes domestic feeling with the upheaval of secession, and it shows a popular novelist of the postwar South at full stretch.
27865-george-borrow-in-east-anglia:
William A. Dutt published this 1896 monograph on George Borrow in East Anglia with David Nutt of London, drawing in part on an article in Good Words. Chapters follow Borrow from early days and a lawyer's clerkship through Norwich, Oulton, pugilism, and the East Anglian gypsies.

Dutt quotes Theodore Watts on Borrow's power to paint England before railways marred her beauty, when the stage-coach was in glory and the horse was the only swift magician. The book is a compact guide to Borrow's East Anglian roots and to the landscapes that shaped his writing.
28034-scenes-in-the-hawaiian-islands-and:
Mary E. Anderson's Scenes in the Hawaiian Islands and California, entered for copyright in 1865, grew from notes kept on a voyage with her father, Rufus Anderson. He travelled in 1863 on business for the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions, and his daughter wrote down what she saw. The American Tract Society published the result in Boston.

The journey runs from New York by steamer to Panama, then across the Pacific to Hawaii and on to California. Anderson describes ports, tropical plants, native homes, and mission schools, often for young readers. The book gives a fresh, first-hand view of Hawaii just as mission work there was changing hands.
28648-a-little-girl-in-old-philadelphia:
Amanda M. Douglas's A Little Girl in Old Philadelphia, published by A. L. Burt of New York with copyright 1890, is a posy culled from quaint gardens. Douglas dedicates the tale, dated Newark 1899, to Mr. and Mrs. Henry Horton Lawrence, praising an old town's youth, its struggles, romance, and unfolding. Earnest hands worked for its welfare and left lasting monuments, she says.

The tale opens with Primrose swinging a faded gingham sunbonnet in late sunshine, her yellow hair a mass of frowzy curls. Aunt Lois scolds her disorder, twists the bonnet strings straight, and orders a clean pinafore, washed face and hands, and combed hair. Chapters follow Bessy Wardour, a new world, a little rebel, native land and loyalty, midnight tidings of great joy, and Polly and Phil.
29055-the-present-state-of-virginia:
Hugh Jones, chaplain to the Virginia assembly and minister at Jamestown, wrote this account of colonial Virginia. The text here is an 1865 reprint. Jones describes the colony's Native, English, and Black inhabitants. He covers their religion, manners, government, trade, and way of living, along with a description of the country itself.

Jones adds a short view of Maryland and North Carolina. He then sets out schemes for promoting learning, religion, inventions, manufactures, and trade in Virginia and the other plantations. Readers get a firsthand colonial survey, valuable for what it shows about how an early Virginia clergyman saw his colony and what he thought it needed to prosper.
29334-the-colonial-architecture-of-phila:
Frank Cousins and Phil M. Riley published this illustrated study in Boston in 1920 with Little, Brown and Company. Nine hundred and seventy-five copies were printed from type, nine hundred and fifty for sale, and this copy is number 201. The first plate shows a doorway at Cliveden in Germantown.

Chapters cover Philadelphia architecture, Georgian country houses of brick, city residences of brick, and ledge-stone, plastered stone, and hewn stone country houses. Later chapters treat doorways and porches, windows and shutters, halls and staircases, mantels, interior wood finish, and public buildings. Readers get a detailed architectural survey, still useful for anyone studying or restoring Philadelphia's colonial buildings.
29496-christopher-columbus-and-his-monum:
J. M. Dickey compiled this 1892 tribute to Christopher Columbus and his monument Columbia, printed by Rand, McNally of Chicago and New York. Its full title calls it a gathering of choice tributes to the great Genoese and his grand discovery, greatness of mind, and purpose. Ancient authors testify beside modern men, and sculptures, scenes, and portraits adorn the pages.

A frontispiece shows the Columbus monument in Genoa's Piazza Acquaverde, sculpted by Signor Lanzio and dedicated in 1862. Dickey's preface calls Columbus and America the brightest jewels in history's crown. Readers of Columbus lore will find a lavish, admiring scrapbook from the age of the Columbian celebrations.
29715-the-princess-virginia:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson published this romance in New York in 1907, with pictures by Leon Guipon. Virginia, the princess of the title, moves through a court world of counts, chancellors, and an emperor. Count von Breitstein asks who she is in the frontispiece scene. The chapters carry her from the news that opens the tale to the emperor's ball and the honors of the day.

A chamois hunter, the eagle's eyrie, and a magic citron add color to the court plot. Leo faces Leopold, the chancellor speaks, and the emperor is at last brought to bay. The Williamsons keep the tone light and the pace brisk. The book is a gay court romance, with a princess at its heart and an empire watching her every step.
30260-a-new-doglike-carnivore-genus-cyna:
E. Raymond Hall and Walter W. Dalquest name a new doglike carnivore from the Pliocene of Texas, in a short University of Kansas Museum of Natural History paper. A study of a right upper jaw bearing premolars and a molar, plus part of a right lower jaw bearing a molar, reveals an unnamed species of cynarctine carnivore.
