The authors call it Cynarctus fortidens, a new species, in volume 14, number 10, pages 135 to 138.

The holotype, a right upper jaw with three teeth numbered 11353 in Kansas collections, came from a bluff on the west side of Turkey Creek, about seventy-five feet above the stream. Dalquest collected it on June 25, 1960, on the Raymond Farr Ranch in Donley County, near Clarendon, from Clarendon fauna of early Pliocene age. Two figures support the brief, technical description.
30635-the-talking-thrush-and-other-tales:
The Talking Thrush and Other Tales from India, collected by W. Crooke and retold by W. H. Drouse, illustrated by W. H. Robinson, was first published in October 1899 and reprinted in July 1902 and October 1922. An illustration warns that a crow is a crow forever, setting the tone for animal wisdom tales.

Contents open with the talking thrush, the rabbit and the monkey, the sparrow's revenge, and the judgment of the jackal. How the mouse got into his hole, King Solomon and the owl, the camel's neck, and the quail and the fowler follow. The king of the kites, the jackal and the camel, and the wise old shepherd close the named tales. Drouse retells Indian folk tales with clarity and humor.
30747-seaport-in-virginia-george-washing:
Gay Montague Moore wrote this history of Alexandria, Virginia, as George Washington knew it, published by the University Press of Virginia with a 1949 copyright and a second printing in 1972. Drawings by Worth Bailey and photographs by Walter Wilcox fill the volume. Moore dedicates it to her husband Charles Beatty Moore, with whom she delved into records that might throw some shadow of those who built and lived in Alexandria's old houses.

The book follows the seaport through its prologue and its growth, using houses, families, and town life to show how Washington's Alexandria worked. It is local history at its best: close, documented, and full of people rather than bare dates. Readers who love Virginia, Washington, or old American towns will find a rich guide to streets and homes that still carry their past.
30888-the-american-church-dictionary-and:
Rev. William James Miller, master of arts and bachelor of divinity, compiled this American Church Dictionary and Cyclopedia, published by Thomas Whittaker in New York in 1901. It is a reference book for churchgoers and clergy, giving short entries in alphabetical order on worship, doctrine, and church practice. Its entries cite rubrics, scripture, and the ordination office, so readers can see where a usage comes from.

Early entries show the method: Ablutions names the ceremonial washing of sacred vessels after Holy Communion, with holy wine and water reverently consumed by the priest. Absolution gives the forgiveness of sins through bishops and priests, with the ordination words on forgiving and retaining sins. It is a useful, old-fashioned guide to American church language and custom.
31096-the-lily-and-the-cross-a-tale-of-a:
Professor James De Mille, author of The Dodge Club, Cord and Creese, and the B. O. W. C. stories, wrote this tale of Acadia, published by Lee and Shepard in Boston in 1874, with pictures. Its frontispiece shows a meeting in mid ocean. Its twenty-six chapters run from A Voice Out of the Deep and A Meeting in Mid Ocean through New Friends, Mimi and Margot, and A Strange Revelation. They end with A French Frigate, Caught in a Trap, and Under Arrest.

Later chapters bring Grand Pré, Alone in the World, A Friend in Need, The Parson among the Philistines, A Stroke for Liberty, and The Manoeuvres of Zac. They continue with Flight, Reunion, Among Friends, and Louisbourg. The tale opens with a schooner belonging to Boston, registered under the name of the Reverend Amos Adams. It is a romance of Acadia, with captives, escapes, and a court martial.
31728-my-brave-and-gallant-gentleman-a-r:
Robert Watson's 1918 romance of British Columbia, published at Toronto, follows a second son. He grows up hearing that Lady Rosemary Granton will someday marry the man who would become Earl of Brammerton and Hazelmere. The narrator, merely the Honourable second son, faces that supposed calamity without much mental agony.

Twenty-six chapters carry him from second sons and a blacksmith named Jim to a viscount captain of the guards. They continue through a coaster voyage, a millionaire, a beach, a fight in the woods, and a knight proved true. Readers get a light adventure romance of the Canadian west, full of rivals, songs, and seaside scrapes.
31923-the-pearl-of-india:
Maturin M. Ballou's Pearl of India, in its second edition of 1895 with copyright in 1894, is a travel book on Ceylon, gem of the Orient. Ballou's preface says readers show growing satisfaction in contemplating foreign lands through the eyes of experienced travelers, and that both author and reader are gratified by such a work.

Asked which place of all he has seen he recommends, Ballou answers that no point presents more varied attractions to the observant traveler. No point more thoroughly exhibits equatorial life than Ceylon, accessible, safe, and healthy for the stranger. Readers get a Victorian travelogue of the fabled isle of Arabian story, for artist, botanist, antiquarian, scientist, and sportsman alike.
32129-area-handbook-for-albania:
Area Handbook for Albania, published in January 1971 as DA PAM 550-98, is a United States Army reference work on Albania, prepared by the Foreign Area Studies program at the American University. Its co-authors were Eugene K. Keefe, Sarah Jane Elpern, William Giloane, James M. Moore, Junior, Stephen Peters, and Eston T. White. Research and writing were completed on July 17, 1970, and the handbook sold for $2.50 through the Government Printing Office.

Its country summary states the essentials: the People's Republic of Albania. Albanians call it Shqiperia. It has been a national state since 1912, and under Communist control after 1944. Government follows the Party-state model of the Soviet Union, with the People's Assembly as highest state organ and the Albanian Workers' Party paralleling government at every level. Readers get a Cold War reference handbook, systematic and official in tone.
32178-los-gringos-or-an-inside-view-of-m:
Lieutenant Wise of the United States Navy published Los Gringos in New York in 1849, with Baker and Scribner. Its full title promises an inside view of Mexico and California, with wanderings in Peru, Chili, and Polynesia. The book belongs to the travel literature of the Mexican-American War era. Wise saw those coasts at first hand, rather than from a library.

Wise's preface begins with his title, Los Gringos, and the volume that follows offers an American sailor's view of Mexican and Californian life, then of South American and Pacific wanderings. Readers get a period eyewitness account: Mexico and California as a serving officer found them in the late 1840s, with Peru, Chile, and Polynesian stops completing a wide Pacific circuit.
32268-the-burning-of-chambersburg-pennsy:
Reverend B. S. Schneck's The Burning of Chambersburg, Pennsylvania, subtitled by an eye-witness and a sufferer, tells of July 30, 1864, when a town of six thousand people was burned. Schneck adds corroborative statements from seven others. They are the Reverend J. Clark, the Honourable A. K. McClure, J. Hoke, the Reverend T. G. Apple, the Reverend B. Bausman, the Reverend S. J. Niccolls, and J. K. Shryock. A notice tells how contributions for the sufferers arrived from friends and strangers abroad.

The citizens, Schneck writes, stated that a demanded sum could not be paid in gold or currency, and could not have been made in good faith. They remonstrated against burning a town as a monstrosity. The burning followed burnings in certain Virginia counties by General Hunter. The raiders, McCausland, Bradley Johnson, and Gilmore, commanded three thousand cavalry with artillery. Readers get a Civil War atrocity narrative, vivid and corroborated.
32507-the-planters-of-colonial-virginia:
Thomas J. Wertenbaker's Planters of Colonial Virginia, copyrighted in 1922 and reissued in 1959, studies the men who built Virginia's plantation society. Chapters move from England in the New World and the Indian weed, meaning tobacco, through the Virginia yeomanry, freemen and freedmen, and the Restoration period. Later chapters treat the yeoman in Virginia history, world trade, and life beneath the black tide, with notes, an appendix, and an index.

Wertenbaker writes from Princeton, where the book was revised in August 1957, and his account stresses land, labour, trade, and social rank. Tobacco, indenture, and the growth of a planter class shape the colony's politics and daily life. The book remains a standard, readable history for readers who want colonial Virginia explained through its planters and their world.
32573-history-of-the-colony-and-ancient-:
Charles Campbell's History of the Colony and Ancient Dominion of Virginia, published in Philadelphia in 1860, follows Virginia from early voyages of discovery through its colonial centuries. Campbell opens with Sir Walter Raleigh's colony, Captain John Smith's early life and adventures, and the landing at Jamestown.

Later chapters treat Smith's explorations and administration, the Indians of Virginia, the sufferings of the colonists, the wreck of the Sea-Venture, Pocahontas in England, and successive governors. Campbell takes Lord Bacon's maxim as his rule, to present events and counsels and leave observations to the reader's judgment.
32627-area-handbook-for-bulgaria:
Eugene K. Keefe and coauthors prepared this Area Handbook for Bulgaria for the Foreign Area Studies program of American University, with research completed in August 1973 and publication in 1974. A country summary opens with size, place, and people: 42,800 square miles, about 8.7 million people in 1973, and borders with Romania, Yugoslavia, Greece, and Turkey.

Four sections then cover social life, politics, economics, and national security in turn. Readers find chapters on land and climate, ethnic groups, faith, government, schooling, and the budget, making the book a compact reference for a country then ruled by its Communist Party.
32700-area-handbook-for-romania:
This handbook on Romania comes from the Foreign Area Studies program, with research completed in February 1972 and publication the same year. Eugene K. Keefe led its coauthors. A country summary gives the shape of the state: over 91,700 square miles, almost 20.6 million people in 1971, and land borders with Bulgaria, Yugoslavia, Hungary, and the Soviet Union.

Sections on social life, politics, national security, and economics follow. Chapters trace the 1965 constitution, Communist Party control, the Carpathians and plains, minorities, labor, and prisons, giving a full reference portrait of Romania in the early 1970s.
32708-the-golden-age-in-transylvania:
Maurus Jókai sets this historical romance in Transylvania near the close of the seventeenth century, translated by S. L. and A. V. Waite. The scene opens with a hunting party in 1666 and follows Prince Michel Apafi, placed on the throne by the Turks, to the murder of Denis Banfi, the last great Transylvanian baron.

Nineteen chapters move through courts, diets, battles, and banquet-hall justice, with figures such as Azraele and Corsar caught in love, fear, and war. Jókai paints wild Carpathian land, proud lords, and sudden turns of fate. The book was praised as his best, and it reads as a full, stirring chronicle.
32755-peasant-tales-of-russia:
V. I. Nemirovitch-Dantchenko offers four peasant tales of Russia, translated by Claud Field and published in London by Robert Scott in 1917. The contents run from the deserted mine through Mahmoud's family and a misunderstanding to the luck of Ivan the Forgetful.

The first tale opens at the Voskressensky mine at dawn, where silent miners in leather jerkins carry flickering lamps to descend into darkness. Old Ivan, thin and withered, insists on going down with them. Later tales follow Mahmoud Bey, a Turkish prisoner talking of families and flight from Adrianople, and Ivan the Forgetful, creeping through a warm spring night toward liberty.
33038-due-north-or-glimpses-of-scandinav:
Maturin M. Ballou's Due North, or Glimpses of Scandinavia and Russia, follows the author's earlier Due South on Cuba, and offers travel sketches from the far north. Ballou opens with the thought that only traveling which reveals the value of home and lets a traveler enjoy it better is truly good. His glimpses take readers through Norway, Sweden, Denmark, and Russia, with notes on castles, canals, and cities whose names he spells as he heard them.

The book is a traveler's notebook rather than a formal history, full of sights, people, and comparisons that a nineteenth-century American reader would enjoy. Its charm lies in Ballou's easy, observant voice and in the period detail of steamers, hotels, and northern light. For readers planning a mental journey north, or studying how Americans saw Scandinavia before modern tourism, it remains an engaging guide.
33272-green-spring-farm-fairfax-county-v:
Ross and Nan Netherton's history traces Green Spring Farm in Fairfax County, Virginia, from the Moss family of freeholders between 1770 and 1835. Orchard and dairy years under Fountain Beattie follow, to the end of the farming era under Michael Straight. Published in June 1970, it pairs historical notes with a full architectural study of the mansion house, the Tobey house, the barn, the log cabin, and the spring house.

The volume adds appendixes with a landmarks survey form, a summary of ownership, and old wills and inventories, making it useful for both visitors and researchers. Its tone is plain and local, rooted in deeds and buildings rather than legend. For readers of Virginia history, it is a thorough guide to one farm and to the county's changing land.
33306-the-king-of-arcadia:
Francis Lynde's novel, published in 1909, bears the title The King of Arcadia, a tale of a man who seeks a pastoral ideal in a modern world. Lynde, author of A Romance in Transit and The Quickening, writes of love, duty, and the pull of a simpler life. A heroine pleads for help in the book's opening scenes. The story is inscribed to his daughter Dorothea, whose loving heart and willing hands aided its writing.

The novel blends romance with a gentle satire of modern haste, as its king of Arcadia tries to hold to his dream against practical claims. Lynde's prose is clear and warm, suited to readers who like a story with both feeling and wit. For fans of early twentieth-century romance, it is a pleasant, well-told tale of an ideal tested by life.
33450-journal-of-a-trip-to-california:
C. W. Smith's Journal of a Trip to California, across the continent from Weston, Missouri, to Weber Creek, California, in the summer of 1850, records a gold-rush journey. Smith writes day by day of the trail, its hardships, and its hopes, in a journal made for readers who wanted the West as travelers lived it. The e-text draws on page images from the Internet Archive.

The journal's value lies in its plain, first-hand detail, from river crossings to camp life, told by a man on the road to gold. Its tone is honest and unadorned, suited to students of the overland trail. For readers of California history, it is a vivid, short record of a summer that changed many lives.
33480-under-fire-for-servia:
Colonel James Fiske, writing the fourth volume of his World's War series, sends American boy Dick Warner into the opening weeks of the First World War. Dick reaches Semlin, a border town in Hungary across the Save river from Belgrade, just as refugees pour through after Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Servia. A visit to the busy American consul starts a chain of dangerous errands.

Across nineteen chapters Dick makes friends, survives a police raid, crosses rivers, rescues a wounded captain, and matches wits with enemy agents. The story moves between Semlin and Belgrade and builds toward flight, explosion, and a final confrontation. It is a boys' adventure tale grounded in the real geography and early wartime tension of the Balkans.
33484-valeria-the-martyr-of-the-catacomb:
W. H. Withrow draws on years of study of the Roman catacombs to tell a story of early Christian life in Rome. His heroine Valeria lives among believers who worship in secret, bury their dead in underground passages, and face arrest, torture, and death for their faith. The preface states his aim plainly: a popular account of primitive Christian character, kept as accurate as his research allowed.

The tale moves between the catacombs, where inscriptions and tombs mark the martyrs, and the pagan city above, where emperors and officials enforce the old gods. Valeria's courage becomes the thread that links scenes of worship, friendship, and persecution. Readers interested in early church history will find both a story and an introduction to what the catacombs reveal about that community.
33748-the-kitchen-encyclopedia:
Swift and Company issued this Kitchen Encyclopedia, twelfth edition, copyrighted in 1911, promising many helpful suggestions, all tried and practical, for ready reference in the kitchen. The volume opens as an advertisement for Swift's Premium Oleomargarine, described as a sweet, pure, clean spread made from rich cream and edible fats. It holds every nutrient found in the best creamery butter.

The book explains that butter fat in oleomargarine matches butter down to the microscope and the chemistry, differing only in how it is secured. These include part by churning, the rest pressed from choice fat of government-inspected animals, called oleo, with rich cream, fancy creamery butter, neutral, vegetable oil, and dairy salt as its only ingredients. Beyond its salesmanship, the encyclopedia preserves period recipes, household advice, and the food industry's early self-presentation.
33753-in-paths-of-peril-a-boy-s-adventur:
J. Macdonald Oxley, author of Donalblane of Darien, writes a boy's adventures in Nova Scotia in this 1903 Toronto book, with six illustrations. Twelve chapters run from the old world to the new, through a great bear hunt, setting a bad example, off to the woods, a moose hunt, in the nick of time.

The story opens with the Huguenot defence of La Rochelle. For more than a year the defenders defied the whole power of France under Cardinal Richelieu, enduring hunger, battle, and pestilence for their faith. From that heroic background, Oxley follows Raoul and his companions through wilderness peril. Young readers and lovers of historical adventure will enjoy its bears, moose, and loyal comradeship.
33812-the-aboriginal-population-of-the-n:
S. F. Cook wrote this University of California study of native peoples along the north coast, issued in 1956. It builds on A. L. Kroeber's 1925 handbook and offers estimates group by group: Yurok, Wiyot, Karok, Hupa, Tolowa, Pomo, Yuki, and many smaller peoples, with a summary of totals at the end.

Cook weighs old reports, mission records, and later counts to judge how many people lived in each area before contact. The work is careful and plain about its limits, and its tables still guide students of California native history. It remains a key source for the size and spread of coastal peoples.
33963-the-valiants-of-virginia:
Hallie Erminie Rives wrote this Virginia romance, copyrighted in 1912 by the Bobbs-Merrill Company, with color pictures by Andre Castaigne. John Valiant comes to Damory Court and finds a family past, a crash, and a secret thirty years old. Chapters follow a hunt, a trespass, a tournament day, and a Virginian Runnymede.

Love, pride, and old wrongs braid through the tale, as Katharine and John weigh what the past demands of them. Rives writes with color and feeling for old Virginia houses and customs. The novel remains a lush, old-fashioned romance of the South.
34015-the-coast-of-bohemia:
Thomas Nelson Page published this book of poems in New York in 1906, with copyrights in 1888 and 1906. The title poem opens a set that runs from The Voice of the Sea and Long Roll at Napoleon's Tomb to Youth, America, and poems on Matthew Arnold and his mother. A closing section gives dialect poems from Befo' de War.

Page moves between high lyric, memory, and Southern dialect voices, with Uncle Gabe and other figures from the old South. The book shows a Virginia writer in two modes: polished verse and folk speech. It remains a varied sample of Page's poetry.
34138-lady-maude-s-mania:
George Manville Fenn wrote this comic novel of a high family, opening with the Earl of Barmouth and his son, Viscount Diphoos, cursing street organs and their grinders. The viscount, heels on the library chimney-piece in a Portland Place mansion, smokes a cigar to steady himself for what he calls the operation. His father, plagued by gout, fears her ladyship may faint on return from church.

Tom, the viscount, grins at the scene his father pictures, recalling a wedding twenty-six years past, since when his mother grew stouter and his father thinner. Fenn writes with broad, cheerful humor. The novel offers a light comedy of an aristocratic household.
34196-porzia:
Cale Young Rice's 1913 verse play Porzia is set at Naples in about 1570, on the wedding day of Rizzio di Rossi, a young leader of men of letters suspected of heresy. His wife Porzia stands at the centre, between her husband, her kin, and officers of the Inquisition.

Giordano Bruno appears among the cast, and the play turns on faith, loyalty, and the risks of free thought under church watch. Rice writes in verse throughout, with terrace, garden, and bay views framing scenes of love, debate, and danger for a household under suspicion. The play is dedicated to Gilbert Murray.
3467-the-life-of-cesare-borgia:
Rafael Sabatini writes a life of Cesare Borgia, Duke of Valentinois and captain general of the Church, in Renaissance Italy. Sabatini warns that his book is no chronicle of saints and no history of devils. Instead it records very human, striving men in a lustful, flamboyant age, red with blood and pale with passion, an age of steel and velvet.

The narrative follows Borgia's rise with his father Pope Alexander the Sixth, his campaigns in Romagna, and his fall after his father's death. Sabatini judges Borgia by the standards of his own time rather than by modern morals. The book suits readers who want a vivid, readable life of one of history's most debated figures.
3607-ismailia:
Samuel White Baker writes an account of his expedition up the Nile for the Khedive Ismail of Egypt, to the province later called Ismailia. Baker commanded a force meant to open Central Africa to trade, plant stations along the river, and suppress the slave trade that ravaged the region. His narrative follows steamers, soldiers, and porters south toward Gondokoro and beyond.

Baker describes the river, its peoples, its wildlife, and the hard labor of moving a modern expedition through swamp and desert. He writes as a Victorian explorer confident in his mission, yet frank about disease, desertion, and resistance. The book suits readers interested in African exploration and in the nineteenth century campaign against the slave trade.
3819-the-euahlayi-tribe-a-study-of-abori:
K Langloh Parker, who lived among the Euahlayi people of New South Wales, wrote this study of their life, law, and belief. Chapters cover Byamee the All Father, relationships and totems, medicine men and leechcraft, and a witch woman. They also follow a girl from infancy to womanhood and a boy to the Boorah initiation. Funerals, mourning, stars and legends, trapping, foraging, costumes, weapons, and amusements all receive their section.

Parker writes as a sympathetic witness of her time, and her notes on twin births, spirit beliefs, and bush bogies show both her care and her era's limits. The book remains a valuable early record of a single people's customs. Readers who study Australian Aboriginal culture should read it with that context in mind, as a pioneer work rather than a modern account.
4641-starr-king-in-california:
William Day Simonds wrote Starr King in California to set the record straight about a critical period in California history, and to deal justly with a man recent historians had slighted. He dedicates the book to Horace Davis of San Francisco, whose friendly interest and help he gratefully acknowledges. Up to Starr King's death, Simonds says, it was generally believed that King, more than any other man, had kept California and the whole Pacific Coast from falling into disunion.

Simonds adds that Abraham Lincoln held the same opinion, quoting Edwin Percy Whipple. Parts cover old New England, California in 1860, California's hour of decision, philanthropist and preacher, and a retrospect. Readers get a warm, partisan biography of a Unitarian minister whose preaching and patriotism shaped a state at war, and a useful guide to California's Civil War politics.
5211-the-famous-missions-of-california:
William Henry Hudson's Famous Missions of California, published in London in 1901, tells the story of the Franciscan missions of Alta California. It opens with Father Junipero Serra and the proposed settlement, follows his arrival at San Diego, and traces the founding of San Carlos at Monterey and San Antonio de Padua, among others.

Hudson, lately professor of English at Stanford, writes for general readers, joining history with affectionate recollection of California days. The book gives a clear, readable introduction to the mission chain, its founders, and the Spanish settlement of California, before later histories revised its romantic view.
5303-the-little-hunchback-zia:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's Little Hunchback Zia is set nearly nineteen hundred and sixteen years ago, in the world of the Nativity. Zia toils up a steep road in the deepest shadows, staggering with weariness, striking his foot on stones, and smothering cries of pain, terrified that any traveller might glance toward him.

Burnett, author of The Secret Garden, writes a Christmas story of a despised child drawn toward Bethlehem. Illustrated by Spencer Baird Nichols and W. T. Benda, the book offers young readers a tender tale of fear, pity, and the hope that reaches even the lowliest wanderer.
5344-journals-of-expeditions-of-discover:
Edward John Eyre's Journals of Expeditions of Discovery into Central Australia, first volume. It records journeys sent by the colonists of South Australia in 1840 and 1841, from Adelaide toward King George's Sound. Its chapters follow the expeditions overland through country no European had mapped, with plates and maps listed in its contents, though not reproduced in this text.

This record holds only the first volume of Eyre's journals, while a companion record in this library carries the complete journals and another carries the second volume alone. Readers get a first-hand account of Australian exploration, with its hardships, discoveries, and encounters, told in the day-by-day form of a journal.
5345-journals-of-expeditions-of-discover:
Edward John Eyre's Journals of Expeditions of Discovery into Central Australia, second volume, continues the journeys sent by the colonists of South Australia in 1840 and 1841. While a companion record carries the first volume alone and another carries the complete journals, this record holds only the second volume. Its own chapters, plates, and maps trace Eyre's route.

The volume follows the expeditions further into the interior and toward King George's Sound, in the day-by-day form of a journal. Readers get the later, harder portion of Eyre's exploration, with its privations and discoveries, told without romance by the explorer himself.
5346-journals-of-expeditions-of-discover:
Edward John Eyre's Journals of Expeditions of Discovery into Central Australia, complete in this record, covers the expeditions sent by the colonists of South Australia in 1840 and 1841. They travelled overland from Adelaide to King George's Sound. Unlike companion records in this library that carry the first or second volume alone, this record holds the whole journals.

Its chapters follow Eyre's parties through the interior, with lists of plates. Maps mark the extent of his journeys, though the plates themselves are not reproduced here. Readers get the full first-hand record of Australian exploration, in journal form, from departure to the far coast.
5789-personal-recollections-of-early-mel:
William Westgarth recalls early Melbourne and Victoria from personal experience, with portraits of pioneers like Edward Henty and John Pascoe Fawkner. Westgarth writes as a participant in the colony's founding decades, recalling streets, businesses, politics, and the men who shaped a new city. His recollections carry the tone of a memoirist who watched a settlement grow into a capital.

Readers get Australian colonial history from inside, without the polish of later official accounts. Westgarth's anecdotes preserve names, dates, and local color that formal histories often lose. The book suits readers of Australian history, Melbourne local history, and pioneer memoirs, offering a firsthand view of a city being built by its first generation.
585-running-a-thousand-miles-for-freedom:
William and Ellen Craft tell how they escaped slavery in Georgia in 1848, travelling a thousand miles to freedom in the North. Ellen, light-skinned, posed as a white gentleman, while William acted as her servant. The Crafts escaped in December 1848, travelling by train and steamer to Philadelphia.

Their narrative moves by train and steamer through dangers, questions, and close calls, told in plain, urgent prose. The Crafts later spoke in Britain against slavery, and their book remains a powerful firsthand account of escape. Their book, published in 1860, aided the abolition cause in Britain as well as America.
6024-the-duke-of-gandia:
Algernon Charles Swinburne stages a Borgia drama set in Rome from 14 June to 22 July 1497. The persons include Pope Alexander VI, Francesco Borgia Duke of Gandia, and Caesar Borgia Cardinal of Valencia. Michelotto the agent, a Tiber waterman, two assassins, Vannozza Catanei, and Lucrezia Borgia complete the cast.

The play opens in the Vatican. There Caesar asks his mother whether he is less her son than his brother, and whether their holy father thrilled her womb with more Italian passion for the elder. Swinburne writes in high verse, turning family rivalry into a contest for Rome itself. Murder waits just offstage.
6037-the-one-woman-a-story-of-modern-uto:
Thomas Dixon Jr. dedicates The One Woman to his mother, whose Scotch love of romantic literature gave him a heritage of eternal youth. The chapters move from the man and the woman through visions in the night, a banker and his fad, a shorthorn deacon, and the cry of the city.

A stolen kiss, sweet danger, a spider, a black cat, and a broken heart-string lead toward the wedding of the annunciation, freedom and fellowship, and a new heaven. Dixon calls the tale a story of modern utopia, where love, faith, and social hope collide. Courtier and queen meet irony of fate.
6060-philistia:
Grant Allen opens Philistia with children of light, the coasts of the Gentiles, Magdalen Quad, and a little music, then Askelon Villa at Gath and a trip down the river. Ghostly counsel, the camp of the Philistines, the women of the land, and the daughters of Canaan follow, with culture set against culture.

Later chapters bring a quiet wedding, fire, literature, music, and drama, the Philistines triumphant, streets of Askelon, and clouds beginning to break. Ronald comes of age, a precontract of marriage is made, and the tide turns. Allen uses biblical names to stage a modern struggle between art and convention.
6081-biographia-literaria:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge opens Biographia Literaria with motives for the work, his first publication's reception, school discipline of taste, and Bowles's sonnets, comparing poets before and since Pope. Later chapters test the supposed irritability of genius against facts and weigh the charge's injustice.

Coleridge treats his debts to critics, modern criticism, Southey's works, the Lyrical Ballads, and the distinction between fancy and imagination. He traces association from Aristotle to Hartley, weighs dualism from Descartes through Spinoza, and defends his own poetic ground. The book is literary autobiography and theory in one.
6083-the-boy-allies-with-haig-in-flander:
Clair W. Hayes opens in Flanders rain, as Hal Paine and Chester Crawford creep from American trenches facing the enemy across No Man's Land. In the trenches all seems silent, as if men were dead or asleep, yet most sleep on their arms, ready for night raids, while vigilant sentinels watch.

Hal and Chester leave with full knowledge of those sentinels, lest they be shot by their own side. The Boy Allies serve with Haig and the fighting Canadians of Vimy Ridge, in a tale of trenches, raids, and alarms. Hayes writes wartime adventure for boys, where caution and courage share the night watch.
6145-tales-of-the-punjab-folklore-of-ind:
Flora Annie Steel gathers Tales of the Punjab, folklore of India. It opens with a preface to the little reader and stories like Sir Buzz, The Rat's Wedding, The Faithful Prince, and The Bear's Bad Bargain. Prince Lionheart and his three friends, the Lambkin, Princess Aubergine, and Valiant Vicky the brave weaver follow.

The Tiger, the Brahman, and the Jackal, the King of the Crocodiles, Little Anklebone, and the Jackal and the Partridge mix cunning with morals. Raja Rasalu's birth, journeys, forsaken friends, and giant-killing close the set. Steel preserves Punjab tales in English, told for children and kept for all.
6424-a-modern-utopia:
H. G. Wells calls this book probably the last of a series beginning with Anticipations, written to clear a muddle in his mind about social and political questions. He meant Anticipations as his sole digression from imaginative writing, but questions he could not keep out of his work distressed him when touched in a stupid, haphazard way. A Modern Utopia answers them in fiction's form.

Old utopias were perfect, static states, Wells argues, a balance of happiness won forever against unrest. A modern utopia must be kinetic, a hopeful stage leading to a long ascent of stages. We build now not citadels but ships of state, floating on the great stream of things. Wells writes a dreamer's topography, where an agreeable, distracting Utopian talks and the author listens, learning his own hopes aloud.
6506-old-mission-stories-of-california:
Charles Franklin Carter gathers seven short tales from the days of the old California missions, when Spanish priests and Native people shared a hard desert land. Most of the stories rest on a scrap of real past fact, while one, about Juana, is made up yet set against that same past. Desert lakes, dry hills, and mission walls give each tale its place.

A sibyl's warning, a priest on the run, hidden money, and a pious woman named Juana all pass through these pages in turn. Carter writes in a calm, plain style, keen to show daily life, faith, and fear as people then knew them. Readers get a gentle, old-style view of Nueva California before the missions faded.
652-rasselas-prince-of-abyssinia:
Samuel Johnson writes a philosophical tale in this 1759 novella, printed here in Cassell's 1889 edition. Rasselas, prince of Abyssinia, lives in a happy valley yet longs to know the world, so he escapes with his sister Nekayah and the sage Imlac to test every way of life. Johnson wrote the tale in a week to pay his mother's debts and burial costs.

Johnson writes with grave, balanced prose, weighing courts, hermits, scholars, and lovers and finding each wanting. The tale asks whether happiness can be found in any single state. It endures as a classic moral fable, where a prince learns that choice itself, not contentment, is the human lot.
6840-queen-lucia:
E. F. Benson opens Queen Lucia on a hot July morning, as Mrs. Lucas walks the half-mile from Riseholme station to her house, The Hurst, on her own brisk feet. Her maid and luggage go on in the fly her husband ordered, for after four hours in a train a short walk will be pleasant. Yet another motive, veiled even from herself, prompts the walk.

All Riseholme will know she arrives by the 12:26, and the village street will be full of friends at that hour. They will see the fly draw up with luggage, and no one but the maid get out, a little thrill for gossips. Benson writes with sly, social comedy. Queen Lucia is a sparkling tale of a village queen and her court.
7071-in-times-of-peril-a-tale-of-india:
G A Henty sets In Times of Peril in India during the uprising of 1857, opening in bright, pretty cantonments at Sandynugghur in early spring. Contents promise life in cantonments, the outbreak, the flight, and broken down, then back under the flag and a dashing expedition. Delhi, a desperate defense, saved by a tiger, and treachery follow, with retribution, dangerous service, and Lucknow.

The besieged residency, spiking the guns, a sortie, and escape from Lucknow lead to the storming of Delhi, a riot at Cawnpore, and the relief and last capture of Lucknow. A sad parting and rest after labor close the tale. Henty writes the Mutiny as a boys adventure of siege, flight, and steadfast courage under fire.
7282-the-captivi-and-the-mostellaria:
Henry Thomas Riley translates two plays of Plautus literally, with notes: the Captivi and the Mostellaria. The Captivi opens in Aetolia with Hegio, father of Philopolemus, seeking a captive son, while Philocrates, an Elean captive, and his servant Tyndarus trade places in a plot of loyalty and disguise. An acrostic argument, supposed to be by Priscian the grammarian, lays out the tale: one son taken in battle, the other sold at four years old by a runaway slave.

Riley's plain version lets students follow Roman comedy without losing its jokes or its twists. The Mostellaria joins it as a second sample of Plautus at his most theatrical. Together the plays show captives, masters, parasites, and slaves in fast, humane farce.
7385-old-calabria:
Norman Douglas travels through Calabria, the toe of Italy, and writes a book that is part travel tale, part history, and part folklore. His chapters wander from Saracen Lucera and Manfred's town to cave shrines, the land of the poet Horace at Venosa, and the Bandusian fountain. He stops in mountain villages, talks with locals, and digs into whatever past each place throws up.

Further south come brigandage, Albanian settlers and their college, the Greek-speaking Sila, and a chapter on Milton in Calabria. Douglas treats the region as a layered country: Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and Norman traces all lie close together. The result is a lively, opinionated guide to a corner of Italy that most travelers skipped, written by a man who plainly loved its rough edges.
7778-history-of-california:
Helen Elliot Bandini wrote History of California to tell the state's story so simply that children read it with pleasure, yet fully enough for older readers and tourists. It runs from Indian occupancy through Spanish and mission days, the gold rush, statehood, and events of yesterday and today.

Chapters also trace California's great industries, and Bandini notes she worked mostly from source material, aided by old Spanish families, manuscripts, and memories of aged residents, each claim checked before use. Roy J. Warren's pictures accompany a history built on firsthand testimony.
8077-the-mind-in-the-making-the-relation:
James Harvey Robinson, author of The New History, wrote this book on how minds are made and how they might be remade for social reform. Its chapters move from disappointed methods of reform through kinds of thinking and rationalising, the animal heritage and the savage mind. The beginnings of critical thought, Plato and Aristotle, medieval civilisation and its intellectual inheritance, to the scientific revolution. The question throughout is why intelligence so often fails to improve the world.

Robinson argues that reform needs clearer thinking more than stronger feeling, and that history explains our mental habits. The book is a classic of progressive-era thought, written for general readers rather than specialists. It still offers a bracing account of prejudice, habit, and the slow work of learning to think.
8185-fountains-in-the-sand-rambles-among:
Norman Douglas rambled among the oases of Tunisia and wrote these fountains in the sand, from his journey en route, by the Oued Baiesh. Through the stones of Gafsa, to Sidi Ahmed Zarroung, the oasis of Leila, Metlaoui, the phosphate works, the Seldja gorge, and the gardens of Tozeur. His chapters mix Roman olive-culture, the work of Philippe Thomas, amusements by the way, cafes, guests, and a mysterious count, with reflections on a watery labyrinth and the dismal chott.

Douglas writes as a learned, witty traveller, at home in history, geology, and local gossip. His Tunisia is ancient and modern at once, with Roman ruins beside French mines. For readers of travel literature, the book is a rich, digressive companion, and one of the best English accounts of the Tunisian south.
853-the-confutatio-pontificia:
An anonymous Catholic reply to the Augsburg Confession, edited by J. M. Reu, bears this Latin title, the Confutation of the Augsburg Confession. It answers the matters laid before the Emperor by the Elector of Saxony and other princes and states of the Holy Roman Empire, on questions of Christian faith and church order.

The text, written for the Diet of Augsburg in 1530, sets out the Roman case point by point against the Lutheran articles. Its tone is formal and theological, aimed at princes and divines rather than lay readers. The book is a key source for the Reformation debates, showing the Catholic answer in its own words.
8544-trivia:
Logan Pearsall Smith published Trivia in 1917. He notes that some pieces were privately printed at the Chiswick Press in 1902, and others appeared in the New Statesman and the New Republic, reprinted with editors' permission. His preface quotes a kindly adviser warning him against thinking too much about style, a warning Smith, a stylist, cheerfully ignores.

Smith's trivia are short reflections, aphorisms, and essays, polished to a shine, on life, books, and manners. Readers get a master of the brief form, in the tradition of La Rochefoucauld and Bacon, but modern and personal. The book suits reading in small doses, one polished piece at a time, and lovers of fine prose.
8869-tales-from-bohemia:
Robert Neilson Stephens gathers Tales from Bohemia, opening with a memory of newspaper life in March 1887. The narrator climbs three rickety flights to the fourth floor of the old Press building to begin work on the news desk. A crude piece of carpentry his companions call the shelf. It is his second night in the novel dignity of editorship, the humblest rank. A first step from the street, and an older hand and a lounging youth greet him with banter.

From that newsroom, the tales move among artists, writers, actors, and journalists living by wit and nerve in the city. Stephens, himself a newspaperman and playwright, writes with insider ease about bohemian work, friendship, and scraping by. The collection suits readers who enjoy O. Henry's New York or stories of the press, and it preserves a vanished world of ink, deadlines, and fourth-floor ambition.
9153-the-history-of-louisiana-or-of-the-:
Le Page du Pratz, a French traveler in Louisiana, wrote this history, here in an English version from the French. It describes the lands on both sides of the Mississippi, with notes on settlements, peoples, soil, climate, and goods. New Orleans, Mobile, and the river mouths get close accounts.

Chapters tell of copper mines, wars with the Natchez, native cures, and French posts pushed toward the Missouri and Kansas. The author sent hundreds of plant samples to the Company. The book remains a key first-hand source on French Louisiana and its native peoples.
9619-who-can-be-happy-and-free-in-russia:
Nicholas Nekrassov, a Russian poet born in 1821, wrote Who Can Be Happy and Free in Russia?, here in Juliet M. Soskice's 1917 translation. First printed in Russia in 1879, the poem asks a plain question of a land of serfs and lords. Seven peasants wander the roads, seeking one happy, free man in all Russia. Their quest frames the whole poem.

Parts follow a pope, a village fair, a drunken night, and a landowner, then a peasant woman's hard life and a feast for the whole village. Nekrassov gives the poor a voice both comic and bitter. A reader gets a landmark of Russian verse, and a portrait of a people asking freedom's question aloud.
9626-buried-cities-volume-2-olympia:
Jennie Hall, a Chicago history teacher, wrote Buried Cities, Part 2: Olympia, for boys and girls. Hall opens by asking young readers if they like to dig for hidden treasure, from arrowheads to graves. The book then tells how Olympia, the Greek sanctuary of games and gods, was buried and found again. Drawings and photos from original sources fill the pages.

Stories follow diggers, crowns, and winners of games, with captions chosen to teach as well as charm. Hall writes in a clear, inviting voice for school readers. A reader gets a lively first history of Olympia, and a tale of dirt, patience, and the thrill of finds.
9775-treasure-and-trouble-therewith-a-ta:
Geraldine Bonner wrote Treasure and Trouble Therewith in 1917, a tale of California gold, outlaws, and romance. Bonner dedicated the book to her father John Bonner, a writer who trained her with pride and belief. Chapters promise hands up, the tules, a marquis de Lafayette, and a derelict. A marked paragraph, a solid gold nugget, and a night rider follow.

Later chapters bring outlaws, revelation, and a last dinner, as George's girls and Michaels the miner cross the plot. Bonner writes with brisk, western color. A reader gets a rousing California adventure, rich in treasure hunts and frontier romance.
a-bird-calendar-for-northern-india: Douglas Dewar arranges this bird calendar for northern India month by month. Each month notes the birds to be seen in the region, drawing on his own notes and those of fellow observers in the Punjab. The sketches first appeared in the press and were gathered here for readers who watch birds through the year. It serves as a seasonal guide to the bird life of northern India.
a-modern-utopia:
H. G. Wells warns his reader at the start that the voice of this book is not quite his own. Two English travelers are lifted to a planet exactly like earth. A world state has been built there. A companion's voice argues with what they find. The contents promise chapters on freedoms, utopian economics, women, failure, and the Samurai.

The travelers inspect a society of world government, personal freedom within strict public rules, and a voluntary ruling order called the Samurai. Wells interrupts the story for essays whenever the argument needs room. He calls the book the last of the series begun by his Anticipations. It remains his fullest picture of the rational world he wanted, freedoms and severities alike.
a-prince-of-bohemia:
Honoré de Balzac frames his tale as a story told among friends, in a translation by Clara Bell and others. A lady draws a manuscript from beneath her sofa cushion and asks leave to make a story of something her friend once told her. The talk turns to the world of young artists and writers in Paris.

At its center stands a prince of Bohemia, a charming, penniless leader of the garret world, and the woman who loves him. Balzac sketches studios, cheap dinners, borrowed money, and fine talk with affection and irony. The dedication goes to Heinrich Heine, and the tale shares Heine's blend of jest, love, and truth about literary Paris.
a-short-history-of-russia: Mary Platt Parmele writes this short history of Russia as the history of a power rather than of a people, as her preface frankly warns. The Russian people, she argues, have had no history yet; only a vast governing system has evolved, wearing a splendid robe of Europeanism over an undeveloped mass. Natural obstacles, ethnic problems, joining the circle of great nations, and a disastrous conflict recently concluded, shape the story she tells.
a-truthful-woman-in-southern-california: Kate Sanborn writes a truthful account of Southern California in this volume, first copyrighted in 1893 and published in 1906. She resolves against soaring into romance or dropping into poetry, against idealizing or repeating prodigious stories. She will write the book she needed to read before travelling. Hints for the journey, Coronado Beach, San Diego, Los Angeles, Pasadena, camping on Mount Wilson, Riverside, and Santa Barbara follow in order.
a-voyage-to-abyssinia:
Father Jerónimo Lobo, a Portuguese Jesuit, tells of his mission to Abyssinia, in Samuel Johnson's translation from the French, printed here in the 1887 Cassell edition. The introduction gives Lobo's life: born in Lisbon in 1593, sent to India in 1621, and chosen in 1624 for the Abyssinian mission. The emperor there favored converting his kingdom to Catholicism.

Part one recounts the dangerous voyage by way of India, shipwreck, captivity, and hardship. Part two describes Abyssinia itself: its court, church, customs, rivers, and animals. The mission failed in the end, but Lobo's plain, curious account kept readers for centuries, and Johnson's English gives it extra polish.
britannica-1911-abbas-i-persia:
Abbas the First of Persia, called the Great, receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbas, son of Shah Mahommed, took the Persian throne in 1586 out of anarchy. Uzbeg raiders in Khorasan felt his first campaigns, beaten near Herat in 1597 and driven out.

Turkish wars fill the reign: Bassora won in 1605, Shirvan and Kurdistan ceded in 1611, Bagdad taken in 1623 after a year's siege. Ormuz fell from the Portuguese in 1622 with British help, and its trade moved to Bander-Abbasi, named for him. Roads, bridges, and trade reforms mark the peace work. Cruelty stains the record: his eldest son slain, other children blinded at his order. His realm ran Tigris to Indus at his death.
britannica-1911-abbazia:
Abbazia receives a resort entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Austrian town in Istria sits on the Gulf of Quarnero under Monte Maggiore, ringed by laurel woods. Some 16,000 visitors a year seek its mild air, fifty degrees in winter by the entry's count.

An old abbey, San Giacomo della Priluca, gives the place its name and now serves as a villa. Rocky, picturesque coast runs north and south, with smaller winter resorts strung along it. Lovrana, five miles south, is the largest of these. Rail joins Abbazia to Trieste, fifty-six miles off. Its 2,343 residents in 1900 lived by the season trade of health and leisure.
britannica-1911-abkhasia:
Abkhasia receives a tract entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The Russian Caucasia district in Kutais government runs from the Caucasus range to the Black Sea, with Mingrelia south-east. Mountains and oak and walnut forest cover most of it.

Deep watered valleys break the heights, and a mild climate grows wheat, maize, grapes, figs, and wine. Cattle, horses, honey, and fine arms fill the produce list. Justinian subdued the land about 550 and brought Christianity; native dynasties then ruled till the Turks made it Muslim in the fifteenth century. Russia took it in pieces from 1829, firm only after 1864. Sukhum-kaleh is the chief town. Some 43,000 folk, two-thirds Mingrelian, held the tract.
britannica-1911-abundantia:
Abundantia, meaning Abundance, was a Roman goddess who personified prosperity and good fortune. Modelled on the Greek Demeter, she was practically the same figure as Copia, Annona, and similar goddesses of plenty. The short Britannica entry treats her less as a goddess with myths of her own than as an image used by the state.

Coins carry her likeness. On coins of the later Roman emperors she often appears holding a cornucopia, the horn of plenty, shaking out her gifts. The picture also praised the emperor or empress for liberality. A later echo appears in Domina Abundia, a kind fairy of medieval French poems who brought plenty to households she visited.
britannica-1911-abydos-mysia:
Abydos in Mysia was an ancient city of Asia Minor at Nagara Point on the Hellespont, where the strait is scarcely a mile broad. Probably a Thracian town at first, it was later colonized by Milesians from Greece. Its position made it a crossing place and, until late Byzantine times, the toll station of the Hellespont.

Two stories dominate the short entry. Xerxes crossed the strait here on his bridge of boats when he invaded Greece. Abydos also resisted Philip V of Macedon fiercely in 200 B.C., and story made it famous as the home of Leander, who swam the strait to Hero. Its importance later passed to the Dardanelles.
britannica-1911-acacia:
Acacia is a genus of shrubs and trees in the legume family, with small flowers in rounded or elongated clusters and compound leaves. About four hundred and fifty species spread across the warmer regions of the globe, abounding in Australia and Africa. In many Australian species the leaflets vanish and flattened leaf-stalks do the leaves' work, turning edge-on to strong sunlight.

Useful products fill much of the entry. True gum-arabic comes from Acacia senegal, catechu medicine from Acacia catechu, and tannin-rich barks from Indian babul and Australian wattles serve tanners. Timber species include Australian blackwood and myall wood. Some acacias bear fierce spines, and Central American bull-thorn acacias shelter ants that defend the plant in return for food.
britannica-1911-acarnania:
Acarnania was a district of ancient Greece on the Ionian Sea, bounded by the Ambracian Gulf, Mount Thyamus, and the river Achelous. Its richest ground was the Achelous plain, commanded by the town of Stratus, though mountains and lagoons cut the coast off from the interior. Its people long lived in semi-barbarism, with little contact with the rest of Greece.

History moves through stronger neighbours. Athens helped the Acarnanians subdue Corinthian posts on their coast, then Sparta and Thebes held them in turn. Their cantonal league, modelled on Aetolia, allied with Philip V of Macedon against Rome, and Rome punished that loyalty by taking Leucas. Augustus finally emptied the land, drafting its people into Nicopolis and Patrae.
britannica-1911-acca-larentia:
Acca Larentia stands in Roman legend as the wife of the shepherd Faustulus, who saved the twins Romulus and Remus after they were thrown into the Tiber. She had twelve sons, and when one died Romulus took his place and founded the college of the Arval brothers with the other eleven. One tradition explains the wolf that suckled the twins by saying Larentia herself was nicknamed lupa, she-wolf.

Another account makes her a beautiful girl won by Hercules at dice, who married a rich Etruscan, inherited his property, and left it to the Roman people. Rome honoured her with the yearly Larentalia festival each December. Some writers made her a symbol of the earth's fertility.
britannica-1911-accoramboni-vittoria:
Vittoria Accoramboni (1557-1585) was an Italian lady famous for her beauty, her accomplishments, and a tragic history that reads like a stage plot. Born in Rome to a family of the minor nobility of Gubbio, she was betrothed to Francesco Peretti, nephew of Cardinal Montalto. Admirers crowded around her, debts mounted, and her brother Marcello had Peretti murdered so she could marry the powerful duke of Bracciano.

Marriage brought flight, not safety. When Montalto became Pope Sixtus V he vowed vengeance, and the couple fled to Venetian territory, where the duke died. Vittoria retired to Padua, and there Lodovico Orsini had her assassinated in a quarrel over property. Her story later fed Webster's drama and Tieck's novel.
britannica-1911-adalia:
Adalia is the largest seaport on Asia Minor's south coast. Its ancient name was Attalia. Crusaders called it Satalia. Trade now ranks it second to Mersina, though. Its harbour suits modern steamers badly. Anchorage outside the harbour is poor too. Railways from Smyrna drew trade away. No good road links it outward. Yet it administers a rich, isolated district.

Medieval history fills much of the entry. Louis VII's army sailed from Adalia in 1148. Richard of England's fleet rallied there. Seljuks made it capital of Tekke province. Venetians and Genoese held it in turn. Ottoman Turks took it finally under Murad II. Dere Beys ruled it in fact for centuries. About twenty-five thousand people live there now.
britannica-1911-agonalia:
Agonalia were festivals of ancient Rome. Four dates in the year carried them. January the ninth was one festival day. March the seventeenth and May the twenty-first followed. December the eleventh closed the year's set. Various divinities received honour at these festivals. Ovid's Fasti is the entry's cited source. His poem covers the Roman calendar in verse.

Word origin gets the remaining space. Agonalia may derive from agonia, a victim. It may derive from agonium, a festival, instead. The entry gives both derivations without choosing. Readers learn the calendar facts plainly here. Four annual festivals shared one name. Their honoured gods varied by the date. A sacrifice word or a festival word explains the title.
britannica-1911-agrionia:
A grim tale sits behind the Agrionia, a yearly Greek feast for Dionysus Agrionius kept at Orchomenus in Boeotia and in other places. Women and priests marked it after dark. For a while the women made a game of hunting for the god, then stopped and said he had taken shelter among the Muses.

Custom linked the rite to the daughters of Minyas, king of Orchomenus. They had scorned the god's worship, the story runs, and madness seized them until they ate the flesh of one of their own children. In the earliest days the priest chased a woman of the Minyan house with sword drawn and slew her, a real killing inside the rite.
britannica-1911-agroteras-thusia:
Agroteras Thusia, an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, records a yearly festival held at Agrae near Athens. It honoured Artemis Agrotera, the huntress form of the goddess. The festival kept a vow the city made before the battle of Marathon. Athens had promised the goddess one goat for every Persian killed in the coming fight.

So many Persians fell that paying the vow in full proved impossible. The city settled instead on offering 500 goats every year, and the rite continued on that scale. Short as the entry is, it names its authorities at the close. They include Plutarch, Xenophon in the Anabasis, Aelian, and a note on a play by Aristophanes, giving readers the ancient sources behind the custom.
britannica-1911-albufera-de-valencia:
Albufera de Valencia is a shallow sheet of water seven miles south of Valencia in Spain, some twelve miles long and four wide, and nowhere more than twelve feet deep. A slim outlet ties it to the sea, and men can open or shut that channel at will. The Crown owns the lagoon.

Fish and wild birds crowd its waters, and that wealth gives the lake its worth. Shore villages plant rice in bulk in the wet soil all around. War fixed the name in men's minds in 1812, when Napoleon made Marshal Suchet duke of Albufera for taking Valencia and granted him the estate. The loss at Vittoria in 1813 stripped Suchet of the land, though the title stayed his. Later the duke of Wellington received the lagoon's income, as a sign of Spanish thanks.
britannica-1911-albuminuria:
Albuminuria, a medical term, is explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It means the presence of albumin, a protein, in the urine. Kidney trouble, acute illness, and venous congestion can all cause it. Yet many cases appear in people who seem in perfect health, once every known disease cause is ruled out. That form is called functional or physiological albuminuria.

Telling that harmless form apart from the albuminuria of Bright's disease is extremely important, the entry stresses. Several kinds are described. Dietetic albuminuria follows meals heavy in albuminous foods such as eggs, or any over-indulgence at table. Cyclic, or postural, albuminuria appears at certain hours of the day in healthy people. It depends entirely on standing upright, and it disappears when the person lies down at night. Exercise forms a third heading in the entry's account.
britannica-1911-algeria:
Algeria, a country of North Africa belonging to France, is covered by one of the longest entries in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is bounded north by the Mediterranean, west by Morocco, south by the Sahara, and east by Tunisia. The country runs about 650 miles along the coast and stretches 320 to 380 miles inland. Politically it forms three departments: Oran, Algiers, and Constantine.

Excluding the dependent Saharan regions, Algeria covers 184,474 square miles. Its coast is severe and inhospitable, with high mountains rising almost sheer from the sea between Dellys and Philippeville. Government, the entry's later sections stress, depends entirely on the will of France. The French chambers alone hold legislative power, and Algeria sends three senators and six deputies to Paris. The franchise is confined to citizens, a restriction the article records without softening.
britannica-1911-anna-amalia:
Anna Amalia (1739–1807) was duchess of Saxe-Weimar. She was born at Wolfenbüttel in October 1739. Her father was Charles I of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. She married Duke Ernest of Saxe-Weimar in 1756. He died only two years later. She became regent for her infant son. Charles Augustus was that son's name. Her regency lasted through his long minority.

She governed with the greatest prudence. The Seven Years' War troubled her duchy. She still strengthened its resources and position. Art and literature flourished under her patronage. Wieland tutored her son at Weimar. Herder, Goethe, and Schiller graced her court. She retired when her son came of age in 1775. In 1788 she toured Italy with Goethe. She died in April 1807. Goethe memorialised her in his works.
britannica-1911-annapolis-nova-scotia:
Annapolis is a town of Nova Scotia, Canada. It is the capital of Annapolis county. Until 1750 it governed the whole peninsula. The town stands on the Bay of Fundy. The Annapolis river meets the bay there. Halifax lies ninety-five miles east. A railway terminates at the town. Its population in 1901 was 1,019. French settlers founded it in 1604.

The French called it Port Royal. It is among North America's oldest settlements. British forces captured it in 1710. The treaty of Utrecht ceded it in 1713. Its new name honoured Queen Anne. A good harbour serves the town. Beautiful surrounding country attracts summer visitors. Apple orchards ring the settlement. May blossom covers miles of trees. Excellent fruit is the region's principal export.
britannica-1911-anne-empress-of-russia:
Anne (1693–1740) was empress of Russia. She was the second daughter of Tsar Ivan V. Ivan was Peter the Great's brother. Her mother was Praskovia Saltuikova. The girlhood home was Ismailovo near Moscow. Her mother neglected and even hated her daughters. Peter acted as second father to the family. In 1710 he married Anne to Courland's duke. Frederick William died on his journey home.

The reluctant widow governed Courland from Mittau. Her revenue was utterly inadequate there. Count Bestuzhev advised her as Russian resident. Biren later supplanted him in her favour. Peter II died in January 1730. The supreme privy council offered Anne the crown. She subscribed nine limiting articles beforehand. Those articles would have reduced her power greatly. Her public entry into Moscow followed in February. The entry follows her repudiation of those limits.
britannica-1911-ararat-victoria:
Ararat is a municipal town in Victoria, Australia. It lies in Ripon county. Melbourne is 130 miles east by rail. Population in 1901 was 3,580. The town sits 1,028 feet high. The Great Dividing Range ends near it. Ararat is the district's commercial centre. The north-western grain and wool district trades there. Gold also made the town notable.

Quartz and alluvial gold-mines operate nearby. Excellent wine is produced locally. Flour-milling leads the town's manufactures. Leather-working, brickmaking, and candle making follow. Soap-boiling is another listed industry. The district yields fine timber abundantly. Granite and bluestone abound in the neighbourhood. Limestone and slate also occur there. The entry is a compact gazetteer notice. It suits a mining and farming service town.
britannica-1911-araucania:
Araucania was a large territory of Chile. It lies south of the Bio-bio river. The Araucanian Indians held it at their independence. Spanish authority never subdued them early. Chilean authority came only later. Loss of political independence followed for them. Most of their territory was lost too. Chile divided it into four provinces.

Those provinces are Arauco and Bio-bio. Malleco and Cautin complete the four. The Indians are much reduced in number now. They live in wooded recesses of three provinces. The entry is a short cross-reference notice. It points readers to the Araucanians article below. That article carries the people's own history. This notice merely fixes the territory's fate. It frames the longer ethnographic account that follows.
britannica-1911-araucaria:
Araucaria is a genus of coniferous trees. The trees are magnificent evergreens. Their branches appear in whorls. Their leaves are stiff, flattened, and pointed. Brazil and Chile host the genus. Polynesia and Australia host species too. The name derives from Arauco in Chile. Trees were first discovered in that district. Araucaria imbricata is the Chile pine.

Monkey puzzle is its popular name. Britain received it in 1796. It usually survives British winters outdoors. Severe cold years have damaged trees, though. Elevated, well-drained spots suit planting best. In Chile it reaches 150 feet. Its cones are broad and long. Its wood is hard and durable. The Brazil pine is less hardy. It needs conservatory protection in Britain. Norfolk Island pine is described last. Cook compared its columnar trunk to basalt.
britannica-1911-arcadia:
Arcadia is a district of Greece. It forms the Peloponnesus's central plateau. Mountain barriers shut it off from coasts. Erymanthus rises 7,400 feet in the north. Cyllene reaches 7,900 feet nearby. Southern peaks exceed 5,000 feet. Subsidiary ranges divide the plateau further. Eastern Arcadia is called locked Arcadia. Parallel heights enclose upland plains there. Their waters escape only underground.

Western Arcadia is more open country. Isolated mountain groups dot it. The Alpheus river drains it complexly. Ladon and Erymanthus feed that river. Ancient inhabitants were shepherds and huntsmen. They worshipped Pan, Hermes, and Artemis. Those were primitive nature deities. Poor communications hindered Greek intercourse. The same population held the land throughout history. No Dorian admixture changed it. Freeman's Federal Government treats its ancient league.
britannica-1911-archelaus-king-of-macedo:
Archelaus was king of Macedonia from 413 to 399 B.C. He was Perdiccas's son by a slave mother. Murder gained him the throne. He killed his uncle and cousin. He also killed his half-brother, the legitimate heir. He nevertheless proved a capable, beneficent ruler. He fortified cities across his kingdom. He constructed roads throughout it. He organised the army thoroughly.

Greek civilisation's refinements attracted him strongly. He spread them among his people deliberately. He moved his court from Aegae to Pella. Celebrated men received his invitations there. Zeuxis the painter came to court. Timotheus the musician came too. Euripides and Agathon completed the famous list. In 399 a favourite killed him while hunting. Another account blames a conspiracy instead. Diodorus and Thucydides are the cited sources.
britannica-1911-archelaus-of-cappadocia:
Two crushing defeats mark Archelaus of Cappadocia's war for Mithradates the Great against Rome. At Chaeroneia in 86 B.C. he was utterly beaten; a fresh army from Mithradates only brought a second loss at Orchomenus in 85, after two days of battle. Peace followed, and with it suspicion: Mithradates took him for a traitor, so Archelaus fled first to the Romans, who welcomed him at Rome.

The campaign had opened in 87 B.C., when he brought a large army and fleet to Greece and took the Peiraeus after three days' fighting. Bruttius Sura checked him there at first; then Sulla shut him in by siege, and pressure drove him back into Boeotia. Nothing more is known of Archelaus himself. His son briefly became king of Egypt, and a grandson later ruled Cappadocia. Strabo and Appian anchor the references.
britannica-1911-austrasia:
Austrasia was the eastern part of the Frankish kingdom. Its name means realm of the east. German Ost Reich explains that meaning. Gregory of Tours uses the word vaguely. Its sense gradually defined itself over time. Metz was usually its capital city. Its inhabitants were called the Austrasii. Later historians apply the name retrospectively. Theuderich I's kingdom receives it first.

Theudebert and Theudebald follow in that usage. Sigebert's kingdom after 561 bears it too. Childebert's kingdom continues the line. Historians read Brunhilda and Fredegond's struggle through it. They frame it as Neustria against Austrasia. Precise textual usage comes later, though. Clotaire II entrusted Austrasia to Dagobert in 623. Pippin and Arnulf guarded the young king. Dagobert handed it to Sigebert in 634. Pfister signs this careful Frankish survey.
britannica-1911-aveia:
Aveia was an ancient town of the Vestini in Italy, on the Via Claudia Nova, six miles south-east of Aquila and north-east of the modern village of Fossa. Some remains of old buildings survive, and the name still clings to the place, the entry reports.

Identification of the site came from V. M. Giovenazzi's 1773 work on Aveia among the Vestini. Paintings in the church of Santa Maria ad Cryptas, from the 12th to 15th centuries, matter for art history. A 3rd-century inscription found in 1902 records a stationarius, a soldier sent on special duty, no doubt against brigandage in the district.
britannica-1911-awadia-and-fadnia:
Awadia and Fadnia are two small nomad tribes of pure Arab blood living in the Bayuda desert of the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, between the wells of Jakdul and Metemma. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry is short, and warns that they are often wrongly classed as Ja'alin.

Both tribes own many horses and cattle, their horses being of the black Dongola breed. At the battle of Abu Klea on 17 January 1885 they won notice for courage, riding against the British square. That single fight carries the entry's judgment of their character. Readers wanting more are sent to Count Gleichen's 1905 work on the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan.
britannica-1911-ayuthia:
Ayuthia is a city of Siam, known to the Siamese as Krung Kao, the Old Capital, where the river Me Nam breaks into creeks around a large island. About 10,000 people live there, most in floating houses moored along the creeks that serve as streets.

On the island stand the ruins of the city that was Siam's capital for over four centuries: palaces, pagodas, churches, and walls recorded by the first European travellers. Burmese armies destroyed it twice, in 1555 and in 1767, after which it stopped being the capital. Today it ships great loads of rice paddi to Bangkok, keeps an elephant-catching enclosure still in use, and heads one of Siam's richest farming divisions.
britannica-1911-bacchanalia:
Bacchanalia was the Latin name for the wild, mystic festivals of Bacchus, the Roman Dionysus. Brought into Rome from lower Italy by way of Etruria, they were held in secret, for women only, on three days a year in a grove near the Aventine hill.

Later, men were admitted and meetings grew to five a month. Their evil fame, with tales of debauchery, crime, and political plotting, moved the senate in 186 B.C. to ban the rites across Italy, allowing them only by special leave under limits. That decree survives on a bronze tablet found in Calabria and now kept at Vienna. Heavy punishments still failed to stamp the festivals out in southern Italy for a long time.
britannica-1911-bactria:
Bactria, or Bactriana, was the ancient land between the Hindu Kush range and the Oxus river, with its capital at Bactra, now Balkh. Mountainous, well watered, and very fertile, it formed the eastern part of Iran and held one of the Iranian tribes.

Tradition ties Bactria to Zoroaster, who likely preached there first. The entry warns against calling the Avesta's language old Bactrian. That term has no good ground and is now dropped. It also rejects the once popular idea that Bactria cradled the Indo-European race. Iranian myth set many hero tales in the east. Later writers inflated them into a great old Bactrian empire. The entry treats that empire as a late reflection of real Persian empires.
britannica-1911-baden-austria:
Baden is a town and watering-place of lower Austria, seventeen miles south of Vienna by rail, beautifully set at the mouth of the Helenenthal valley on the Schwechat river. Its 12,447 people host some 20,000 visitors a year as the capital's chief summer resort.

Thirteen warm springs, from 72 to 97 degrees, rich in sulphate of lime, gave the town its very name, Baths; fifteen bathing houses serve them. Romans knew the place as Thermae Pannonicae. Ruined castles, Rauheneck and Rauhenstein, guard the valley. The Vienna waterworks aqueduct strides across it. Up the valley lies Mayerling. That hunting lodge is where Crown Prince Rudolph was found dead in 1889. Imperial family villas dot the town.
britannica-1911-bagheria:
Bagheria is a town of the province of Palermo in Sicily, eight miles east by south of Palermo by rail. Its population in 1901 was 18,218, a large town by the measure of its neighbours. What sets it apart in this short entry is not trade or history but houses.

Bagheria holds many villas of the Palermo aristocracy, great houses raised mostly in the 18th century when the nobles built their summer seats within easy reach of the capital. By the time of the entry most had fallen into decay, their glory faded with their owners' fortunes. Town, rail distance, population, and that ring of decaying villas: the record is complete in four short facts.
britannica-1911-baldwin-i-emperor-of-rom:
Baldwin I (died 1205), count of Flanders and Hainaut, was a leading figure of the Fourth Crusade. That campaign took Constantinople and founded the Latin empire of Romania. Offered first to the doge of Venice, who refused it, the imperial crown went to Baldwin, elected on 9 May 1204.

The 1911 Britannica entry describes an empire run on feudal lines, with Baldwin holding Constantinople, lands on both shores nearby, and islands such as Lemnos, Lesbos, Chios, and Tenos. Much land still had to be won. His push into Thrace and toward Thessalonica brought him into clash with Boniface of Montferrat, his rival for the crown.
britannica-1911-baldwin-ii-emperor-of-ro:
Baldwin II (1217–1273) was the last emperor of Romania, the Latin empire set up at Constantinople. A younger son of Yolande, sister of Baldwin I, he came to the throne in 1228 at the age of eleven, after the death of his brother Robert. John of Brienne was chosen as regent for life.

By the time Baldwin ruled alone, his realm was little more than Constantinople itself, and Greek power was gaining ground. The 1911 Britannica entry shows a life spent begging at the courts of Europe for money and men. Trips west in 1236 and 1245 raised troops, yet he could not win back the lost lands.
britannica-1911-baluchistan-persia:
Persian Baluchistan is a province of Persia, forming the western part of the wider region of Baluchistan. It covers about 60,000 square miles along the north shore of the Arabian Sea. British and independent Baluchistan bound it on the east, Seistan and the central Persian desert on the north, and Kerman on the west.

Water is scarce, and only a small part of the land is farmed. The rest is dry plains, stony or sandy desert, and bare hills. The 1911 Britannica entry lists twenty districts under Kerman's administration, from Bampur to Makran on the coast. Rivers such as the Mashkid run inland and die in salt flats rather than reach the sea.
britannica-1911-bandini-angelo-maria:
Angelo Maria Bandini (1726–1800) was an Italian author, born at Florence on 25 September 1726. Orphaned in infancy, he was raised by his uncle Giuseppe, a lawyer of note, and educated among the Jesuits. From the start his bent ran to antiquities, and his first work, in 1749, treated ancient dances.

A trip to Vienna as secretary to the bishop of Volterra brought him before the emperor, to whom he dedicated a specimen of Florentine literature. Taking orders, he settled at Rome and worked in the Vatican library and the libraries of cardinals. The 1911 Britannica entry highlights his learned folio on the newly dug-up obelisk of Augustus, and his later post as librarian of the Marucelli library at Florence.
britannica-1911-bartet-jeanne-julia:
Jeanne Julia Bartet (1854– ), a French actress born in Paris under the name Regnault, is the subject of a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. She trained at the Paris Conservatoire, the national school for music and drama. In 1872 she began a successful career at the Vaudeville theatre. Seven years later, in 1879, she was engaged by the Comédie Française, and in 1880 she became a sociétaire, a full member of that company.

Leading parts kept Bartet at the centre of the French stage for many years. She played the chief roles in both tragedy and comedy. The entry praises her grand style and her fine, exact touch, calling her supreme among the younger actresses of her time in France. A London season in 1908 let English audiences judge for themselves, when she showed her art, the entry says, in a number of different parts.
britannica-1911-bastia:
Bastia is a town and seaport on the eastern coast of Corsica, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as the island's chief port. It lies ninety-eight miles north-north-east of Ajaccio by rail and held 24,509 people in 1906. The old port quarter is dense, a maze of steep, narrow streets, while a more modern quarter has grown around the new port to the north. Rising from the shore like an amphitheatre, the town is dominated by a citadel with a 14th-century keep.

Trade fills the working portrait. Bastia was the seat of courts for the whole island, of the military governor, and of a chamber of commerce. It also had a lycée and a library of up to 40,000 volumes. Its new port offered 1100 feet of quay; 721 vessels entered in 1907. Exports included chestnut extract, citrons, oranges, fish, and copper and antimony ores.
britannica-1911-batrachomyomachia:
Batrachomyomachia is a Greek title built from the words for frog, mouse, and battle, and the poem it names is set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The “Battle of Frogs and Mice” is a comic epic, a parody of Homer's Iliad. Small pond and field creatures fight the grand war of heroes in mock form. 

Who wrote it is left in doubt. The Romans flatly gave the poem to Homer himself. Plutarch, in his work on Herodotus, named instead Pigres of Halicarnassus, the brother or son of Artemisia, queen of Caria and ally of Xerxes.
