Some modern scholars of the entry's day set both claims aside. They gave the poem to an unnamed poet of the time of Alexander the Great. An edition by A. Ludwich, from 1896, is listed at the end.
britannica-1911-battaglia:
Battaglia is a town of Venetia, Italy, in the province of Padua, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies eleven miles south-south-west of Padua by rail, and its people numbered 4456 in 1901. The town stands at the edge of the volcanic Euganean Hills, the old cone-shaped hills that rise from the plain south-west of Padua. 

Warm water made the town's name. Battaglia is famed for its warm saline springs, springs of salty water rising warm from the ground, and for a natural vapour grotto, a cave full of warm steam. A fine palace in the Palladian style was built in the 1600s by the Marchese Benedetto Selvatico-Estense. He then owned the springs, and his palace showed the wealth those healing waters brought.
britannica-1911-berkeley-california:
Berkeley is a city of Alameda county, California, on the east shore of San Francisco Bay. It takes its name from Bishop Berkeley, for his line “Westward the course of empire takes its way.” Its people leapt from 5,101 in 1890 to 40,434 by 1910.

Two transcontinental railways and electric lines to San Francisco and Oakland serve the city, seven miles across the bay from San Francisco. Its outlooks make it a favoured home suburb. Berkeley’s heart is the University of California, opened there in 1873, ringed by theological schools of several churches and the state institution for the deaf, dumb and blind. Farms covered the site until the university was planted on it in the years before 1873.
britannica-1911-bernicia:
Bernicia was the northern of two English kingdoms later joined as Northumbria. Its land ran from the Tyne northward, in time reaching the Forth. Its western border grew at Welsh expense. The chief royal seat was Bamburgh, near the island of Lindisfarne. The first recorded king is Ida, said to have taken the throne about 547.

The 1911 Britannica entry gives the kingdom a short, dense outline. Æthelfrith of Bernicia united Deira to his realm about 605. The union held under his successor Edwin. Bernicia split from Deira again under Eanfrith in 633 to 634. After that date its kings ruled supreme in Northumbria. Bede, Nennius, and Simeon of Durham are the cited sources.
britannica-1911-bestia:
Bestia was the name of a family in ancient Rome. The 1911 Britannica article treats its best-known members in turn. First comes Lucius Calpurnius Bestia, tribune in 121 BC and consul in 111. Sent against Jugurtha in Numidia, he campaigned hard at first. Then, heavily bribed, he made a disgraceful peace. On his return to Rome he stood trial and was condemned. Sallust and Cicero still rated his abilities highly.

A second Bestia appears in the Catiline conspiracy story. He was to give a signal for revolt, but the plot was crushed first. A third, an aedile who sought the praetorship in 57 BC, faced a bribery charge. Cicero defended him, yet he was condemned all the same. In 43 BC he joined Antony's party, hoping for the consulship. Ancient sources cited include Sallust, Appian, and Cicero's letters.
britannica-1911-bithynia:
Bithynia was an ancient district in the north-west of Asia Minor. It adjoined the Propontis, the Thracian Bosporus, and the Euxine, or Black Sea. The river Sangarius bounded it east by the commoner reckoning, or the Parthenius further east. The Rhyndacus split it from Mysia on the west. Mountains and forests cover much of its ground. Fertile valleys and coastal districts break up that rough land. The Mysian Olympus, 7,600 feet high, towers above Brusa.

Snow caps that summit for much of the year, and it can be seen from Constantinople, 70 miles off. The Ala-Dagh range runs east for over 100 miles from the Sangarius. The 1911 Britannica article traces the land's history under its own kings. Nicomedes I founded Nicomedia, which rose to great prosperity. Chalcedon, Heraclea Pontica, and Prusa are named among its trading cities. Ismid and Scutari hold their places in the modern map.
britannica-1911-boiardo-matteo-maria:
Matteo Maria Boiardo (1434–1494), count of Scandiano, was an Italian court poet of Ferrara and the author of Orlando Inamorato. Born at Scandiano near Reggio, he studied at Ferrara and learned Greek, Latin, and even Oriental tongues, taking degrees in philosophy and law. Dukes Borso and Hercules d'Este favoured him with high posts.

He served as governor of Reggio in 1478 and captain of Modena three years later, and he died at Reggio in 1494. Most of his verse was written to please the Ferrara court, composed away on his own estates. The great poem is praised as the first romantic epic fit to serve as a model, the seed of Ariosto's Orlando Furioso. Its matter came from the old Charlemagne tales, not from Homer, the entry argues.
britannica-1911-bolivar-colombia:
Bolívar was, until 1908, a department of Colombia on the Caribbean coast, and the entry gives its bounds and make-up. The sea bordered it north and west, Magdalena and Santander lay east, and Antioquia and Cauca south. Its area was 27,028 square miles, much of it low, wet, thickly wooded plain.

That plain was thinly farmed and ill-suited, the entry says, to labour by north Europeans. The people, put at 323,097 in 1899, were largely of mixed race, in some parts four-fifths of the whole. Cartagena, the capital, had once been Colombia's chief trading port. Other towns named are Barranquilla and Mompox on the Magdalena river, and Corozal and Lorica near the western coast.
britannica-1911-boothia:
Boothia, or Boothia Felix, is a peninsula of British North America in the Franklin district, covering 13,100 square miles. It lies between about 69 and 72 degrees north. Its Murchison Point is the northernmost point of the American mainland. Captain James Ross found it on his expedition of 1829–1833 and named it for Sir Felix Booth, who had chiefly paid for the voyage.

Boothia forms the west side of Boothia Gulf and is nearly cut off from the continent by lakes and inlets, with Bellot Strait between it and North Somerset Island. The peninsula matters in the Franklin search story, and in science too. On its western shore Ross first fixed the place of the north magnetic pole, at 70 degrees 5 minutes north, 96 degrees 47 minutes west.
britannica-1911-brieg-silesia:
Brieg is a German town in the Prussian province of Silesia, on the left bank of the Oder 27 miles south-east of Breslau. Its people numbered 24,090 in 1900. A castle of the old counts, a lunatic asylum, a gymnasium with a good library, churches, hospitals and a theatre mark it out. Old walls pulled down by the French in 1807 have given place to fine promenades.

Trade is brisk, with linen, embroidery, cotton and woollen goods, ribbons, leather, machines, hats, pasteboard and cigars among its makes, plus large cattle markets. Town rights came in 1250 from Duke Henry III of Breslau, and the name derives from the Polish Brzeg, meaning shore. Hussites burned it in 1428, war hurt it again and again, and French and Bavarian troops took it in 1807. From 1311 to 1675 it was capital of its own line of dukes.
britannica-1911-brighton-australia:
Brighton in Australia is a watering-place in Bourke county, Victoria, 7 and a half miles by rail south-east of Melbourne, and in practice a suburb of that city. It stands on the east shore of Port Phillip, the great bay on which Melbourne also sits. Seaside use, not trade or farming, defines the place in the short notice.

Two piers reach into the bay, a long stretch of sandy beach draws visitors, and rows of handsome villas house its residents and holiday guests. The count for 1901 gives 10,029 people, a large figure for a resort suburb of the day. Those few facts, position, piers, beach, villas and population, make up the whole of the brief gazetteer entry.
britannica-1911-bristol-pennsylvania:
Bristol is a borough of Bucks county, Pennsylvania, on the Delaware river opposite Burlington, New Jersey, 20 miles north-east of Philadelphia. Its people numbered 6553 in 1890, 7104 in 1900 and 9256 in 1910, served by the Pennsylvania railway. Level ground a few feet above the river holds the town amid attractive farming country.

Mill Street holds the chief business houses while Radcliffe Street runs along the river. Machine shops, rolling mills, a planing mill, yarn, hosiery and worsted mills, and factories for carpets, wall paper and patent leather make up its works. Just outside the borough, Bath Springs still draw notice for chalybeate waters famed early in the 18th century. Bristol was among the first places settled after William Penn received his charter in 1681, served as county seat until 1725, was laid out in 1697 and incorporated in 1720.
britannica-1911-brunswick-georgia:
Brunswick is a city and county-seat of Glynn county, Georgia. A port of entry, on St Simon Sound about 12 miles from the Atlantic Ocean and about 100 miles south of Savannah. Its people numbered 8459 in 1890, 9081 in 1900, of whom 5184 were of negro descent, and 10,182 in 1910. Three railways and coastal steamboat lines serve the port.

The federal government dredged a channel in the inner harbour 21 feet deep at mean low water and one across the outer bar 19.3 feet deep, with a tidal rise of 7.2 feet. St Simon Island and Jekyl Island, a winter resort of wealthy men, shelter the harbour from the ocean. Growth has been slowed by the rivalry of other cities, notably Savannah. Export trade is considerable, chiefly in lumber, cross-ties and naval stores, valued at 13,387,838 dollars in 1908, with planing mills, cooperage works and oyster canneries among its factories. Settled about 1772, it received a city charter later.
britannica-1911-caledonia:
Caledonia was the Roman name for North Britain. It is still used, chiefly in poetry, for Scotland. This 1911 Britannica article traces the name and the Roman wars there. The name appears first in the poet Lucan, about A.D. 64. It named a district north of the Clyde and Forth isthmus. It also named a forest and a tribe, the Caledones.

The Romans first invaded under Agricola, about A.D. 83. They fortified the Forth and Clyde line with forts. They pushed into Perthshire and fought at Mons Graupius. Tacitus claims a victory on those slopes. Rome then recalled Agricola and gave up his conquests. About A.D. 140 a new advance annexed land up to the Forth. The Wall of Antoninus Pius was drawn across the isthmus. The article weighs the fort sites and the contested battle site. Inchtuthill is offered as the likely camp of Agricola's army.
britannica-1911-capodistria:
Capodistria is a town and seaport of Austria, in Istria. It lies 15 miles south-west of Trieste by rail. Its population in 1900 was 10,711, mostly Italians. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town and its past. It stands on a small island at a bay's end. A causeway half a mile long joins it to the mainland. The old town keeps narrow streets and a Venetian air.

The cathedral, town hall and Loggia stand in the main square. Salt works near the town draw salt from the sea. Fishing and shipbuilding employ many people as well. Trade runs chiefly in sea-salt, wine and oil. The town is usually linked with Pliny's Aegida. In the 6th century it took the name Justinopolis, from Justin II. Its present name means the capital of Istria. Venice captured it in 1279, and Austria gained it in 1797.
britannica-1911-cappadocia:
Cappadocia was an inland district of ancient Asia Minor. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys its land and history. In Herodotus' time its people held a vast region. It ran from Mount Taurus to the Black Sea. The Persians called them Katpatouka, the entry says. The Greeks called them Syrians, or White Syrians. Later Persian rule split the land into two governments.

One part kept the name Cappadocia for Greek writers. The other became known simply as Pontus. The split was fixed before Xenophon's time. After Persia fell, the two provinces stayed apart. This article treats the inland province alone. It was sometimes called Great Cappadocia. The Taurus chain bounded it to the south. The Euphrates bounded it to the east. Pontus lay north, and the salt desert west. The article gives its true size against Strabo's larger figures. It then treats towns, roads, kings and Roman rule.
britannica-1911-capraia:
Capraia is an island of Italy, off its north-west coast. Its ancient name was Capraria, from the Latin for wild-goat. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives its facts. The island belongs to the province of Genoa. It lies 42 miles south-south-east of Leghorn by sea. Its highest point is 1466 feet above the sea. Its population in 1901 was 547. The island is of volcanic origin.

Part of Capraia holds a penal agricultural colony. The island produces wine for its living. It is also a centre of the anchovy fishery. Genoa took the island in 1527, and fortified it strongly. In 1796 Nelson occupied it for a short time. The entry adds a note on a neighbour island. Gorgona lies about 20 miles to the north. Its highest point is 836 feet. It is famous for its anchovies, like Capraia itself.
britannica-1911-capua-campania:
Capua is a town of Campania, in southern Italy. It stands in the province of Caserta. It lies 7 miles west of the town of Caserta by rail. Its population in 1901 was 14,285. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the modern town. It is an archiepiscopal see of the church. Bishop Landulf founded it in 856, after a disaster. The Saracens had destroyed the ancient Capua in 840.

The new town rose on the site of Casilinum. It took only the south bank of the river. Its cathedral of San Stefano also dates from 856. It has a handsome atrium and a tall Lombard bell-tower. Ancient granite columns stand in both structures. The Romanesque crypt below has been restored with care. It holds a fine paschal candlestick. An Exultet roll and a bound gospel book survive too. In 1232 Frederick II built a castle by the bridge.
britannica-1911-caracal-rumania:
Caracal is a town of Rumania, in eastern Europe. It is the capital of the department of Romanatzi. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives its facts. The town stands in plains between two rivers. They are the lower reaches of the Jiu and the Olt. A railway runs beside it from Corabia, on the Danube. The line runs on to Hermannstadt in Transylvania. Its population in 1900 was 12,055.

Caracal has little trade, the entry says. Grain is the one real exception to that rule. Its chief buildings are the prefecture and a school. That school teaches arts and crafts to the town. Several churches also stand in the town. Ruins of a tower survive from Roman times. The emperor Caracalla built it in A.D. 217. The town takes its name from that emperor. In 1596 Michael the Brave beat the Turks near Caracal.
britannica-1911-caria:
Caria was an ancient district of Asia Minor. It lay in the south-west of the peninsula. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys its coast and history. Ionia and Lydia bounded it on the north. The Aegean Sea washed its west and south. Lycia and a part of Phrygia lay to the east. Its coast is a chain of headlands and deep inlets.

The Ceramic Gulf runs inland for 70 miles. It ends between Myndus and Cape Krio. North of it lies the Gulf of Iasus. The Maeander river has silted up the old Latmic Gulf into a lake. South of Cape Krio lies the Gulf of Doris. The bay of Marmarice, a fine modern harbour, comes next. Almost the whole of Caria is mountainous, the article says. Cadmus and Salbacum are its two great masses. Both belong to the Taurus chain that crosses Asia Minor.
britannica-1911-carlisle-pennsylvania:
Carlisle is a borough of Cumberland county, Pennsylvania. It is the county-seat of that county. It stands 18 miles west by south of Harrisburg. Philadelphia lies 118 miles to the east by south of it. Its population was 7620 in 1890. It rose to 9626 in 1900 and 10,303 in 1910. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the borough and its schools.

The borough sits in the fertile Cumberland Valley. The valley is 12 miles wide at that point. Two railways serve the town and its farms. Dickinson College stands in Carlisle, founded in 1783. Presbyterians founded it, and John Dickinson gave it his name. It was reorganized as a Methodist Episcopal college in 1833. President Buchanan and Chief Justice Taney were its graduates. Metzger College for young ladies also stands there. A famous United States Indian industrial school opened in 1879.
britannica-1911-cartagena-colombia:
Cartagena is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a city and seaport in Colombia, South America, the capital of the department of Bolívar. It stands on the Caribbean coast, and its population was officially estimated at 14,000 in 1905. The mean yearly temperature is 82 degrees, and the port had a name for being very unhealthful, above all for newcomers. Well-off residents kept country houses on the cooler Turbaco hills.

The harbour is the best on the north coast of South America. Two long islands lying parallel to the mainland shut in a bay of about 62.5 square miles, giving deep and safe anchorages. Large vessels could not reach the city landing stages, but a railway pier on the mainland let them moor alongside. The entry also describes the harbour's two old entrances, the Boca Grande and the Boca Chica. The Boca Grande was filled with stone after a capture of the city.
britannica-1911-castalia:
Castalia is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a celebrated fountain in Greece, now called the Fountain of St John. It rises in a chasm of Mount Parnassus, near Delphi. The spring was sacred to Apollo and the Muses. Its water served in the ritual purifications of the Pythian pilgrims who came to the oracle.

Through its link with the Muses, late Greek writers and Latin poets spoke of Castalia as a source of inspiration. Lucian and Ovid are named among those who used it so. That figure of speech passed into a commonplace of modern literature, where the name still signals poetic inspiration. The entry also records two accounts of the water's origin. Some authorities made the nymph Castalia a daughter of Achelous. Others derived the spring from the Boeotian Cephissus river.
britannica-1911-cilia: Cilia, the plural of the Latin cilium, an eyelash, are in biology the thread-like processes by whose vibration many lowly organisms move through water. The same structures serve movement in a second case named by the entry, the male reproductive cells of higher organisms. A name taken from eyelashes thus covers fine hairs whose beating drives tiny living things and cells along. The entry is a single definition sentence, giving the word's Latin root, its field and its function, and nothing further about form, place or kinds.
britannica-1911-cilicia:
Cilicia, in ancient geography, was a district of Asia Minor along the south coast, from the Alara Su to Mount Amanus, with the crest of Taurus as its northern limit. The Lamas Su divided it into Cilicia Trachea in the west and Cilicia Pedias in the east. Trachea is rugged mountain country, its Taurus spurs ending in rocky headlands with small sheltered harbours. Pirates used that coast in classical times, and Genoese and Venetian traders held it later.

Pedias holds a large rich plain watered by the Cydnus, Sarus and Pyramus, with Tarsus, Adana and Mopsuestia on the great east-west highway. The Cilician Gate carried that road down from the plateau to Tarsus. Cilicians appear as Khilikku in Assyrian inscriptions and ranked among the chief powers of western Asia early in the first millennium B.C. Goat's hair cloth, Cilicium, was a Roman-era export.
britannica-1911-citta-vecchia:
Città Vecchia, or Città Notabile, is a fortified city of Malta, seven miles west of Valletta and joined to it by railway. Its people numbered 7,515 in 1901, and it lies on high, sharply rising ground with a view over much of the island. A bishop has his seat there, in an ornate cathedral rebuilt after an earthquake in 1693. Tradition says that cathedral occupies the site of the house of Publius, who welcomed the apostle Paul.

Catacombs cut in the rock beneath the city are partly pre-Christian, yet they hold evidence of early Christian burial as well. A grotto said to have sheltered Paul is shown below the church of San Paolo, and Roman building remains have been excavated. Romans called it Civitas Melita, Saracens called it Medina, and the knights called it the old city. It was the island's capital until Valletta superseded it in 1570.
britannica-1911-civita-vecchia:
Civita Vecchia is a seaport town and episcopal see of Italy in Rome province, 50 miles north-west by rail from Rome, with 17,589 people in 1901. It is the ancient Centum Cellae, founded by Trajan, and Pliny the Younger and Rutilius described it. Modern harbour works rest on the ancient foundations near it. Remains of an aqueduct and other Roman buildings survive, and the imperial family had a villa here.

Saracens destroyed the place in 813, and Leo IV built a new city inland for its people, who returned to the shore site in 889 and rebuilt it as Civitas Vetus. Julius II began the castle in 1508 from Bramante's designs, with Michelangelo adding the central tower, a work Burckhardt called the finest of its kind. The town was the chief port of the Papal State and still holds considerable trade.
britannica-1911-collingwood-australia:
Collingwood is a city of Bourke county, Victoria, in Australia. It forms a suburb of Melbourne on the north-east side, set on the Yarra Yarra river. Its people numbered 32,766 in 1901. The town holds a place of note in the state's growth. It was the first town in Victoria to gain incorporation after Melbourne and Geelong.

One claim more fills the short entry. Collingwood is held to be one of the healthiest suburbs of the capital. No trade, church or public work is named in the piece. Its facts are place, river, count of people, rank in incorporation and good health. Readers who want more must look to the Melbourne entry. The brevity fits a suburb whose story runs with that of its great neighbour.
britannica-1911-croatia-slavonia:
Croatia-Slavonia was a kingdom of the Hungarian monarchy, lying between Carniola, Styria, and Hungary to the north and Servia, Bosnia, and Dalmatia to the south. Its coast ran along the Adriatic, and its surveyed area in 1900 was 16,423 square miles. Until 1881 a strip of the Austrian Military Frontier divided Croatia in the north-west from Slavonia in the north-east. That strip, now the county of Bjelovar, forms part of the united kingdom.

The entry divides the land into western highlands and eastern lowlands between the Drave, the Danube, and the Save. Sections cover minerals, climate, farming, forests, industries, roads, and chief towns, with Agram as capital. Further sections treat population, constitution and government under the fundamental law. A long history then runs from early times through the national revival of the Croats. A full list of authorities, from Klaić to Farlati, closes the survey.
britannica-1911-crypteia:
The crypteia was a kind of secret police in ancient Sparta, said by Aristotle to have been founded by Lycurgus. The entry notes that no real proof fixes its date. The ephors supervised it, and each year on taking office they proclaimed war against the helots. That proclamation freed from guilt any Spartan who killed a helot. The watch was set chiefly against the standing danger of a helot revolt.

Young Spartans were sent out by the ephors to watch the helots and kill any who seemed dangerous. Training for the young men may have been a second aim. After the revolt of 464 the darker purpose grew stronger, the entry judges. It cites the secret massacre of 2,000 helots who had claimed rewards for good service. Plato, in the Laws, stresses the guard against revolt rather than the killing. Thucydides supplies the massacre story.
britannica-1911-cryptomeria:
Cryptomeria, or Japanese cedar, is a genus of conifers with a single species, C. japonica, native to China and Japan. The Royal Horticultural Society brought it into Great Britain in 1844. It ranks among the finest trees of Japan, rising 100 feet or more. Its trunk stands bare below and carries a conical crown. Narrow pointed leaves, set in spirals, last four or five years, and small round cones sit at the tips of the branchlets.

In Japan the tree serves widely for replanting bare land, since its timber is valuable. It also lines public roads as an avenue tree. Sargent praised the groves at Nikko, where cryptomerias of 100 to 125 feet guard temples and tombs. Japanese growers have raised many odd varieties, some of them dwarf shrubs a few feet high. In Britain the tree asks for deep, drained soil, plenty of moisture, and shelter from cold winds.
britannica-1911-daphnephoria: The Daphnephoria was a festival held every ninth year at Thebes in Boeotia in honour of Apollo Ismenius or Galaxius. A procession formed its centre, and the chief figure in it was a boy of good family and noble looks. Both his father and his mother had to be alive for him to take the part. The entry gives only these few facts about the rite.
britannica-1911-darlingtonia:
Darlingtonia, named after the American botanist William Darlington, is a Californian pitcher-plant of the order Sarraceniaceae. Its single species grows at 5000 feet on the Sierra Nevadas, in sphagnum bogs with sundews and rushes. The pitcher leaves stand in a cluster one to two feet high, slender and erect. Each ends in a rounded hooded top, from which a fish-tail blade hangs over the pitcher's mouth.

Bright colouring draws insects to the leaves, and downward-pointing hairs guide them into the narrow funnel and bar their climb back out. The trapped insects rot in a mass at the pitcher's bottom. The entry supposes that the leaf absorbs the products of that decay as food.
britannica-1911-elyria:
Elyria is a city and the county-seat of Lorain county, Ohio, on the Black river, eight miles from Lake Erie and about 25 miles west-south-west of Cleveland. Its population was 8791 in 1900 and 14,825 at the 1910 census. Two railways serve the city. Elyria stands about 720 feet above sea level where the two forks of the Black river join. Each fork falls about 50 feet there, giving water-power.

The city's factories make oxide of tin and other chemicals, iron and steel, leather goods, cars and bicycles, and electrical and telephone supplies. Factory output in 1905 was valued at $2,933,450, well over double the value in 1900. Flagging, building stone, and grindstones from the Berea Grit quarries nearby are shipped from Elyria in large amounts. The town was founded about 1819 by Heman Ely, in whose honour it was named. It became the county seat in 1823 and a city in 1892.
britannica-1911-emilia:
Emilia is a territorial division, or compartimento, of Italy. It is bounded by Venetia and Lombardy on the north, Liguria on the west, and Tuscany on the south. The Marches lie on the south-east, and the Adriatic Sea on the east. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the Emilia article within it. Its area is 7967 square miles, and its population was 2,477,690 in 1901. Eight provinces make up the division.

Those provinces are Bologna, Ferrara, Forlì, Modena, Parma, Piacenza, Ravenna, and Reggio nell' Emilia. The north is one great plain running from the Via Aemilia to the Po, with lagoons at the Po mouth and the Valli di Comacchio. South of the Via Aemilia the ground rises to the Apennines, reaching 7103 feet in Monte Cimone. The main railway runs from Piacenza to Rimini.
britannica-1911-emporia:
Emporia is a city and the county-seat of Lyon county, Kansas, on the Neosho river, about 60 miles south-west of Topeka. Its population was 8223 in 1900 and 9058 at the 1910 census. Two railways serve the city. Emporia holds a Carnegie library and is the seat of the state normal school and of the College of Emporia, a Presbyterian college founded in 1883.

The city's business turns mainly on trade with the farming country round it, though it has small flour mills, machine shops, and foundries. Factory output in 1905 was valued at $571,601, and the town runs its own water-works and electric-light plant. Emporia was settled in 1856 and chartered as a city in 1870. His 1896 editorial “What's the matter with Kansas?” made a great stir, and he also wrote well-liked short stories, among them The Court of Boyville.
britannica-1911-encaenia:
Encaenia is a festival marking a dedication, from a Greek word built on kainos, new. The entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica is only a few lines long. It says the term is used above all of the anniversary of the dedication of a church. A cross-reference sends the reader to the article on Dedication for the church sense.

The term carries a second, academic use. At the university of Oxford it names the annual Commemoration, held in June, of founders and benefactors. A cross-reference sends the reader to the article on Oxford for that ceremony. Nothing more is given: no history of the festival, no list of churches, and no account of the Oxford rite. The notice simply fixes the word's two homes, the church calendar and the Oxford year, and points onward for the rest.
britannica-1911-encyclopaedia:
Encyclopaedia is traced by this long entry to the Greek idea of instruction in the whole circle of learning, education in arts and sciences. Pliny, in the preface to his Natural History, says his book treated all the subjects of the Greek encyclopaedia. Quintilian directs that boys be taught the other arts before rhetoric, so as to complete that “orbis of doctrine.”

The word was likely first used in English by Sir Thomas Elyot, who in the Governour calls it “Encyclopedia” in Greek. The entry then follows the form through later ages to the great French Encyclopédie. That work, the entry says through its quoted critics, was a war machine against the church and a despotic government. It was met by opposition and persecution unmatched in the history of encyclopaedias, and its making was uneven and loosely overseen.
britannica-1911-etna-pennsylvania:
Etna is a borough of Allegheny county, Pennsylvania, on the west bank of the Allegheny river. It stands about 2 miles north of Pittsburg, of which it is a suburb. Its population rose from 2,334 in 1880 to 5,830 in 1910. The Pennsylvania railway and electric lines serve it. Its works include rolling mills, tube and pipe works, furnaces and steel mills. A brass foundry and makers of boxes, asbestos coverings and ice are also listed.

Industry began in 1820 with a small factory making scythes and sickles. Natural gas piped from Butler county fired the iron mills early on. The place was first called Steuart's Town. It was incorporated as a borough in 1869. The entry is a short gazetteer notice of a working mill town. Its figures trace steady growth across four censuses.
britannica-1911-etruria:
Etruria was an ancient district of Italy whose bounds shifted greatly over time. Its name matches the Greek Tyrrhenia, and the Romans also called its people Tusci, the root of Tuscany. Early on it may have covered the north from the Tiber to the Alps. By about 100 B.C. the Arno, the Apennines and the Tiber bounded it. Under Augustus it formed Italy's seventh region, reaching north to the river Macra.

Etruscan power once spread north past the Po and south into Latium and Campania. The Tarquin kings of Rome are read here as Etruscan lords holding sway before 600 B.C. A treaty with Carthage gave the Etruscans Corsica and command of Tyrrhenian trade. Decline followed fast. Hiero of Syracuse destroyed their fleet in 474 B.C. Veii fell to Rome in 396 after a ten years' siege. The Vadimonian Lake defeat in 309 ended Etruscan independence.
britannica-1911-flaminia-via:
The Via Flaminia was an ancient high road of Italy, built by Gaius Flaminius during his censorship in 220 B.C. It ran from Rome to Ariminum and was the most important route to the north. Emperors improved it often. Augustus, restoring Italy's roads, kept the Flaminia for himself and rebuilt every bridge except the Pons Mulvius over the Tiber and one other. Triumphal arches in his honour stood on that bridge and at Ariminum, the latter still standing.

Vespasian cut a new tunnel through the Furlo pass in A.D. 77, and Trajan repaired several bridges, as inscriptions show. The entry follows the road's course north from Rome, noting surviving pavement in the modern highway. It passes the Etruscan site of Falerii, Ocriculi and Narnia, where a great four-arched bridge crossed the Nar. One arch and all its piers still stand, a measure of the road's solid building.
britannica-1911-foggia:
Foggia is a town and episcopal see in Apulia, Italy, capital of the province of Foggia. It stands 243 feet above sea-level in the centre of the great Apulian plain, 201 miles by rail south-east of Ancona and 123 miles north-east of Naples. The town counted 49,031 people in 1901, the commune 53,134. Its name probably comes from the foveae, the pits or cellars where the people store their grain. It is the medieval successor of ancient Arpi, three miles north.

The Normans, after taking the district from the Eastern empire, gave Foggia its first importance. Its cathedral, built probably about 1179, keeps traces of Norman work and a fine figured cornice by Bartolommeo da Foggia, though an earthquake in 1731 forced much rebuilding. A gateway of the emperor Frederick II's palace of 1223 also survives. His third wife Isabella, daughter of King John of England, died here, and Charles of Anjou died here in 1284.
britannica-1911-fontana-lavinia:
Lavinia Fontana (1552-1614) was an Italian portrait-painter, daughter of Prospero Fontana. She was much employed by the ladies of Bologna. Going from there to Rome, she painted the likenesses of many famous persons. She stood under the special patronage of the family of Pope Gregory XIII, who died in 1585. Roman ladies from that pontiff's days to those of Paul V favoured her no less than the women of Bologna had done. Paul V himself sat for her, a rare honour for a woman painter of the age.

Some of Lavinia's portraits have been wrongly credited to Guido. In other kinds of painting she joined care and delicacy with boldness. The entry names a Venus in Berlin, a Virgin in the Escorial, and a Queen of Sheba visiting Solomon. Her youthful self-portrait was perhaps her masterpiece.
britannica-1911-fostoria:
Fostoria is a city lying partly in Seneca, partly in Hancock and partly in Wood county, Ohio, 35 miles south by east of Toledo. Its population grew from 7,070 in 1890 to 9,597 in 1910, with 584 foreign-born residents in 1900. Five railways serve it, with two interurban electric lines. The city stands in a farming region, and oil abounds in the neighbourhood, a pairing of field and well typical of north-west Ohio in its boom years of growth.

Fostoria's factories make glass, flour, brass and iron goods, carriages, barrels, lamps, carbons, wire nails, automobile engines and railway torpedoes. The waterworks belong to the city itself. In 1832 the first settlers laid out two rival towns on the site, Rome and Risdon. A bitter rivalry arose between them before they grew into one city. The entry joins that founding quarrel to the long list of manufactures of the merged town it became.
britannica-1911-francia:
Francia (about 1450-1517) was a Bolognese painter whose real name was Francesco Raibolini. His father, Marco di Giacomo Raibolini, was a carpenter of an old and creditable family. The boy was apprenticed to a goldsmith currently named Francia, and from him probably came the nickname by which he is generally known. He also studied design under Marco Zoppo. The youth was first a goldsmith, and an engraver of dies and niellos, arts in which he became extremely eminent.

Francia was famed for his dies for medals and rose to be mint-master at Bologna. A famous medal of Pope Julius II is ascribed to his hand. As a type-founder he made the first italic type for Aldus Manutius. At a mature age he turned to painting.
britannica-1911-franklin-pennsylvania:
Franklin is a city and the county-seat of Venango county, Pennsylvania, where French Creek meets the Allegheny river. Its population grew from 6221 in 1890 to 9767 in 1910. Four railways serve it, and its broad shaded streets, parks, library, and fine houses mark a settled, prosperous place.

The city stands at the centre of the chief oil region of the state, ships great quantities of refined oil, and makes oil-well supplies, boilers, engines, and steel castings. Its site saw Fort Machault, built by the French in 1754, then Fort Venango, taken by Indians in 1763, and Fort Franklin, built in 1787. The town was laid out in 1795 and chartered as a city in 1868, most growth following the oil find of 1860.
britannica-1911-fredericia:
Fredericia is a seaport of Denmark near the south-east corner of Jutland, on the west shore of the Little Belt facing the island of Fünen. It held 12,714 people in 1901, with rail links north and south and a steam ferry to Middelfart. Shipping trade is large, and local works make tobacco, salt, chicory, cotton goods, and hats.

Christian IV raised a small fort on the site, and Frederick III resolved about 1650 to build a strong fortress town, first called Frederiksodde and renamed Fredericia in 1664. Swedes stormed it in 1657. In 1849 it stood a two-month siege ending in a famed Danish sortie on 6 July, marked by the bronze Land Soldier statue. In 1864 the Danes abandoned it after a six-week siege, and the Austro-Prussian army partly destroyed the works.
britannica-1911-frederick-william-i-of-p:
Frederick William I (1688-1740), king of Prussia, was born on 15 August 1688, son of Frederick I. Raised under strict tutors, he took a passion for military life, deepened by meeting Marlborough in 1709 and Prince Eugene at Tournai. In temper he was his father opposite: frugal, plain, fierce of will, and devout, yet tolerant toward Catholic subjects, the Jesuits excepted.

He came to the throne on 25 February 1713 and at once cleared the palace of needless officials and sold much of its fine furniture. The entry rates him among the greatest administrators to wear the Prussian crown. Abroad he gained most of Gelderland at Utrecht in 1713, then by the treaty of Stockholm in 1720 won Stettin and Hither Pomerania from Sweden for two million thalers. His claim to Jülich and Berg failed, and he renounced it in the Wüsterhausen settlement.
britannica-1911-fredonia:
Fredonia is a village of Chautauqua county, New York, about 45 miles south-west of Buffalo and three miles from Lake Erie. Its population reached 5285 in 1910. It holds a State Normal School and the Darwin R. Barker public library, and sits in the grape country of western New York, shipping grapes and running large nurseries.

Wine and unfermented grape juice are leading products, with canned goods and patent medicines also made. First settled in 1804 as Canandaway, the place took its present name in 1817 and was incorporated in 1829. A gas well sunk in 1821 lit the village streets, making Fredonia one of the first American places to use natural gas in public. In its Baptist church a Woman Temperance Union formed in December 1873, a seed of the wider temperance movement.
britannica-1911-freesia:
Freesia is a genus of plants in the iris family holding a single species, F. refracta, native at the Cape of Good Hope. The plant grows from a corm, a solid bulb like that of the gladiolus. A tuft of long narrow leaves rises first, then a slightly branched stem carrying loose one-sided spikes of sweet-smelling, narrow funnel-shaped flowers.

Known varieties differ in flower colour, running white, cream, or yellow, and newer large-flowered forms include rose shades. Freesias make pretty greenhouse plants and grow readily from seed. Growers in Guernsey, England, and America raise them widely for market. By potting fresh corms in turn through the autumn, a grower can keep flowers coming all through winter and spring. The entry is a short gardener note on the genus and its culture.
britannica-1911-friedland-austria:
Friedland is a town of Bohemia, Austria, 103 miles north-east of Prague by rail, with 6229 people in 1900. Beyond the old walled town lie three suburbs, and the chief work is the making of woollen and linen cloth. The place is known above all for its old castle on a small hill looking down over the town.

A round watch-tower is said to have stood on the castle site as early as 1014, and the present castle dates from the 13th century. It was besieged several times in the Thirty Years and Seven Years Wars. In 1622 Wallenstein bought it and took from it his title of duke of Friedland. After his death Ferdinand II gave it to Count Mathias Gallas, and since 1757 it has belonged to the Count Clam Gallas family. The castle was grandly restored in 1868-1869.
britannica-1911-friedland-prussia:
Friedland is a small town of Prussia on the Alle river, 27 miles south-east of Königsberg, with about 3000 people. Its fame is the battle fought there on 14 June 1807 between Napoleon French army and the Russians under General Bennigsen. The Russians took the town on the night of the 13th, and fighting began before dawn in the Sortlack Wood.

Bennigsen had nearly 50,000 men across the river by six in the morning, cramped between the Alle and the mill-stream. Napoleon reached the field at noon and set Ney, Lannes, and Mortier in line, with Victor and the Guard in reserve. At five, Ney stormed the Sortlack Wood, and after a cavalry check Dupont infantry and Sénarmont massed guns broke the Russian left at case-shot range. The town burned as French troops pursued. Russian losses were put at 10,000 of 46,000, French at 12,100 of 86,000.
britannica-1911-fuenterrabia:
Fuenterrabia, in Latin Fons Rapidus, is a town of northern Spain in Guipúzcoa, on the French frontier near the Bay of Biscay. It stands on a hill slope on the left bank of the Bidassoa where the estuary begins. From some 750 people in 1870 it grew to 4345 by 1900, as visitors from inland Spain made it a summer resort.

Inside the heavy, half-ruined ramparts lie narrow steep streets, gabled houses, a fine old church, a castle, and a massive town hall. Outside them spread hotels, villas, and a fishermen quarter. The fortress was long fought over by France and Spain: French attempts failed in 1476 and 1503, succeeded in 1521, and were reversed in 1524. Condé was beaten under its walls in 1638, and Philip IV then granted it the rank of city. It fell to Berwick in 1719 and to the French again in 1794, and Wellington forced the ford opposite it in October 1813.
britannica-1911-gaetulia:
Gaetulia was an ancient district of northern Africa. In Roman usage it covered the tribes of the southern Atlas slopes, west to the Atlantic and south to the oases of the Sahara. Its people were Berbers, clad in skins and living on flesh and milk. They were famed horse-breeders; Strabo credits them with 100,000 foals in a year. Their manufacture was a purple dye, famous from Augustus's time, made from shellfish on the coast.

The Gaetulians first appear in the Jugurthine war of 111 to 106 B.C., fighting beside Jugurtha when they had not heard Rome's name. Later they backed Caesar against Juba I. Augustus gave part of Gaetulia to Juba II in 25 B.C., but the tribes rose and massacred the Roman residents. A defeat in A.D. 6 under Lentulus Cossus, who took the name Gaetulicus, brought submission. Gaetulians later served in the empire's auxiliary troops.
britannica-1911-galatia:
Galatia was a district of Asia Minor, named for the Gaulish tribes that settled it in the 3rd century B.C. It covered the vilayet of Angora, some 200 miles long and 100 broad, on a plateau 2000 to 3000 feet. The Halys divides an eastern part from a western part drained by the Sangarius. Most of it is upland pasture for sheep and goats, with few cities and a climate of extremes.

The Gauls crossed into Asia in 278 to 277 B.C., invited by Nicomedes of Bithynia. They had split from the host that invaded Greece under Brennus. After 46 years of ravaging, Attalus fixed them there about 232 B.C.: Tectosages round Ancyra, Tolistobogii round Pessinus, Trocmi round Tavium. Rome curbed them in 189 B.C., and Deiotarus united the tetrarchies as king. On Amyntas's death in 25 B.C. Augustus made Galatia a province. The Phrygians and Cappadocians formed the bulk of its people.
britannica-1911-galicia-austria:
Galicia is a crownland of Austria, its largest province, with 30,299 square miles between Russia, Bukovina, Hungary and Silesia. The Carpathians cover a third of it along the south, sinking to the valleys of the Vistula and Dniester, while the north and east run into the Russian plains. Its climate is the severest in Austria, shut from warmth by the mountains. The land is mostly farmed or forested, and no Austrian province grows more potatoes.

Galicia had 7,295,538 people in 1900, Poles at 45 per cent and Ruthenians at 42. Its wealth includes salt at Wieliczka, coal near Cracow, zinc, and petroleum fields in the Carpathian foothills, with ozocerite besides. Distilling, refining and saw-milling lead its industries. The province joins the kingdoms of Galicia and Lodomeria, the duchies of Auschwitz and Zator, and the grand duchy of Cracow. It came to Austria at the partition of Poland in 1772 and won autonomy after 1861.
britannica-1911-grisi-giulia:
Giulia Grisi (1811–1869) was an Italian opera singer born in Milan, the daughter of one of Napoleon's Italian officers. Music ran through her family: her aunt Josephina Grassini was a celebrated singer, her mother sang, and her sister Giudetta and cousin Carlotta were both highly gifted. Giulia made her stage début in 1828.

Rossini and Bellini both backed her, and at Milan she created the part of Adalgisa in Bellini's Norma opposite Pasta. Paris heard her in 1832 and London in 1834, and her brilliant dramatic soprano held prima donna rank for thirty years. London remembered her seasons alongside Lablache, Rubini, Tamburini and Mario as the palmy days of Italian opera. She toured America with Mario in 1854 and died in Berlin in 1869.
britannica-1911-hampton-virginia:
Hampton is a city of Elizabeth City county, Virginia. It is the county-seat, at the mouth of the James river. Norfolk lies about 15 miles to the south-east. The 1910 population was 5,505. The Chesapeake & Ohio railway serves the city. Hampton ships farm produce, fish and oysters. Canned crabs, fish oil and brick are manufactured. St John's church dates from 1727.

The Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute dominates the account. The American Missionary Association opened it in 1868. It was founded for the education of black students. Samuel Chapman Armstrong superintended it until 1893. Indian students were admitted from 1878. Booker T. Washington was its most famous graduate. Its industrial training model shaped many other schools. Work students, day students and trade students form its three schemes. Confederates burned Hampton in August 1861. It became a city in 1908.
britannica-1911-hanover-pennsylvania:
Hanover is a borough of York county, Pennsylvania. Harrisburg lies 36 miles to the north. The state border is six miles south. Its population in 1910 was 7,057. The Northern Central and Western Maryland railways serve it. It stands on level ground in the fertile Conewago valley. Turnpikes to Baltimore, Carlisle, York and Frederick cross there. The main streets take their names from those roads.

Foundry and machine-shop products lead its manufactures. Flour, silk, waggons, shoes and gloves are also made. Furniture, wire cloth and cigars join the list. Germans began the settlement in the mid-18th century. Colonel Richard MacAllister laid out the town in 1763 or 1764. Incorporation came in 1815. On 30 June 1863 Kilpatrick's and Stuart's cavalry clashed there. That fight preluded Gettysburg, and a state statue marks it.
britannica-1911-henrietta-maria:
Henrietta Maria (1609–1666) was queen of Charles I of England and a daughter of Henry IV of France. She was little more than fourteen when her marriage was arranged in 1624. Louis XIII agreed only if the penal laws against English Roman Catholics were eased. Married by proxy on the 1st of May 1625, she came to England pledged to a course sure to make her and her husband unpopular.

The early marriage was unhappy, but after Buckingham was killed in 1628 the pair grew close. Six children followed, among them Charles II and James II. From 1637 she backed aid for English Catholics, which alarmed Protestant England. In the Civil War she raised money, crossed to the Continent, and in February 1643 landed at Burlington Quay to lead loyalists to the king near Oxford. She left him in April 1644 and never saw him again. She died at Colombes on the 31st of August 1666.
britannica-1911-hestia:
Hestia, in Greek myth, is the fire-goddess, daughter of Cronus and Rhea, and goddess of hearth and home. She is not named in Homer, though the hearth there is already a refuge for suppliants. In later religion she is one of the twelve Olympians, yet she never leaves Olympus. When Apollo and Poseidon sought her hand, she swore to stay a maiden for ever.

Zeus gave her rule over sacrifices, with the first and last libations poured to her. Her fire burned always, and if it died only sacred fire could relight it. She stands for the family union, and so, the city being the family writ large, for the state. Her chief shrine was the prytaneum, whose common hearth-fire burned before the magistrates. Colonists took fire from it for the hearth of their new home.
britannica-1911-hibernia:
Hibernia, in ancient geography, is one of the names by which Ireland was known to Greek and Roman writers. Others were Ierne, Iuverna and Iberio, all from a stem that also gives Erin. Traders' reports made the island well known to Rome, at least along its coasts. Yet it never became part of the Roman empire.

About A.D. 80 Agricola planned its conquest and judged it easy, but the government in Rome vetoed the plan. Irish pirates were an on-and-off nuisance during the Roman years in Britain. The best-attested Irish movement of the age is that of the Scots into Caledonia. Roman civilization entered the island only in post-Roman days, perhaps with missionaries such as Patrick. Ireland thus stood known, named and traded with, but never ruled from Rome.
britannica-1911-hierocles-of-alexandria:
Hierocles of Alexandria was a Neoplatonist writer who flourished about A.D. 430. He studied under Plutarch at Athens and taught for some years in his native city. Banished from Alexandria, he settled in Constantinople. There his religious opinions gave such offence that he was jailed and cruelly flogged.

His only complete surviving work is a commentary on the Carmina Aurea of Pythagoras. It won a great name in the middle ages and the Renaissance, and passed into many European languages. Other writings, on providence and fate and a consolation for Olympiodorus of Thebes, are known through Photius and Stobaeus. The jest-book Philogelos, credited to him and Philagrius, has no link with him. The Elements of Ethics fragments in Stobaeus belong to a Stoic Hierocles of Epictetus's time.
britannica-1911-john-don-of-austria:
Don John of Austria (1545–1578) was the natural son of the emperor Charles V by Barbara Blomberg of Regensburg, where he was born on the 24th of February 1545. Raised in Spain in ignorance of his birth, he was owned as a son in Charles's will and received by Philip II in 1559. His segment sits in a hosted file shared with several other John entries.

Philip meant him for the Church, but he chose the life of a soldier. He fought Algerian pirates and the rebel Moriscos of Granada. In 1571 he led the joined fleets of Spain and Venice against the Turks, and at Lepanto on the 7th of October he won a complete victory. Made governor of the Netherlands in 1576, he signed the Perpetual Edict, then broke with the states and won at Gemblours in January 1578. He died of fever on the 1st of October 1578.
britannica-1911-john-of-bohemia:
John (1296–1346), king of Bohemia, was a son of the emperor Henry VII, born on the 10th of August 1296. He became count of Luxemburg in 1309 and was offered the Bohemian crown about the same time. He married Elizabeth, a sister of the last Premyslide king, and was crowned at Prague in February 1311.

Restless and warlike, he soon tired of governing. Bohemia slipped back toward disorder while its king won fame as a fighter across Europe. He fought Metz and Brabant, led the Teutonic knights in Lithuania, and brought Silesia under his rule. He helped the emperor Louis defeat Frederick the Fair at Mühldorf in 1322. At home his German followers were disliked and he grew unpopular. A closing note treats the tale that the prince of Wales took his feather badge and motto Ich dien from John after Crécy, and finds no proof John bore it.
britannica-1911-kaffraria:
Kaffraria was the name given to the southeast part of the Cape province in South Africa. It was no longer an official term. It once covered the districts of King William's Town and East London. Those districts formed British Kaffraria and were joined to Cape Colony in 1865. The name also covered the land past the Kei River as far as the Natal frontier.

As a term of geography it still served for the Transkeian territories of the Cape. Those lands, the Transkei, Pondoland, Tembuland, and Griqualand East, were taken into Cape Colony at dates between 1879 and 1894. They cover 18,310 square miles and held 834,644 people in 1904, of whom 16,777 were white. The land rises from the sea in a set of terraces to the rugged Drakensberg range. Between that range and the coast lie lesser ranges with rich valleys, cut by many rivers.
britannica-1911-karamania:
Karamania was once a separate inland province in the south of Asia Minor. It took its name from Karaman, granted Laranda in fief and made governor of Selefke in the years 1223 to 1245. On the fall of the Seljuk empire his grandson Mahmud, who ruled from 1279 to 1319, founded a state on the land.

That state took in Pamphylia, Lycaonia, and large parts of Cilicia, Cappadocia, and Phrygia, with Laranda as its capital in place of Konia. It warred often with the kings of Lesser Armenia, the Lusignan princes of Cyprus, and the knights of Rhodes. It also fought a long struggle for mastery with the Ottoman Turks, which ended only in 1472, when Mahommed II annexed it for good. The Ottomans split it into two parts across the Taurus and restored Konia as its chief city. In later geography the name clings chiefly to the southern part.
britannica-1911-labicana-via:
The Via Labicana was an ancient highroad of Italy running E.S.E. from Rome. It may first have led only to Tusculum, then been carried on to Labici, and later still become a through route. It may even have displaced the Via Latina as the road to the south-east. The two roads run much the same distance from Rome to their main junction at Ad Bivium, but the Labicana's summit level is 725 ft. lower than the Latina's, a little west of the pass of Algidus.

Beyond the junction the combined road probably kept the name Via Latina rather than Via Labicana. For the first six miles out of Rome the ancient course matches no modern road, yet it can be followed clearly by surviving stretches of pavement and by buildings along the line.
britannica-1911-laconia:
Laconia was the ancient name of the south-eastern district of the Peloponnese, with Sparta as its capital. It covers some 1,048,000 acres, a little more than Somersetshire, and falls into three zones running north and south. The Eurotas valley holds the centre. Taygetus, 7900 ft., bounds it on the west and ends in the promontory of Taenarum, Cape Matapan. The east is broken hill country rising in Parnon to 6365 ft. and ending at Cape Malea.

Taygetus was well watered and forested, with hunting for the Spartans, iron mines, and quarries of bluish marble and the famous rosso antico. Parnon's slopes are mostly barren limestone. The Eurotas valley is fertile, growing maize, olives, oranges and mulberries. The coast, especially in the east, is rugged and dangerous, with few good harbours and only Cythera lying off it. Besides Sparta and Gythium, the chief towns were Bryseae, Amyclae and Pharis.
britannica-1911-lagos-nigeria:
Lagos is a seaport of West Africa and capital of the British colony and protectorate of Southern Nigeria, at 6° 26′ N., 3° 23′ E. It stands on an island in the lagoon that shares its name, with Iddo Island between it and the mainland. An iron bridge of 2600 ft. for road and railway joins Lagos to Iddo, and another of 917 ft. joins Iddo to the mainland. The town lies a foot or two above sea-level.

Its chief buildings are the government house, the law courts, the Glover memorial hall, a club-house and the police quarters. The town has electric light and a good water service, and its stores and depots line the lagoon banks. The swamps that once made up Lagos Island have been reclaimed, a canal 25 ft. wide cut through the island, and a sea-wall built round its western half. Shifting sand banks bar the lagoon's sea entrance.
britannica-1911-lamellibranchia:
Lamellibranchia names the fourth of five classes inside the mollusc group in the 1911 Britannica, a class marked by a small head and a body kept even on both sides. The shell grows as two plates, one on each side, and the foot most often takes a plough-like shape used for digging in sand and mud.

Large paired gills do the central work. Their fine hairs drive water flows that carry food to a weak mouth, so feeding matters more here than breathing. The account then works through points of change across the group: gill build, one muscle or two, rear tubes for water flow, shell balance, and foot shape from disc to burrowing tube.
britannica-1911-limburg-prussia:
Limburg is a German town in Hesse-Nassau, Prussia. The Lahn flows past it under a bridge of 1315. Rail lines run to Coblenz, Cassel, and Frankfort. The count of 1905 gave 9,917 people. A Roman Catholic bishop sits there.

The cathedral of St George stands on rock above the river. Seven towers mark its small frame. Conrad Kurzbold founded it early in the 900s. Consecration came in 1235. Restoring work ran from 1872 to 1878. A castle, a new town hall, and a priests' school fill out the town. Cloth, tobacco, soap, machines, pots, and leather are made there. Its own counts ruled till 1414. Trier then bought the place, and Nassau took it in 1803. Austrians beat the French here in September 1796.
buried-cities-volume-2-olympia:
Jennie Hall wrote the Olympia part of her buried cities tales for the young, as part two of the set. Hall taught history and English at the Francis W. Parker School in Chicago. The same foreword on dug wealth opens this book as the first. Drawings and photos from first sources fill its pages.

Temple ground rules this part. A boy named Charmides walks the old temple of Hera in the tale's heart. Rows of statues in marble, gold, and ivory line its side rooms. Zeus and Hera stand at the front, with priests at prayer. One small room stops the boy cold: his Hermes, with the baby Dionysus in its arms. Gold sandal and soft joy mark the meet. Games ground, gods, and the long dig that freed the site form the rest. Part one holds Pompeii and part three Mycenae.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abecedaria:
Abecedaria are alphabet lists, whole or partial, cut into ancient monuments in Greek and Latin, on pagan and Christian stones alike. The Latin alphabet settled into a fixed system near the start of the Christian era, while Greek shapes drew closer to Latin forms. Three extra letters added by Emperor Claudius never appear in Christian inscriptions. Formal monumental lettering differed widely from everyday cursive, and uncial script stayed in books until the fourth century.

Christian examples are rare, apart from two Carthage vases, while pagan ones include stonecutters' practice tablets and puzzling catacomb letter strings. One stone from the cemetery of St. Alexander looks like a schoolboy exercise in paired letters, a memory drill St. Jerome describes. A Rome stone found in 1877, of sixth- or seventh-century date, apparently served a school as a model alphabet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abyssinia:
Abyssinia, stretching between the sixth and fifteenth degrees of north latitude, south of Nubia, is likened to a vast fortress towering above eastern Africa's plains. It is a huge granitic and basaltic mass, a great mountainous oval, ridged mainly eastward. A chain over 650 miles long runs north to south. From the Red Sea it resembles a vast wall, about 8,000 feet high near Kasen and over 10,000 feet at Angolala.

On the west the mass breaks into plateaux of varying height, split by volcanic mountains, with Tigre summits over 6,500 feet and Simien summits from 13,000 to 16,000. Lake Tana hollows the highlands to the southwest, Gojam rises above 13,000 feet, and Kaffa's peaks reach some 12,000. That remarkable elevation gives Abyssinia a peculiar climate, which scholars divide into three chief zones, beginning with the low valleys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acacia:
Acacia in the Bible is the Hebrew shittah, plural shittim, linked to Egyptian shent, Coptic shonte, and Arabic sunt, all pointing to thorn. Hence the Greek akantha and Latin acanthus for the Egyptian acacia. The Septuagint calls its wood incorruptible wood, and the Vulgate calls it setim-wood. The biblical acacia, genus Mimosa, is no doubt the Acacia seyal or Acacia tortilis, called torrent trees, from sayl, torrent.

They grow in Sinai's desert wadis, or torrent valleys. Their wood is light, hard, and durable, blackening almost to ebony over time. The ark of the covenant and the table of the loaves were made of setim-wood. So were the holocaust altar, the incense altar, and the wooden parts of the tabernacle, as Exodus 25:5 records.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acadia:
Acadia's precise location and extent were disputed, with consequent warfare, between French and English colonists in America for over one hundred and fifty years. Henry IV of France granted the Sieur de Monts the territory called La Cadie. The grant was to cultivate it, people it, and hunt for gold and silver mines between the 46th and 40th degrees of north latitude. The Marquise de Guercheville, who bought the claim, imagined she owned Florida to the St. Lawrence.

Later Acadia was taken as the present peninsula of Nova Scotia. Now it usually means the small district on the Bay of Fundy's south shore, from Annapolis to the Basin of Minas. His concession came on 8 November 1603, and with Champlain and Pontgrave he reached Port Royal, now Annapolis. The entry closes with the Acadian dispersion and its descendants, put at 270,000 by Richard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achaia:
Achaia, also called Aegialeia, was, before Rome's conquest in 146 BC, a coastal strip between the Gulf of Corinth and Elis and Arcadia, holding twelve cities leagued together. The Achaean League stood prominent in the Greek struggle against Roman domination. Probably for that reason the name later spread across the country south of Macedonia and Illyricum, roughly modern Greece.

Under Rome, Achaia was usually a senatorial province, governed by an ex-praetor titled proconsul, with Corinth as capital. When St. Paul came into Achaia, Gallio, Seneca's brother, held the proconsulship. His refusal to meddle in Jewish religious affairs, and the tolerance of his rule, favoured the spread of Christianity, and Paul founded a flourishing church at Corinth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acmonia: Acmonia, a Phrygian Pacatiana titular see in Asia Minor, is now Ahat-Keui. Cicero mentions it in his speech Pro Flacco, and it stood on the road from Dorylaeum to Philadelphia. The entry gives this brief identification of site, classical mention, and road position, and cites Smith's geography and Mas Latrie's chronology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acolouthia:
Acolouthia, from Greek akoloutheo, to follow, means in church language the Divine Office's order or arrangement, and, broadly, the office itself. The parts follow closely in order, which explains the name. The office joins musical and rhetorical elements, with music given in one of eight modes, four primary and four secondary.

Greeks seldom used notated texts, so they learned a standard hymn or canticle by heart as a model for others of the same rhythm. A model stanza is called a hirmos, and a final one a catabasia by some writers. The basic element is the troparion, a short hymn, with forms like the contakion explaining a feast, the oikos praising its subject, and the apolytikion proper to the day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-actus-et-pote:
Actus et potentia is a technical expression in scholastic language, translating Aristotle's energeia or entelecheia and dynamis. No single English word renders either exactly. Act, action, and actuality express shades of actus, while potency, power, and capacity express shades of potentia. Generally, potentia means an aptitude for change, for acting or being acted on, or for a new form. Actus means fulfilling such a capacity.

Potentia thus points to something future, existing now only as a germ to be evolved, while actus denotes the full reality that answers it. In short, potentia is determinable being and actus determined being. Actus extends further than act or operation, since every perfection and form counts as actus, not only operations. The entry closes by noting today's drift toward actuality theories in the sciences, which on analysis still yield potential elements awaiting their full form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adria:
Adria is an Italian bishopric, suffragan to Venice, comprising 55 Rovigo-province towns and part of one town in Padua. Tradition dates gospel preaching in Adria from St. Apollinaris, consecrated bishop by St. Peter. That Bishop of Ravenna holds singular importance in the legends of northeast Italy. Recent investigation shows, however, that even if Emilia, Romagna, and Venetian territory were Christianized before Piedmont, their conversion goes no further back than the end of the second century.

The first bishop of Adria whose name is certain is Gallonistus, present at a Roman synod in 649 under Martin I. Venerable Bede mentions a St. Colianus, Bishop of Adria, in his Martyrology, but nothing more is known of him. Among later bishops stands Blessed Aldobrandinus of Este. The diocese counts 80 parishes and 300 churches, chapels, and oratories, served by 250 secular priests, among 190,400 people. Sources include Ughelli, Cappelletti, and Gams.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agria:
Agria, also Erlau, Eger, and Jager, is Hungary's archiepiscopal see; Pius VII made it an archdiocese in 1304, after its 1009 founding. It counts 633,804 Latin Catholics and 81,217 Greek Catholics, plus 503,407 Schismatics and Protestants in part, with a sprinkling of Jews. Its parishes number 200, served by 342 secular clergy and 51 religious; Hungarian and German dominate the vernacular, with Croat, Slavonic, and Armenian also spoken.

Its suffragan dioceses are Kosice, Rozsnyo, Szathmar, and Szepes. Together the figures sketch Catholic life in early twentieth-century Hungary. Hundreds of thousands of Latin and Greek Catholics live alongside a large mixed population of Schismatics and Protestants, served by nearly four hundred clergy across two hundred parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alba-pompeia:
The diocese of Alba Pompeia in northern Italy takes in eighty towns in the province of Cuneo and two in the province of Alexandria. Its entry follows the bishops of Alba from early tradition toward firmer records. Tradition heads the list with St. Dionysius, said to have served at Alba before becoming Archbishop of Milan. He suffered exile in 355 for opposing Arian teaching, the belief that Christ was not fully divine.

A list of nine early bishops, drawn from inscriptions found in Alba cathedral late in the fifteenth century, was later proved a forgery. The first bishop whose existence is certain is Lampradius, present at a Roman synod in 499 under Pope Symmachus. Benzo stands out later as an opponent of Gregory VII and a backer of the emperor in the Investiture struggle over who appointed bishops. The entry closes with the diocese's scale: 101 parishes, 276 secular priests, 403 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albania:
Albania, the ancient Epirus and Illyria, was in this entry's day the westernmost land in Europe held by the Ottoman Turks. Roughly 290 miles long and forty to ninety miles wide, it lies between the Adriatic and Ionian seas and the mountains inland. The entry divides it into three regions. Upper Albania runs from the Montenegrin frontier to the river Shkumbi, Lower Albania or Epirus runs south to the Gulf of Arta, and Eastern Albania lies beyond the Schar-Dagh range.

Much of the entry covers religion. For four centuries Catholic Albanians held to their faith under hardship, aided by Franciscan missionaries, while adopting Islam brought rank and the right to bear arms. It maps the church provinces of the region and describes its towns, including Scutari and Yanina. Near Yanina stand the ruins of Dodona, the ancient oracle site, in a rugged land where faith and Ottoman rule met.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alberic-of-os:
Alberic of Ostia was a Benedictine monk who became Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia in 1138 and died at Verdun in 1147. Born at Beauvais in France in 1080, he entered the monastery of Cluny and served as sub-prior and then prior of St. Martin-des-Champs. He was called back to Cluny in 1126 to help restore discipline there. He went on to serve as Abbot of Vézelay before Pope Innocent II raised him to the cardinalate.

Right after his consecration, Alberic travelled as papal legate, a pope's personal envoy, to England. A council gathered at London in December 1138 with eighteen bishops and about thirty abbots present. The entry then follows his further legatine missions and closes with its sources, including the life and works of St. Bernard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albi-albia:
Albi is a French diocese covering the Department of the Tarn. It was an archiepiscopal see from 1678 until the French Revolution, with suffragan bishops at Rodez, Castres, Vabres, Cahors, and Mende. It was re-established in 1822 with a new grouping that joined the ancient bishopric of Castres. Local tradition from the twelfth century credits its foundation to St. Clarus, though the Bollandists doubt the legend. The first bishop known to history is Diogenianus, about 406.

The diocese is rich in memories. The first monastery of the Gauls was founded at Vieux late in the fifth century. Two great local families, the Salvia and the Ansbertina, gave many saints to the Church between the sixth and eighth centuries. St. Dominic's fight against the Albigensian heresy is still recalled there, and the Council of Albi in 1254 organized the Inquisition in the region. Its cathedral of St. Cecilia was built between 1282 and 1512.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandria-d: Alessandria della Paglia is a diocese in Piedmont, Italy, under the archdiocese of Vercelli. Alexander III raised it to a see in 1175, suppressed in 1213, united to Acqui in 1405, suppressed again in 1803, and re-established as fully independent in 1817. It stood vacant from 1854 to 1867. The entry counts 116,000 Catholics, 61 parishes, 143 secular priests, and 188 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandria:
Alexandria is an important Egyptian seaport on the left bank of the Nile, founded by Alexander the Great in 331 B.C. to replace the small borough of Racondah or Rakhotis. Under the Ptolemies it became the world's intellectual and commercial metropolis. Caesar visited it in 46 B.C. and left it to Cleopatra, but Octavius in 30 B.C. turned the Egyptian kingdom into a Roman province, and the city stayed prosperous under Rome before declining somewhat in later Roman times.

After the Byzantines yielded Alexandria to Amru in October 642, Arab rule hastened its ruin. Christianity came there through the Evangelist St. Mark, and the city grew illustrious through learned doctors such as Pantaenus and Clement. The entry then surveys its Christian communities one by one: Copts, Greeks, Latins, Armenians, Maronites, Syrians, Chaldeans, and Protestants, alongside the Catholic missionary orders and their schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alleluia:
Alleluia is a liturgical expression found in Tobit and the Psalter, where it heads psalms of praise or closes them as a glory-giving ovation. In the New Testament it appears only in Revelation 19. In the old Greek Tobit, the Septuagint Psalter, and the original Greek Apocalypse it is transcribed Allelouia. The Vulgate gives it as Alleluia in both Testaments. The English Reformers instead put translated words into the Protestant Psalter and Book of Common Prayer.

From the Temple, through the Coenaculum's thanksgiving hymn, the word passed into Christian worship. Its language, like that of the Septuagint and New Testament, was at first Greek. Its character stayed unchanged, but Christian memories gave it a Paschal sense. Among holy words it gained a mystic meaning. As divine acclaim its force was intensified and the feeling it evoked deepened, so that Alleluia became the worship-word of creation itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-almeria:
Almería, a suffragan see under Granada's archdiocese in Spain, traces its founding at Urci to Indaletius, a follower of St. James the Greater. After a long eclipse, Ferdinand and Isabella gave this little seaport its episcopal honour back in 1489, when Granada fell. Meanwhile it had taken the Arabic name Almería, meaning mirror.

In 1900 all 230,000 of its people were Catholic. Its clergy then numbered 110 parish priests, 32 vicars, and 28 canons and prebendaries. Its buildings counted 122 churches and 50 chapels, with Dominican convents numbering 3 and houses of female religious numbering 4. The see's history runs from its apostolic foundation through centuries of eclipse to its restoration at the fall of Granada. Its early-twentieth-century statistics show a fully Catholic diocese served by a large clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amasia:
Amasia, or Amasea, is a titular see and metropolis of Pontus in Asia Minor on the Iris River, now Amasiah. Its bishops are listed from the third century. It was Strabo's birthplace. The geographer left a vivid portrait of his native city in a deep, extensive gorge beneath a lofty rock, steep on all sides and falling abruptly to the river.

The city was famous for rock cisterns reached by galleries, some traces remaining, and for the Pontic kings' tombs hewn in solid rock. A gorge city crowned by rock, it joined natural strength to ancient fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amelia:
The Diocese of Amelia covers seven towns in Perugia province, Italy, under the Holy See's immediate jurisdiction. Its Umbrian mountain town's Christian origin is wrapped in mystery, and its bishopric appears late. Ughelli names Orthodolphus about 344 and a traceless Stephen, while Flavius seems present at Rome's synod of 14 November 465 under Hilary. Ughelli adds Tiburtius, Martinianus, and Sallustino at Symmachus's 502 synod, plus a fifth-century Sincerus whose very existence the Bollandists question.

A Bishop of Amelia still appears in 649 at Martin's Lateran provincial synod. The city mattered politically in the eighth century, as popes' temporal power grew between iconoclast Byzantine emperors and conquering Lombards. The diocese counts 20 parishes, 31 secular priests, 43 regular priests, 78 churches and chapels, and 19,500 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anaesthesia:
From Greek words meaning without feeling, anaesthesia names a state of numbness to outside impressions. Disease may cause it, or drugs or hypnotic suggestion may bring it on. In nervous disease it often covers a patch of skin, traced by the nerves that serve it. In functional disorders feeling may stop sharply at a line, as if after an amputation, without following any nerve at all.

The practice is ancient in story, from Homer's nepenthe to tales told by Herodotus. Reliable modern use waited for the nineteenth century. Davy described nitrous oxide in 1800 and Faraday proved ether's effect in 1818. The first practical use came in December 1844, when dentist Horace Wells had a tooth drawn under laughing gas. William Morton followed about two years later with ether. Surgeons, the article adds, should warn patients of the risks, since Christian duties performed leave a patient calmer and less open to shock.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andalusia:
Andalusia takes its name from Al-Andalus, the Arab name for the part of Spain under their rule. Saavedra dates the name to after Las Naves in 1212, when the Sierra Morena divided Christian and Moorish lands, for the Moorish territory matching present Andalusia. It fills Spain's south, between Portugal and the Mediterranean. Its area runs about 33,950 square miles, with 3,433,693 people by the census verified in 1900.

Sierra Morena, Sierra Nevada, Sierra Almagrera, and Sierra de Gador rise here, and the Guadalquivir with its tributaries waters the land. Early Iberian peoples included the Turdetani, Turduli, Bastuli, and Bastetani, spread across Seville, Huelva, Jaen, Cordova, Granada, Malaga, Guadix, Baza, and Almeria. Phoenicians settled Cadiz about 1100 before Christ. Carthaginians followed them, and Romans expelled the Carthaginians in turn. Seville's Holy Week and Granada's Corpus Christi show its character. Its famous sons include Suarez, Luis de Granada, Murillo, and Gonsalvo de Cordova.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-della-:
Andrea della Robbia, nephew, pupil, assistant, and sharer of Luca's secrets, was born at Florence in 1431 and died in 1528. His works are often hard to tell from Luca's, but several are certainly his. They include the Foundling Hospital medallions of infants and the Annunciation at its entrance. The Meeting of Saint Francis and Saint Dominic in the loggia of San Paolo and the Madonna of the Architects in the Bargello are his too.

Other certain works include the Virgin adoring the Child in the crib, Saint Francis at Assisi, the Madonna della Quercia at Viterbo, and the marble high altar at Arezzo. His sons Giovanni, Girolamo, Luca the Younger, and Ambrogio carried on the workshop. Giovanni made the reliefs for the Ospedale del Ceppo at Pistoia. Girolamo worked much in France, where he died. The school slowly lost power, its later works often crowded and full of clashing colour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-doria:
Andrea Doria, Genoese admiral and statesman, was born at Oneglia in Italy in 1468 and died at Genoa in 1560. His family belonged to the four great houses disputing supremacy in Genoa, but the Adorni and Fregosi shut the Doria from power. His father died young, and his mother placed him under a relation who captained the guard of Pope Innocent VIII.

At first a condottiere, he served in Innocent's guards from 1487 to 1492. He then served in Alfonso of Aragon's Neapolitan army, to whom he alone stayed faithful after Charles VIII conquered Naples in 1495. He joined the Knights of Saint John and made pilgrimage to the Holy Land. In 1528 he quarrelled with Francis I over unpaid service and entered Charles V's service. At Genoa he was received with enthusiasm, broke the old noble clans, and rebuilt order. In 1547 he crushed the Fieschi and Cibo conspiracy with much cruelty.
