catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andria:
Andria is a diocese in Italy comprising three towns in the Province of Bari and one in the Province of Potenza, in the Archdiocese of Trani. Information about the Christian origin of Andria is impossible to find. Tradition assigns it an Englishman, Saint Richard, as bishop, chosen by Pope Gelasius I about 492. The bishopric probably dates from the time of Gelasius II, elected pope in 1118.

The name Richard is genuine, since a Richard of Andria attended the Eleventh Ecumenical Council, the Third Lateran, in 1179 under Pope Alexander III. The first Bishop of Andria known to history appears unnamed in the Translation of Saint Nicholas Pilgrim, celebrated in Trani in 1143. Like all principal cities of Apulia, Andria holds many artistic remains, notably the Castel del Monte nearby. Andria has 15 parishes, 200 secular priests, 6 regulars, 41 seminarists, and 53 churches or chapels, with 101,000 inhabitants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anne-garcia:
Anne Garcia, the Venerable Anne of St. Bartholomew, was a Carmelite nun and Teresa's companion, born in 1550, died in 1626. Of humble origin, she spent her youth tending flocks. When she first went to Avila, she was refused as too young; for years after, her brothers made her suffer. Finally she entered as lay sister and made her vows in 1572. For ten years she was infirmarian; her prayer and humility endeared her to Teresa, whose companion and secretary she became. Teresa died in her arms at Alba in 1582.

Anne afterwards was prioress at Pontoise, Paris, and Tours, with heavy trials, not least differences with superiors. Warned by a vision, she went to Belgium in 1611 and founded an Antwerp convent, which she governed for life. Twice she delivered the town. In 1735 she was declared Venerable; her beatification is incomplete. Her writings include preserved letters, an Antwerp autobiography, and Paris treatises of 1646.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apameia: Apameia was a titular metropolitan see, a former archbishop's seat now given as a title, in Syria. It stands in the valley of the Orontes river, with a bishops' list dating from the first century. Still flourishing in Crusader times and known to Arabs as Fâmieh, it left vast ruins of very ornate character nearby. The entry also notes two other places of the same name, Apameia Cibotos in Phrygia and a Bithynian see whose list runs from the fourth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aquileia:
Aquileia was a former city of the Roman Empire at the head of the Adriatic. It stands on what is now the Austrian coast at the meeting of the Anse and Torre rivers. For centuries it was the seat of a famous western patriarchate. It therefore plays a large part in church history, above all in the story of the Holy See and northern Italy. Today its site is Aglar, a village of 1,500 people.

Founded in 180 BC on a strip between mountains and lagoons during the Illyrian wars, as a check on a warlike people, its trade grew fast. Marcus Aurelius made it in 168 the empire's chief fortress against northern and eastern barbarians, and it rose to 100,000 people. Pillaged in 238 by Emperor Maximinus, it was so utterly destroyed by Attila in 452 that its site was hard to recognize, and its people fled to the lagoons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arabia:
Arabia, called here the cradle of Islam and probably the primitive home of the Semitic peoples, is a great peninsula. It is bounded by Syria and its desert to the north and the Indian Ocean to the south. The Persian Gulf and Babylonia lie to the east, and the Red Sea to the west. Its western coast runs about 1,800 miles, its breadth about 600 miles, and its area about a million square miles. That area is four times Texas.

Its general shape is a central tableland ringed by a desert belt, sandy west, south, and east and stony north. A line of low sterile mountains rises toward Yemen and Oman. From that geography the long article moves through peoples, history, and religion, above all the rise of Islam and the missions and churches that followed. Readers get a peninsula surveyed as land, peoples, and faith together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-araucania: Araucania, located in Chile, was established by Leo XIII in 1901 and entrusted to the Capuchin friars. The entry counts twenty-eight missionaries at work across the mission territory. Battandier's Annuaire Pontifical Catholique for 1906 is cited as its source, and the note records a mission district rather than a settled diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aristaces-aza:
Aristaces Azaria, a Catholic Armenian abbot and archbishop, was born at Constantinople on 18 July 1782 and died at Vienna on 6 May 1854. Sent at fifteen to Rome's College of the Propaganda, his studies were broken in 1798 by the French invasion. Taking refuge with the Mechitarists of Trieste, he joined their order in 1801 and was ordained priest the same year.

When the short-lived Kingdom of Illyria confiscated his convent's property in 1810, the monks settled at Vienna after vain pleas for restitution. There they lived by teaching Armenian youth and running a printing press. Azaria served as missionary among his compatriots and servant of the Holy See, became general abbot in 1826 and titular archbishop of Caesarea in 1827. Under him the Vienna community prospered, its library grew, and a bookstore joined the press.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armenia:
Armenia, a mountainous region of western Asia southeast of the Black Sea, takes its biblical name Ararat, identical with Urartu of the cuneiform inscriptions. Yet Armenia itself occurs twice in the Vulgate, the Latin Bible. Lacking fixed natural borders, its extent has varied by age, and even Roman times knew a Lesser Armenia as well as a Greater one, the former reaching into Asia Minor. Politically it has been partitioned among Turkey, Iran, and formerly the Soviet Union, Turkey holding the largest share.

The country covers about 120,000 square miles, mainly an elevated plateau crossed by mountain ranges running parallel to the Caucasus in the north. Ararat, the holy mount, is its most noted peak. The article moves from land and borders to peoples, ancient kingdoms, and the Armenian church, giving a region whose map kept shifting under empires while its people and faith endured.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnold-of-bre:
Arnold of Brescia, born toward the end of the eleventh century with death date uncertain, was a reformer whose life is tangled in disputed evidence. Otto of Freisingen says he studied under Abelard, which would put him in Paris about 1115 and explain his later affection for the French master. Abelard summoned him to his cause after the Lateran Council of 1139, as Bernard hints. Other critics find Otto's word alone too thin for that first French stay.

Aspiring to a perfect life, Arnold entered a house of canons regular in his home city, was ordained priest, and became prior or provost of his house. He was fitted by austerity, detachment from earthly things, love of discipline, clarity of intellect, and eloquence. The long article follows his preaching, his clashes with church authority, and his Roman career, weighing sources that praise and sources that condemn a priest who demanded a poorer church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnulf-of-bav:
Arnulf of Bavaria, son of Luitpold of the Agilulfing line and Kunigunde, was duke of Bavaria from 907 to 937, in a troubled time. Magyars had begun predatory raids into Germany, destroying all where they penetrated, and in 907 they advanced on Bavaria in greater numbers than ever. Margrave Luitpold summoned his people's full fighting force, but Bavarians were completely defeated on 5 July 907, with Luitpold, nearly all Bavarian nobles, and several bishops killed.

The land became easy prey and was ruthlessly devastated, while King Louis of the East Franks withdrew westward. In almost hopeless conditions Arnulf began his reign, yet he did not lose courage and on 11 August 909 defeated Magyars on the Rott as they returned from Swabia. That victory did not end raids, but the entry credits Arnulf with restoring Bavarian defence and ducal power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-artoklasia:
Artoklasia, from Greek artos, bread, and klao, to break, the breaking of bread, is a rite in the Greek church performed as the closing part of Vespers, evening prayer. Five loaves of bread, wine, and oil are set on the reading stand before the iconostasis, the screen in front of the altar. They are first incensed, then the priest, taking one loaf in hand, blesses them.

His prayer recalls Christ blessing five loaves in the desert and feeding five thousand, asking him to bless these loaves, wheat, wine, and oil. It asks him to multiply them in this holy abode and throughout the world. It also asks him to sanctify the faithful who partake of them, since he blesses, hallows, and nourishes all good things. Psalm 33 follows, ending with the chanting of its eleventh verse on the rich grown poor. The entry walks readers through a rite of blessed bread.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asia:
Asia, in this article, receives a rapid survey of its geography, peoples, and political and religious history, above all the rise, progress, and present state of Asiatic Christianity and Catholicism. Readers are sent to special articles for single countries. Asia is the largest continent, about 17,000,000 square miles, roughly a third of all dry land, and the oldest known part of the globe. It is the earliest seat of civilization, and probably the cradle of humanity.

Scholars differ on humanity's primitive home: southwestern Asia, above all the Tigris-Euphrates valley, as Genesis tradition suggests, or Central Asia, above all the Indo-Iranian plateau. From that opening question the survey moves across a continent of empires and missions, giving a framework for the encyclopedia's many Asian entries rather than a single country's story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assyria:
Assyria is hard to treat without its sister, or rather mother country, Babylonia, since Semitic Babylonians and Assyrians share race, religion, language, literature, and civilization in ethnographic and linguistic terms. Assyro-Babylonian religion, mythology, and religious literature, above all in relation to the Old Testament, are therefore treated under Babylonia. The history of modern exploration and discovery in both countries is given here.

Geographically Assyria holds the northern and middle part of Mesopotamia between Euphrates and Tigris, while the southern half reaching the Persian Gulf forms Babylonia and Chaldea. Assyria first occupied only a small triangular land between those rivers. The long article follows its growth from that triangle to empire, its kings, its wars, and the digs that brought its palaces and tablets back to light.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-attalia: Attalia, also called Attaleia, was a titular metropolitan see in Pamphylia on the southern coast of Asia Minor. It is likely the same place as modern Adalia, the chief port of that coast. Its bishops are listed for the years 431 to 879 in Gams. Acts mentions it as the harbor where Paul and Barnabas sailed for Antioch after their travels in Pisidia and Pamphylia. A second city of the same name stood in Lydia, with its own list for the same years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atto-of-pisto:
Atto of Pistoia was born at Badajoz in Spain in 1070 and died in 1155, after a career that moved from monastery to bishopric. He became Abbot of Vallombrosa in Tuscany in 1105, and thirty years later he was made Bishop of Pistoia. The entry presents him as a churchman of the reforming age, steady in office and active as a writer.

His writings included lives of St John Gualbert and St Bernard of Vallombrosa, bishop of Parma. In 1145 he brought certain relics of St James of Compostella to Pistoia, an event his surviving correspondence records. That letter exchange, preserved in Ughelli's Italia Sacra, is the main source the entry cites for the transfer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-australia:
Australia is a long survey article on the island-continent, also called New Holland until about 1817. Politically it treats the mainland with Tasmania as the Commonwealth of Australia, under the British Crown, federated on 1 January 1901 from six states. Those states became separate colonies in turn: New South Wales in 1788, Tasmania in 1803, Western Australia in 1826, South Australia in 1836, Victoria in 1851, and Queensland in 1859. The Commonwealth spans 2,980,632 square miles, about a quarter smaller than Europe.

At the census of 1901 the six states together held 3,782,182 people, rising to an estimated 4,002,893 by December 1905. The north and west coasts already appear on Spanish and Portuguese maps from about 1530, but white settlement followed the American War of Independence. The article then traces the convict system that shaped early settlement, the growth of the colonies, and the church's place within them. It closes with a long source list from Moran, Britton, Jose, and the Catholic directories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auxentius-of-:
Auxentius of Mopsuestia is a bishop dated to 360, whom Baronius placed in the Roman martyrology on the strength of a story from Philostorgius. The tale runs that Auxentius had been an officer in the army of the emperor Licinius. He gave up his commission rather than obey an order to offer grapes before a statue of Bacchus, the wine god. The refusal reads as a quiet act of Christian conscience against an idolatrous rite.

Tillemont, however, leans toward a different verdict: Auxentius was probably an Arian, a follower of the heresy that denied Christ's full divinity. His patronage of the heretic Aetius points that way, the entry says. The piece is short, weighing a martyr-like anecdote against a heretical leaning, and leaving the bishop's true standing uncertain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-babylonia:
Babylonia is a vast survey of the ancient empire between the Euphrates and the Tigris, from Baghdad to the Persian Gulf. The article opens by tying Babylonia to Assyria, its northern neighbor and colony. Assyria shared its race, language, and nearly its religion and civilization. Their political fortunes intertwined for over a thousand years. Readers are sent to the Assyria article for sources, exploration, language, and writing, and for much history under Assyrian supremacy.

The land runs diagonally from northwest to southeast, some 300 miles long and 125 wide, about 23,000 square miles, the size of Holland and Belgium together. Its soil is largely river alluvium, like those low countries. A striking feature is the southern land's gain on the sea: the Persian Gulf now recedes about a mile every seventy years. The source list runs from Boscawen and Bezold to Sayce, Jastrow, and Delitzsch on texts bearing on the Old Testament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-o:
Bartholomew of Brescia was an Italian church lawyer, born late in the twelfth century at Brescia, who died in 1258. He studied Roman and church law at Bologna, where he himself became a teacher. He is believed murdered when Ezzelino captured Brescia in 1258. His work was almost all rework of other writers' books.

His Brocarda reworked Damasus's church rules, and his Casus decretorum revised Benencasa's Casus. His Historiae reproduced an unknown author's work, and both Casus and Historiae entered Paris's 1505 edition of Gratian's Decretum. He also revised Tancred's Ordo Judiciarius. Chief was his Glossa Ordinaria on Gratian, fixing Johannes Teutonicus's Glossa. His only sure work of his own was the Quaestiones, lectures given on Sundays and Fridays.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basil-of-sele:
Basil of Seleucia was a bishop and church writer who died, it seems, between 458 and 460. His surviving writings, though wordy and tangled, show great writing skill. Made Bishop of Seleucia in Isauria between 432 and 447, he joined Flavian's 448 Synod of Constantinople against Eutyches. Yet he then attended Ephesus's Robber Synod, voting, likely under threats, to restore Eutyches and depose Constantinople's patriarch.

Taking Pope Leo's letter to Flavian, he joined in damning Eutyches and Dioscurus, saving his see. He stayed a fierce foe of the Monophysites, joining Isauria's bishops in a 458 appeal to Emperor Leo I. Forty-one sermons on Old Testament passages survive under his name, with a life of the first martyr Thecla and her wonders. Most sermons count as genuine, though some are now assigned to Nestorius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-batavia:
Batavia is a vicariate apostolic seated in Java's capital, where Portuguese first brought Christianity. After the Dutch conquered Java in 1596, they set about destroying Catholicism, and priests entering Java were hunted out. In 1807 Pius VII made Batavia the seat of an East Indies prefecture, and missionaries Nelissen and Preffen reached it in 1808. The government first gave them a ruinous Calvinist chapel, then helped them build Our Lady of the Assumption, blessed in 1829.

In 1842 Gregory XVI raised the prefecture to a vicariate, with Monsignor Groof as first vicar apostolic. Vrancken, his coadjutor from 1847, succeeded him in 1852. The vicariate now spans over 340,000 square miles, more than Germany plus Great Britain and Ireland combined. Its stations run from Medan and Padang in Sumatra to Macassar and Menado in Celebes, with 170 Ursuline sisters at Batavia and Surabaya.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-pa:
Bernard of Pavia, a noted canonist, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Provost of Pavia's cathedral chapter, he became Bishop of Faenza in 1190 and Bishop of Pavia in 1198, dying in 1213. About 1190 he compiled the Breviarium Extravagantium, a book of papal decrees outside Gratian's great collection, bringing church law down to his own day.

He quotes authorities in shortened form, hence the title Breviarium, or summary. Bologna welcomed the work, and from Tancred's time it was called the First Compilation. Later decrees and fragments of Roman and German civil law appear beside the papal texts, making it a working book for canon lawyers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethulia:
Bethulia, the city saved by Judith from the siege of Holofernes, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. The Book of Judith tells how Judith slew the Assyrian general and freed her town. The view that Bethulia is merely a symbol for Jerusalem or a made-up town has found little favour, even among critics who doubt the book's history.

Bethulia stands clearly apart from Jerusalem in the text, and its topography points to a definite place, though its site remains disputed, with Sanur and Mithiliye among the candidates. The entry defends a real town behind a story that may itself be a pious romance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-simon-of-c: Blessed Simon of Cascia, an Italian preacher and spiritual writer, was born at Cascia and died at Florence in 1348. He joined the Augustinian Hermits young, distinguished for learning and monastic virtue, and preached with great fruit at Perugia, Bologna, Siena, and Florence. He worked notably among fallen women, founding a house of penance for them and a convent at Florence, and wrote a history of the Gospels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bohemia:
Bohemia, a crown province of Austria-Hungary and an independent kingdom until 1526, fills a mountain-rimmed trough drained by the Elbe. Its area covers 20,058 square miles, ringed by the Bohemian Forest, the Ore Mountains, and the Sudetic range. The Moldau joins the Elbe, which leaves the country at Tetschen in the north.

The 1900 census counted 6,318,697 people, with Czechs at 63 percent and Germans at 36 percent. Beyond geography and population, the entry traces Bohemia's national history and the coming of Christianity. It then surveys present dioceses, religious orders, schools, charities, and the legal ties between Church and state, including marriage, wills, and burial law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bolivia:
Bolivia, a landlocked South American republic since its war with Chile ended in 1881, stretches across the Andes and the Amazon basin. It covered 702,767 square miles, ranking third in size on the continent. Its 1905 population was estimated at 1,816,271, with Catholics outnumbering others by about seventy-two to one.

The country divides into nine departments plus a National Territory of Colonies, with La Paz the most populous and, since 1899, the capital. The southwest rises to great altitude, while eastern rivers, broken by rapids, give the only transit. The entry then treats government, the Church, schools, and the peoples of Bolivia, warning that its statistics are still recent and tentative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brescia:
Brescia, a Lombard diocese between the Mella and Naviglio rivers, grew from a Gallic town taken by Rome in 197 before Christ. Constantine fought Maxentius there in 312, Attila besieged it, and Charlemagne seized it from the Lombards in 774. Its bishops, titled counts from Louis II, ruled city and county until Arduin slew a bishop loyal to Henry II and Henry confirmed the citizens' commune.

Brescia joined Lombard leagues against the emperors and beat off Frederick II's siege in 1238 after Cortenova. Henry VII besieged it for six months in 1311, losing three-fourths of his army. Scaligeri, Luxemburgers, and Visconti then fought over it, Pandolfo Malatesta seized it in 1406, and Filippo Visconti sold it to Venice in 1426. Milan tried again and lost at Maclodio in 1427.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-british-colum:
British Columbia, Canada's westernmost and largest province at 357,600 square miles, is a sea of mountains broken by lakes, valleys, and forests. Vancouver and Queen Charlotte Islands lie offshore, and the mainland runs from Washington and Idaho to the 60th parallel, with Alaska holding a coastal strip north of Portland Canal. Only the Chilcotin plateaus offer level, grassy ground above 3,000 feet.

Ranges include the Lillooet, Cariboo, and Babine mountains, with sierras joining the Rockies to the Coast Range. Great lakes like Babine, Stuart, Kootenay, and Okanagan feed rivers that turn to spring torrents, above all the Fraser with its Nechaco, Quesnel, and Thompson branches. Forests of conifers, with some hardwoods and rare prairies, cover nearly all the rest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bulgaria:
Bulgaria, a Balkan kingdom of 37,200 square miles between the Black Sea, the Rhodope Mountains, Serbia, and the Danube, counted 3,744,283 people in 1900. Greek Orthodox formed the vast majority, with 28,579 Latin and Uniat Catholics, 4524 Protestants, 13,809 Gregorian Armenians, 33,663 Jews, and 643,300 Muslims. By nationality, Bulgarians led with 2,887,860, followed by Turks, Gypsies, Rumanians, Greeks, Jews, Tatars, and Armenians.

At the Christian era's start, the land formed Roman Moesia and Thrace, where the 343 Council of Sardica proves an early church. Slavs pressed in during the migrations, and Bulgars of Hunnic and Finnic stock, driven from the Volga, conquered Moesia and Thrace and founded a kingdom about 680. Prince Boris accepted baptism in 864 or 865, first courting Rome, then joining Byzantium. His son Symeon took the tsar's title in 917 and won an autocephalous patriarchate at Ochrida in 924, before decline set in under Peter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-california:
California, the second state in area and twenty-first in population in 1900, stretches 800 miles from Oregon to Mexico between the Pacific and Nevada. The Coast Range and the Sierra Nevada, rising past 14,000 feet, frame a great valley drained by the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers. Sacramento is the capital, and San Francisco, with 342,000 people in 1900, is the metropolis, ahead of Los Angeles, Oakland, and San José.

Its returns list vast crops of grain, fruit, and vegetables, with lumber, wool, and wine among its products. Its population, counted in the census of 1900, had already grown sharply by 1907, when San Francisco neared 400,000 and Los Angeles 245,000.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-candia:
Candia stands on the north shore of Crete, where an ancient city called Heracleion once stood. Arabs built a new city near the old site in 825, calling it Khandak, from which the Italian name Candia comes, used also for the whole island. Nicephorus Phocas retook it in 960, Venetians held it from 1204, and Turks from 1669.

Under Venice, Crete held eleven Latin sees, with Candia as an archbishopric, and Lequien lists twenty-seven archbishops from 1213 to 1645. Among them were Saint Peter Thomas and Blessed Francis Quirini, but the hierarchy vanished with the Turkish conquest. Pius IX restored the see in 1874 as a suffragan of Smyrna. The diocese counts only about 300 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-passagl:
Carlo Passaglia was an Italian theologian born at Lucca in May 1812 who died at Turin in March 1887. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1827, taught at the Sapienza before thirty, and served as prefect of studies at the German College. After solemn vows in 1845 he took the Gregorian University chair of dogmatic theology. In 1850 he helped prepare the definition of the Immaculate Conception, writing three large volumes on it.

His historical and linguistic method drew fire, with critics saying he put grammar in place of dogma. His works ranged from an annotated Augustine Enchiridion to studies of St. Peter's prerogatives and of the Church. Trouble with his superiors ended in his leaving the Society in 1859, a Turin summons from Cavour in 1861, and late attempts at reconciliation in 1867. He retracted only a few months before his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carpasia:
Carpasia was a titular see of Cyprus, also called Karpasia or Karpasion and sometimes confused with Karpathos. Tradition says King Pygmalion founded it near Cape Sarpedon, today Cape St. Andrea, at the northeast tip of Cyprus a short way north of modern Rhizokarpaso. St. Philo, its first known bishop, received ordination from St. Epiphanius in the fourth century, and left notes on the Canticle of Canticles with a letter and fragments.

Hermolaus attended Chalcedon in 451, and later names come from chroniclers, a seal, and Alexander IV's Constitutio Cypria of 1260, most of them undated. The papal legate Cardinal Pelagius suppressed the see in 1222, yet it lived on in later see lists. Under Latin rule the Greek Archbishop of Arsinoe, of Famagusta, had to reside at Rhizokarpaso.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cartagena-col:
Cartagena in Colombia is a city on an island north of Tierra Bomba, built and fortified by Heredia in 1533. Philip II granted it the title of city in 1579, and it now serves as capital of the State of Bolívar. Clement VII made it a bishopric in 1534. Leo XIII gave it metropolitan rank in 1900. The Dominican Tomás del Toro became its first bishop in 1535.

Later bishops include Antonio de Hervia, first professor at the University of Lima, and Juan de Labrada, who rebuilt the cathedral. José Diaz de Lamadrid built churches and hospitals. He enriched the cathedral with a marble pulpit, mosaics, and a monstrance worth ninety thousand dollars. Pedro Adán Brioschi became the first archbishop. The diocese counts 300,000 people in 98 parishes, with a Jesuit university and college, a seminary, and girls' schools run by nuns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cassovia:
Cassovia, Hungarian Kassa, German Kaschau, and Slavic Kosice, is a Hungarian diocese founded in 1804 by dividing the Diocese of Agria. It covers Abauj, Saros, and Zemplen, and its first bishop was Andrew Szabo, who served from 1804 to 1819. Its episcopal city on the Hernad, 130 miles northeast of Budapest among vine-clad hills, ranks among northern Hungary's chief towns, with a population near 40,000 in 1900, mostly Catholic Magyars.

Benefactors such as Palugyay, Perger, and Schuster shaped the diocese, whose St. Elizabeth Cathedral, restored from 1882 to 1896, counts among Hungary's finest Gothic monuments. It holds 197 parish churches and about 300 priests, a seminary of some fifty theology students, and houses of Premonstratensians, Franciscans, Piarists, Ursulines, and Sisters of Charity. Latin Catholics numbered 307,186 in 1900 with 160,527 Greek Catholics, and a centenary history and picture account appeared in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-castellammare:
Castellammare di Stabia is a diocese whose seat is an industrial city on Naples Bay. It stands on a slope of Monte Gauro, famed for health-giving mineral springs and serving as a naval station. It rose near ancient Stabiae, buried under Vesuvius in 79, and its history runs largely with Naples. Fortified since Angevin times, it took Christianity early, though no bishop register survives from before Ursus at the Roman synod of 499.

Later bishops include Lubentius at Rome in 649, St. Castellus in 827, and Palmerio, champion of church rights against Frederick II. Fonseca was a Trent theologian, Gravina and Maso were theologians and canonists, and del Pezzo was an accomplished orator. Pius VII joined Torre Patria, ancient Liternum, to the see in 1818. The diocese counts 70,400 people in 26 parishes, with 90 churches and chapels and 250 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-castoria:
Castoria was a fortified lakeside town in Macedonia whose name changed with its rulers. Ancient writers knew a settlement near a lake in Orestis as Celetrum, and later writers linked it with Diocletianopolis, rebuilt by Justinian, and with Castoria itself. By the tenth century Bulgarians held it, and in the fourteenth it passed from Byzantine hands to Serbia and then, in 1386, to the Turks.

The town also had a long church history. From at least the reign of Basil II it ranked first among the suffragan sees of Achrida. The see still existed for the Greeks as a metropolitan see when the article was written. Latin bishops survive in records covering the thirteenth through the fifteenth centuries. By 1908 Castoria counted about 10,000 people, Turks, Greeks, and Bulgarians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catalonia:
Catalonia is a principality in the northeast corner of the Iberian Peninsula, inside the Spanish monarchy, covering 12,414 square miles. Its name may come from the Goths and Alans who settled there. Other derivations point to Gothaland, or to a hero of the eastern Pyrenees said to have beaten the Saracens around 756. The land slopes from the Pyrenees toward the Mediterranean. The Ter, Llobregat, Noguera, and Segre rivers water it.

Beyond geography, the article surveys Catalonia's history, its present conditions, and its church life. It describes the ecclesiastical divisions of the region and gives separate accounts of Tarragona, Barcelona, Gerona, Lerida, Solsona, Tortosa, and Urgel, closing with the sources on which the survey rests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catania:
Catania is a Sicilian seaport on the eastern flank of Mount Etna, in fertile country. Founded around 730 B.C. by Chalcidian settlers from Naxos, it grew quickly, changed hands under Syracuse and Rome, and shared Sicily's later fortunes. Eruptions of Etna buried most of its old monuments under lava, so little of the ancient city survives above ground.

The article also traces the Christian history of Catania. Legend credits St. Beryllus with first preaching the faith there, and St. Agatha suffered martyrdom under Decius. Bishops appear at Ephesus in 431 and on missions from Pope Hormisdas, and the modern city supports a university and a library founded in 1755 holding 120,000 volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cervia:
Cervia, a city in Ravenna province, Italy, stands on the ancient Via Flaminia in marshy country near the sea, as seat of a diocese suffragan to Ravenna. Anciently called Phicoclæ, it took its present name before 997, perhaps after a destructive fire in 708. Its political fortunes largely followed those of Ravenna.

The first known bishop, St. Gerontius, was killed by bandits while returning from the Roman council of 501, which had met over accusations against Pope Symmachus. Later bishops of note include the Venetian Pietro Barbo, afterwards Pope Paul II, and Bonifacio Bevilacqua, later cardinal and friend of Gregory XV. The diocese counted 12,696 people, 12 parishes, and 43 secular priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chioggia:
Chioggia, a seacoast city in Venice province, with an important harbour and wide fisheries. Known in antiquity as Fossa Clodia and in the Middle Ages as Clugia, it sheltered refugees from Attila in 452, then passed under Goths, Lombards, and Pepin, King of Italy. It became a republic in the tenth and eleventh centuries, was ruined by the Genoese in their war with Venice, and was freed by the Venetian general Zeno in 1381.

In 1106 Bishop Enrico Grancarolo moved his see from the deserted island of Malamocco to Chioggia. Later bishops include the Dominican Marco Medici, a noted theologian at the Council of Trent, and Gabriello Fiamma, a great preacher of his age. Cardinal Pietro Bembo served as a canon of the cathedral, famed for its pulpit and baptistery. The diocese counts 93,500 people, 31 parishes, and thirteen religious houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-bis:
An entry on Christian, the first Bishop of Prussia, who died in 1245. Before his mission he was a Cistercian monk, probably at Lekno in Poland. In 1209 Innocent the Third charged him with the Prussian missions between the Vistula and the Memel, begun two years earlier. He was made bishop in 1212 and consecrated at Rome in 1215, bringing two converted Prussian nobles for baptism by the pope.

Back in Prussia, pagans rose against foreign settlers and forced converts back to paganism. Christian raised too few crusaders to win, founded the Knights of Dobrin about 1228, and at last called in the Teutonic Order through Duke Conrad of Masovia. In 1230 he gave the order his Culmerland lands and a third of his Prussian lands, keeping church jurisdiction for himself, and under Herman Balk the order pressed the conquest onward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cimbebasia:
An entry on Cimbebasia, long the name for the western part of southern Africa, and on the Prefecture of Upper Cimbebasia. The region first lay in the vast vicariate of Senegambia and the Guineas erected in 1842 under Bishop Barron. Propaganda cut Cimbebasia from it in July 1879 as a prefecture apostolic under the Holy Ghost Fathers, with Father Duparquet as first prefect.

The new field held three regions: the Portuguese north of Amboella and Gangela, the German south of Ovamboland and Damaraland, and Bechuanaland. After attempts in all three, the missionaries concentrated on the north. In August 1892 Propaganda gave Upper Cimbebasia to the Holy Ghost Fathers, Lower Cimbebasia to the Oblates of Mary, and Bechuanaland to the Orange Free State vicariate. Upper Cimbebasia, bounded by the Kassai, the Kunene, and the twenty-second meridian, is worked by twenty priests and eight brothers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claudia:
Claudia, called Klaudia in Greek, Saint Paul conveys her greeting to Timothy with Eubulus's, Pudens's, Linus's, and all the brethren's; she was a Christian woman of Rome. Evidently she stood prominent in the Roman community. The Linus of the text is identified by Saint Irenaeus with Peter's successor as Bishop of Rome. The Apostolic Constitutions call him the son of Claudia, which implies fame at least equal to Linus's.

Attempts have been made to prove her the wife of Pudens. Further, some identify her with Claudia Rufina, wife of Aulus Pudens, the friend of Martial. On that theory she is a lady of British birth, probably King Cogidubnus's daughter. Unfortunately the evidence does not carry the identification beyond possibility, and it remains no more than possibly true.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claudiopolis-:
Claudiopolis in Isauria, a titular see of Asia Minor, stood in Cilicia Tracheia, or Byzantine Isauria, at the central Calycadnus valley's lower end. Its old name was perhaps Kardabounda, and under Claudius it became the Roman colony Colonia Julia Augusta Felix Ninica Claudiopolis. No coins of the city are known. Leake identified it with Mut, a caza's chief village in the Adana vilayet, a view confirmed by inscriptions.

The city was suffragan to Seleuceia. Lequien names only six bishops, from Aedesius at Nicaea in 325 to John at Constantinople in 533, probably the friend of Severus in 508 to 511. In the tenth century Constantine Porphyrogenitus counts it among the ten cities of the Isaurian Decapolis, and it still figures in lists of bishoprics in the twelfth or thirteenth century. Mut, in that era, has about nine hundred inhabitants and vast ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clement-of-al:
Clement of Alexandria, properly Titus Flavius Clemens, was an early Greek theologian heading Alexandria's catechetical school. His birth date is unknown, and he died about 215. Athens, probably his birthplace, stands as the starting-point of his journeyings. Converted to the Faith, he travelled seeking higher instruction. He attached himself in turn to masters in Ionia, Magna Graecia, and Coele-Syria, then to an Egyptian, an Assyrian, and a Palestinian Jew.

At last he met Pantaenus in Alexandria and found rest in his teaching. It was a great centre of culture and trade, with a university grown under state patronage. Its temper was broad and tolerant, and Plato was the favoured old master. Philo, its foremost Jewish thinker, became a sort of Jewish Plato. In the later second century a school of oral instruction arose, with lectures open to pagans and advanced teaching for Christians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colombia:
Adolph Francis Bandelier's entry describes Colombia at the northwest corner of South America. The Caribbean Sea bounds it on the north, Venezuela on the east, and Brazil and Peru on the south. Ecuador lies southwest, the Pacific west, and Panama and the Gulf of Darien northwest. Its area runs from 450,000 to about 500,000 square miles. At least eleven volcanoes, active or dormant, rise within it. Huila, near 19,000 feet, seems its highest point. Since 1870 no census of its people had been tried.

History here runs from 1500, along the Magdalena valley into the interior. German agents of the Welser family entered from the east in 1529. New Granada gained its own audiencia in 1563 and became the Republic of New Granada in 1831. The Church, working with the Spanish king, reached the natives early, and lately turned again to Casanare, where a vicariate Apostolic rose. Article 41 of the constitution ties public schooling to the Catholic religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colonia:
A titular see of Armenia, Colonia is the subject of Sophrone Pétridès's entry. Procopius reports that Justinian restored a fortress once taken by Pompey, fortified it, and named it Colonia. The city appears in the Synecdemus of Hierocles and in the Notitiae episcopatuum as a suffragan of Sebaste, metropolis of Armenia Prima. Lequien names five of its bishops. They run from Euphronius, friend and correspondent of Saint Basil, to Callinicus in 680 and 692.

Other bishops fill out the line. Eustathius served in 458. Saint John the Silent died a monk at Saint Sabas in 557. Proclus was exiled by Emperor Justin in 518 as a Severian. In the ninth century the city became capital of a Byzantine theme. Its modern name is Koilu Hissar, chief town of a caza in the vilayet of Sivas, with about 1,800 people, among them Greeks and Armenians. A second Colonia in Cappadocia gets a brief note.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constantia:
Siméon Vailhé's entry follows Constantia, suffragan see of Arabia under Bostra. It figures in Hierocles's Synecdemus about 533, in Anastasius I's Notitiae episcopatuum in the sixth century, and in Georgius Cyprius's Descriptio early in the seventh century. Only two bishops are known: Chilon at Constantinople in 381, whom Lequien wrongly places at Nicaea in 325, and Solemus at Chalcedon in 451. Eubel lists three Latin bishops of a Phoenician Constantia in the fourteenth century, otherwise unknown and possibly this see.

Waddington likely named Constantia as Brâk, north of Ledja in Trachonitis. Brâk kept a special era, and carved stones prove Constantine adorned it, giving the name Constantia. Its ruins rank important, and Circassian settlers lately came there. Do not mix this Constantia with Amida's see in Mesopotamia, Tella's Jacobite bishopric at Viran-Shehir between Mardin and Edessa, or Salamis, Cyprus's chief city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coria:
Eduardo de Hinojosa y Naveros's entry covers the Diocese of Coria, Cauria, Cauriensis, in Spain, suffragan of Toledo. It includes nearly the entire province of Cáceres, except a few parishes belonging to Salamanca's diocese. Coria's diocese first appears in 589, when Bishop Jacintus subscribed the Third Council of Toledo's acts. Under Visigothic rule Coria was suffragan of Mérida.

During the Arab conquest titular bishops continued the episcopal list. One of them, Jacobus, assisted at Compostela's church consecration in 876. After the city's reconquest in 1142, Alfonso VII turned its mosque into a cathedral, reconstructed in honour of the Blessed Virgin and all saints. Iñigo Navarrón became the new series' first bishop. Statistics for 1906 list 171,041 Catholics, 124 parishes, 159 churches, and 186 chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
The Councils of Aquileia stretch from 381 to 1596, five gatherings in a northern Italian see. The first, under St Valerian with thirty-two bishops, deposed stubborn partisans of Arius and asked emperors to summon an Alexandrine council to end the Meletian schism at Antioch. A council of 553 then opened a century-long breach with Rome over the Three Chapters.

Later synods turned to arson and sacrilege in 1184, and to rival popes in 1409. There Gregory XII declared Benedict XIII and Alexander V schismatical, yet offered to resign if they would. In 1596 Patriarch Francesco Barbaro restated Trent's renewal in nineteen decrees.

Two councils at Bostra in Arabia, in 246 and 247, confronted Beryllus, bishop of the see, and others teaching that the soul perished and rose again with the body. Origen attended these synods and convinced the heretics of their errors, according to Eusebius and Baronius. Harnack, Wright, and Mansi supply the modern sources behind the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-croatia:
A country entry presents Croatia with Slavonia as an autonomous state, bounded by the Danube, the Drave, the Save, and the Adriatic. Its name comes from the Croats, a people whose migrations from White Croatia toward Illyricum and Dalmatia began in the early fifth century.

History follows the Croats from settlement in Pannonia and Dalmatia, through wars with the Avars, to a state headed by the ban, a leader and governor of unlimited power. Later sections cover education and religion, with a university at Zagreb, and the causes of emigration: heavy taxes, unjust tariffs, state monopolies, and a bureaucracy that hampered trade. The entry is a compact portrait of a land on the edge of empires.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-croia:
A short entry describes Croia, a titular see of Albania whose name means Spring. It stands on the site of Eriboea, mentioned by Ptolemy, and appears as a fortress in 1251. Held by the Castriots from 1395, it was the birthplace of George Castriota, called Scanderbeg, the Lion of Albania.

Captured by Mohammed II in 1478, its whole population was slaughtered alongside the Venetian garrison, except for the few who embraced Islam. From the thirteenth century Croia stood as a Latin suffragan of Durazzo, with fourteen bishops recorded from 1286 to 1694. Today it is a chief town in the Scutari region, all Muslim, its Venetian citadel still preserved above the sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cydonia:
A short entry describes Cydonia, a titular see of Crete. Old legend says King Kydon founded it on the north-west shore, and Achaeans and Aeolians later occupied it. It stayed a chief city of the island until Quintus Metellus took it in AD 69. Venetians rebuilt and fortified it in 1252, and Turks captured it in 1645.

Arabs called it Rabdh el-Djebn, modern Greeks and Turks Khania, and western peoples Canea. Lequien's list holds only two Greek bishops: Sebon (458) and Nicetas (692), with Meliton added in 787. After Frankish occupation a Latin see arose, counting sixteen bishops from 1310 to 1645. Canea, now about 20,000 people, mostly Greeks with 200 Latins, keeps a Capuchin parish, Christian Brothers, and Sisters of Saint Joseph.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyrus-of-alex:
A biographical entry examines Cyrus of Alexandria, a seventh-century Melchite patriarch, counted among the authors of Monothelism, dead about 641. Bishop of Phasis since 620, he was consulted by Emperor Heraclius during the Persian campaign about a plan to win Egypt's Monophysites back to the Church and empire.

The plan, from Sergius of Constantinople, kept Chalcedon's two natures of Christ while admitting one divine-human will and operation. Cyrus at first hesitated, then became a staunch supporter and was raised to Alexandria in 630. His nine-article Satisfactio of union was welcomed by Monophysites yet soon fell into discredit as the washy union. Cyrus persisted, accepting the imperial Ecthesis of 637, even as Arab invasion overtook Egypt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dalmatia:
A country entry describes Dalmatia, a strip of the Croatian kingdom along the Adriatic's eastern shore, from Croatia to Montenegro, bounded by Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Velebit and Dinaric ranges wall it inland, Mount Orjen rising highest at 6,225 feet. Its steep, rocky coast is lined with islands: Pag, Rab, Krk, Brac, Hvar, Korcula, and many more.

Poor in water, with only the Krka and Cetina rivers of note, Dalmatia lives chiefly by pasture, fishing, and trade through harbours like Zadar, Split's neighbour Trogir, Sibenik, and Dubrovnik. Its name means land of shepherds. History runs from Illyrian leagues against Rome through Venetian, French, and Austrian rule, while religion and schools, with a seminary at Zadar, anchor its Catholic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daulia:
A short entry describes Daulia, a Greek titular see. Daulis, later Daulia, was a town of Phocis on the Cephissus, some fifteen Roman miles north-east of Delphi. By the end of the seventh century it had become an Athenian suffragan.

In 1393 Talantion was severed from Daulia and made a distinct see, a division Daulia's bishops long protested. Near the close of the fifteenth century the two sees reunited as Daulia and Talantion, and in 1653 the double see briefly became an archbishopric through a Turkish pasha's influence. Suppressed in 1833, Daulia counts about fifteen known Greek bishops, from Germanos, dead in 919, to Neophytos Metaxas, later Metropolitan of Athens.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dei-gratia-de:
A formulary entry explains two phrases added to ecclesiastical titles: By the grace of God, and By the grace of God and the Apostolic See. The first, in the form N. Dei gratia Episcopus N., appears among signatures at Ephesus in 431 and Chalcedon in 451, though it became prevalent only in the eleventh century.

The second form is current since the eleventh century, but archbishops and bishops used it generally only from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The first points to the episcopal office's divine origin, the second the bishops' union with Rome and submission to it. Temporal rulers since Pepin the Short in the eighth century also used the first phrase, and from the fifteenth it signified complete independent sovereignty. Hence bishops in parts of southern Germany must say instead, By God's mercy and the Apostolic See's grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-derry-deria:
A diocesan history of Derry in Ireland, suffragan of Armagh, covering most of County Derry with parts of Donegal and Tyrone. Saint Columba founded its monastic root between 546 and 562, yet no resident bishop appears before Gervase O'Cervallen about 1230. Union of the older Rathlure and Ardstraw sees shaped the diocese, fully defined by the mid-thirteenth century.

Derry's monastery grew into the chief house of Columban monks, and Gelasius, once its abbot, rose to Armagh in 1136. Bishops followed without break until the Reformation, and Redmond O'Gallagher, named in 1569, stood out as Ulster's most active Catholic defender before soldiers killed him in 1601. Vicars then ruled the see until 1683, and later pages trace schools and religious houses into modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-fernand:
Diego Fernandez de Palencia was a Spanish soldier turned historian. He went to Peru about 1545, shortly after the conquest, and fought in the civil wars that tore the colony apart. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he served under Alonso de Alvarado against the rebel Hernandez de Giron in 1553 and 1554.

Charged by the viceroy Hurtado de Mendoza to write the history of those troubles, he set to work at once. Later he widened the work to cover Pizarro and his followers, publishing the whole as a History of Peru at Seville in 1571. The entry values him as an eyewitness who knew the men he described and checked facts with care before setting them down.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dionysius-of-:
Dionysius of Alexandria, bishop from about 247 to 265, was called the Great by Eusebius, Saint Basil, and others. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry places him second only to Saint Cyprian among third-century bishops. Like Cyprian, he excelled more as an administrator than as a theologian, and letters make up most of his writing. Both men were converts from paganism.

Both faced the same three disputes: restoring those who lapsed under Decius, the Novatian schism, and whether heretics needed rebaptism. Both wrote to the popes of their day, yet strangely neither names the other. Only one letter of Dionysius survives in Greek canon law, and the rest is known through Eusebius and Saint Athanasius, his great successor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominic-of-pr:
Dominic of Prussia, born in Poland in 1382, was a Carthusian monk who wrote on the ascetic life. His first teacher was a pious Dominican parish priest, and he later studied at Cracow, where he was noted for intelligence. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he fell into bad habits and a vagabond life until twenty-five, when Adolf of Essen, prior of Saint Alban near Trier, helped him reform. He entered the Carthusian order in 1409.

In the monastery he practiced severe penance with great fervor, and many visions are credited to him. At Mainz he trained novices, and at Saint Alban he served as vicar. With Adolf he spread a prayer form, Dominic's Psalter, which some count among the original shapes of today's Rosary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dulia:
Dulia, from the Greek for service, is the honor paid to the saints, set against latria, worship owed to God alone. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry adds hyperdulia, the higher veneration given to the Blessed Virgin Mary. Saint Augustine distinguished two kinds of service, one due to men, called dulia, and latria, the service of God's worship. Saint Thomas grounded the split in the gap between God's supreme rule and any rule one man holds over another.

Catholic theologians insist the difference is one of kind, not of degree, as wide as the gap between creature and Creator. Even Leibniz, a Protestant, owned an infinite gulf between the honors. The entry points readers to articles on images, relics, and saints for the fuller account of dulia in practice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durazzo-alban:
Durazzo is an archdiocese in Albania on the Adriatic, a town with a good port and chief place of a district in the region of Scutari. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry counts about nine thousand people. Appian credits its founding and its name Epidamnum to a barbarian king, Epidamnus. Dyrrachium came from Dyrrachus, nephew of one of Epidamnus's daughters, who built the port. Thucydides and Strabo more likely make it a colony of Corcyra.

It helped cause the Peloponnesian War, and after Illyrian kings and Roman conquest it won many privileges from Rome. Its port linked Italy to Greece, and Cicero and Pompey sheltered there in disgrace. The entry closes with its modern state, twenty priests, twenty-two parishes, and schools for boys and girls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egfrid-king-o:
Egfrid, also called Ecfrid and Egferd, was King of Northumbria from 670 to 685, born in 650. He took the throne at the death of his father Oswy, beat back Picts who tested his youth, and broke the power of Wulphere of Mercia for a time. Fresh war with Mercia in 679 cost him his brother Aelfwin, but Archbishop Theodore of Canterbury made peace, and Egfrid took the lawful blood price instead of vengeance.

By treaty, annexation, and diplomacy he brought Cumberland, Galloway, and north Lancashire under Northumbrian sway. Hunger for conquest then led him astray. A raid on Ireland in 684 hurt a friendly people who had done the Angles much good, and in 685, against his counsellors' advice, he marched on the Picts. Lured into mountain passes, he was trapped and slain, and his victors buried him on Iona.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-encyclopedia:
An encyclopedia is a summary of human knowledge, whole or in one large field, treated from one point of view. Though the technical word dates only from the sixteenth century, encyclopedic writing reaches back to antiquity. It was born from the needs of general culture in great empires. The learning every free-born Greek and Roman had to gain was grammar, music, geometry, astronomy, and gymnastics. It was called the circle of sciences, and in the Middle Ages the liberal arts.

Systematic encyclopedias fall into two kinds: those arranged by a fixed system of thought, and those arranged alphabetically like a dictionary. Suidas compiled an alphabetical work in the tenth century, though that type grew common only in the seventeenth. Aristotle first tried a summary built on philosophy, while Cato, Varro, Pliny, and Martianus Capella merely gathered materials. Medieval summae and specula likewise strung facts together without a philosophic base.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epiphania:
Epiphania was a titular see in Cilicia Secunda in Asia Minor, suffragan of Anazarbus. Ancient geographers such as Ptolemy, Pliny, and Stephanus Byzantius mention it. It was first called Oiniandos, then Epiphania after Antiochus IV Epiphanes, King of Syria from 175 to 164 before Christ. Cicero once camped there, and Pompey settled some subdued pirates there.

The city kept a special era beginning in the year 37. Seven of its bishops are known, from 325 to 692, the first being Saint Amphion, who suffered under Diocletian and sat at Nicaea in 325. Epiphania was also the birthplace of George, the usurping Bishop of Alexandria in the fourth century. Its ruins stand near Piyas, with walls, a temple, an acropolis, an aqueduct, and many houses in basalt, near the Cilician Gates and the field of Issus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ethiopia:
Ethiopia comes, through the Greek aithiopia, from aitho, I burn, and ops, face: the land of scorched faces. But many writers claim a different origin: the Greeks borrowed it from the Egyptians, who knew the land as Ksh or Kshi by the Twelfth Dynasty. One form, with the aleph prefix, Ekoshi, would thus be the root-word. Others derive it from the Arabic atyab, plural of tib, meaning spices or perfumes, or from an Arabo-Sabean word, atyub, of the same meaning.

It is not easy to say where the name Ethiopia properly applies in history. The territory it covered, and even the word's use for a territory, have varied across ages and writers. In the early Bible Ethiopia designates the lands of the sons of Cush, applied to all their scattered regions. Elsewhere in the Bible it denotes a definite region without regard to race, and is thus geographical.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-euaria:
Euaria was a titular see of Phoenicia Secunda or Libanensis, in Palestine. A Syriac inscription dating from the fourth to the sixth century gives the city's true name as Hawârin. Ptolemy placed it in the Palmyrene province. Georgius Cyprius gives it as Euarios or Justinianopolis. The sixth-century Notitiae episcopatuum of Antioch gives it as a suffragan of Damascus.

Thomas, one of its bishops, is known in 451, and some uncertainty surrounds another, John, who lived a little later. Today El Hawârin is a large Mohammedan village three hours north of Karyatein, on the road from Damascus to Palmyra. Ruins of a Roman castellum and a basilica are still visible there. Euaria, or Hawârin, must not be confused with Hauara or Havara, another titular see in Palaestina Tertia, south of Petra.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eucarpia:
Eucarpia was a titular see of Phrygia Salutaris in Asia Minor. Eucarpia, mentioned by Strabo and other geographers, lay on a road from Dorylaeum to Eumenia. It stood between the Dorylaeum-Acmonia and Dorylaeum-Synnada roads, probably at modern Emin Hissar, in the vilayet of Brusa. Hamilton saw imposing ruins there in 1837; they have almost vanished. Nothing is known about the city's history.

It struck its own coins from the time of Augustus till the reign of Volusianus. The bishopric, a suffragan of Synnada, figures in the Notitiae episcopatuum until the twelfth or thirteenth century. Six bishops are known. They are Eugenius at Nicaea in 325, Auxomenus in 381, Cyriacus in 451, Dionysius in 536, Constantine or Constans in 787, and Constantine in 879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eudocia:
Ælia Eudocia, sometimes wrongly called Eudoxia, was the wife of Theodosius II, dead about 460. Her original name was Athenais, daughter of Leontius, one of the last pagans who taught rhetoric at Athens. Leontius, dying, left nearly all his property to his two sons. To Athenais he left only 100 pieces of gold, saying her luck was greater than that of all women.

She came to Constantinople to dispute the will, and was seen by Pulcheria, Theodosius II's elder sister, who ruled for him until he came of age. The emperor, just twenty, had already expressed his wish to marry, and both he and Pulcheria were greatly delighted with Athenais. She was instructed in the Christian Faith and baptized by Patriarch Atticus. On 7 June 421 she married Theodosius. At her baptism she had taken the name Eudocia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eulogia:
Eulogia is a Greek word for a blessing, and this short entry traces how the Church used it for blessed things. At times in the early Church it stood for the Holy Eucharist itself. That use is frequent in Saint Cyril of Alexandria and rooted in Saint Paul's words about the cup of blessing. More often, though, it meant bread, wine, and other food blessed and handed out after the celebration of the Divine Mysteries.

Saint Augustine notes that such blessed bread was given in his day to catechumens, people still preparing for baptism. He calls it holy, though not the Body of Christ. The entry also gives the word a monastic sense. Under the Rule of Saint Benedict, monks could not take letters, blessed gifts, or small presents without the abbot's leave. Blessed bread was also shared in the refectory after Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eumenia:
Eumenia was an ancient city of Phrygia Pacatiana in Asia Minor, now remembered as a titular see, a former bishopric kept on the Church's list. King Attalus II Philadelphus founded it between 159 and 138 before Christ. It stood by the Cludrus springs near the Glaucus, where modern Ishekli stands, and took its name from the founder's brother Eumenes. Coins and inscriptions show it was a rich and busy city under Roman rule, proud of its claimed Achaean origin.

The entry stresses its Christian story above all. By the third century much of its people were Christian, and it suffered heavily in the persecution under Diocletian. Its bishop and martyr Saint Thraseas belongs to that age. Later bishops are known from council records: Theodore in 361, Leo in 787, and Paul and Epiphanius in 879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-of-a:
Eusebius of Alexandria is a shadowy church writer known for homilies, or sermons, widely read in the sixth and seventh centuries and prized for teaching on conduct and doctrine. Almost nothing about his life is sure. The old biography said to come from his notary, the monk John, makes him a monk near Alexandria. Cyril chose him as successor in 444, against his will, and he later retired to the desert. Yet neither Eusebius nor his supposed successor Alexander appears in the lists of bishops of Alexandria, where Dioscurus follows Cyril.

Scholars have therefore assigned the homilies to Eusebius of Emesa, to Eusebius of Caesarea, to a fifth-century monk, or to a court chaplain of Justinian I. Whoever wrote them, they cover many subjects and rank among the earliest witnesses to the teaching on Christ's descent into Hell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-of-n:
Eusebius of Nicomedia was the court bishop who led the Arian party after the Council of Nicaea and spent his career trying to undo its work. He moved, against church canons, from Berytus to Nicomedia, home of the eastern emperor Licinius, whose wife Constantia favored him. When Arius was condemned at Alexandria, Eusebius took up his cause and wrote letters for him. He taught that the Son was created, other in nature and power from the Father, and begotten by God's free will.

At Nicaea in 325 his Arian confession won only about seventeen backers out of three hundred bishops. He signed the Nicene Creed but not the condemnation of Arius, for which Constantine exiled him for two years. Recalled through Constantia's influence, he headed the compact Eusebian party. He helped depose Eustathius of Antioch and other Nicene bishops and pressed the Arian cause at court until his death in 341.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-euthanasia:
Euthanasia, from Greek words for well and death, means an easy, painless death. This short entry treats it only as far as it may be brought about by drugs. When such drugs take away the sufferer's use of reason, Catholic teaching does not approve their use at the supreme hour of life. The reason given is that the dying person loses the power to act well at the moment when such action matters most and bears final fruit.

A further reason is that giving such drugs amounts in effect to shortening life. So long as the sick person has not yet made due ready for death, it is gravely wrong to bring on a state of feeling nothing. No positive approval can ever be given to means meant to make a person die without knowing it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eutropius-of-:
Eutropius of Valencia was a Spanish bishop who died about 610. He began as a monk in the Monasterium Servitanum, a house in the province of Valencia founded in the sixth century by Donatus, a monk driven from Roman Africa by Vandal persecution. Eutropius succeeded Donatus as abbot. He is known for three letters: one to Licinianus of Carthagena, two to Peter of Iturbica.

His letter to Peter on the ruin of monasteries, which Saint Isidore says every monk should read, holds that earnest monks matter more than many monks. He defends strict correction of faults as a first duty of a superior. His second letter to Peter treats the deadly sins, counting eight after Cassian: pride, vanity, faint-heartedness, sadness, anger, covetousness, lust, and gluttony. He traces their links and urges Christians to fight them with God's help. He became Bishop of Valencia in 589.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evangeliaria:
Evangeliaria are liturgical books holding those Gospel parts read at Mass or in the Church's public offices. The name itself dates only from the seventeenth century. Greeks called such collections the Euangelion, or Gospel, while the Latin Church more often grouped Old Testament lessons, Epistles, and Gospel parts in one book, the Comes or Lectionary. 

Following synagogue custom, the early Christians read Scripture at their assemblies, and as the New Testament canon took shape, Gospel extracts joined the readings. Bishops at first chose passages, then fixed lists grew, and notes in the margins of manuscripts grew into full collections. Greek fragments survive from the fourth century, and Gregory counts over a thousand from the ninth century on. The entry also notes their rich ornament, their small value for textual criticism, and their lasting liturgical interest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feria:
Feria, Latin for free day, began as a Roman public and legal holiday. On feriae the people, especially slaves, were not obliged to work. No courts sat, and the days marked public rest. Christian feasts and fasts later took the name for days of religious rest and worship.

Great feast crowds drew markets, giving rise to the English word fair. Today feria names the weekdays except Sunday and Saturday. Major feriae of Advent, Lent, and Ember days must at least be commemorated. Ash Wednesday and Holy Week days keep their own office always.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florilegia:
Florilegia are systematic collections of excerpts from the Fathers and early church writers. They served dogmatic or ethical ends, gathering approved teaching for ready reference. The need arose in fifth-century Christological disputes, when councils wanted handy summaries. Cyril laid such a summary before Ephesus in 431; others served Chalcedon in 451.

Dogmatic florilegia reached full form in the seventh century, notably at the Sixth Council in 680. The oldest great example, the Doctrina Patrum, holds 977 citations from 93 writers. Ascetical florilegia gather moral sentences on virtues, vices, and duties of religious life. The Sacred Parallels, long ascribed to John Damascene, contrasted virtues with vices side by side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-foggia:
Foggia is a diocese in Apulia, in a rich farming plain between the Cervaro and Celone. It grew around the church of the Madonna of the Seven Veils, built in 1072 by Robert Guiscard. Its name comes from fogia, or marsh, for the swampy ground it stands on. Frederick II built an imperial fortress there; Charles of Anjou destroyed the city in 1268.

Made a diocese by Pius IX in 1855, it was united with Troia in 1907. Its cathedral, often restored, holds the tombs of the Princes of Durazzo. The city counts 81,000 people in nine parishes, with schools and religious houses. A severe earthquake greatly damaged Foggia in 1781.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fortunato-of-:
Fortunato of Brescia, born in 1701 and dead at Madrid in 1754, was a Franciscan Minorite, philosopher, theologian, and pioneer of modern morphology. Morphology is the study of the forms and structures of living things. He took the religious habit in 1718, became secretary general of his order, favoured at the Bourbon court of Spain. His philosophical writing tried to bring scholastic thought together with the new discoveries of physical science.

His fame rests on the microscope. Following Malpighi, he studied the fine structure of organs. He argued that microscopic anatomy holds the key to nature. He was the first to draw a clear line between tissues, parts with a definite structure seen under the microscope, and organs built from them. He described connective and bony tissue and classified tissues and organs years before Bichat, who later got the credit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-ant:
Francesco Antonio Zaccaria, born at Venice on 27 March 1714 and dead at Rome on 10 October 1795. He was a Jesuit theologian, historian, and astonishingly prolific writer, with 161 printed works to his name. He joined the Austrian province of the Society of Jesus in 1731, was ordained at Rome in 1740, preached and lectured in Ancona, Fermo, and Pistoia. In 1751 he succeeded the great Muratori as ducal archivist and librarian of Modena.

Removed in 1768 for his Antifebronio, a vigorous defence of the rights of the Holy See, he became librarian at the Jesuit professed house in Rome. He drew a papal pension, and was made professor of church history at the Sapienza and director of the Academy of Noble Ecclesiastics. He belonged to at least nineteen Italian academies. His works include histories of bishoprics, defences of the Bollandist saints' lives, and editions of canonists and historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-lor:
Francesco Lorenzo Brancati di Lauria, born at Lauria in the Kingdom of Naples on 10 April 1612 and dead at Rome on 30 November 1693. He was a Conventual Franciscan cardinal and theologian. Stricken with a dangerous illness at seventeen, he vowed to enter the Minor Conventuals if he recovered and took the habit at Lecce in July 1630. He taught philosophy and theology with notable success in the noted convents of his order.

In 1653 he took the chair of dogmatic theology at the Roman University and became consultor of the Holy Office, whom Alexander VII called a mainstay of the Apostolic See. He was chief librarian of the Vatican under Clement X. Innocent XI made him cardinal in 1681. He served on at least ten Roman congregations, coming within fifteen votes of the papacy itself after Innocent's death, blocked only by Spain's veto. His ascetical writings show a master of the spiritual life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francia:
Francia, born Francesco Raibolini at Bologna about 1450 and dead in 1517, was a goldsmith, engraver, and painter who shows what Italian art owed to the minor arts. His father carved wood. Francesco joined the goldsmiths' guild in 1482 and led it the next year, taking the name Francia from his master Duc, either in gratitude or as a valuable trade mark. In his age painting had not yet been ranked above crafts, and the goldsmith's care for detail, ornament, and beauty lifted painting above routine pious imagery.

His medals, nielli, enamels, jewellery, armour, and type founding display the industrial side of his art. His paintings, pure and original, kept him apart from the pagan and rationalist movement of his century. The entry calls him the leading personality in northern Italian art before Titian and Correggio, a solitary man of great and noble gifts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-borgi:
Francis Borgia, born 28 October 1510 and dead 30 September 1572, was a Spanish saint whose life ran from the highest court in Europe to the leadership of the Jesuits. Great-grandson of Pope Alexander VI on his father's side and of King Ferdinand of Aragon on his mother's, he grew up at the court of Charles V. He married Eleanor de Castro in 1529 and became Marquess of Lombay, equerry to the empress, and a model courtier gifted in sacred music.

The empress's death in 1539 turned him toward a stricter Christian life. As viceroy of Catalonia from that year he reformed justice, finance, and monasteries, and in 1543 he became Duke of Gandia. After his wife's death in 1546 he joined the Jesuits in 1548 and became commissary-general in Spain in 1554. He took charge of all Jesuit missions and was canonized by Clement X in 1670.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-of-vi:
Francis of Vittoria, born about 1480 at Vittoria in Old Castile and dead on 12 August 1546. He was a Spanish Dominican theologian called the father of the Salamanca school and of the new scholasticism. Moving young with his parents to Burgos, he entered the Dominicans and studied at the order's chief house in Paris. He taught there from 1516 with Dominic de Soto among his pupils, and returned to Spain in 1522, teaching at Valladolid until 1524. He then took the principal theology chair at Salamanca, holding it until 1544.

 He left many valuable manuscripts, but his sole published work is the twelve theological relections, printed at Antwerp in 1604. His commentary on the whole Summa of St. Thomas remains among his unpublished writings, a monument to his teaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-de-:
Francisco de Vargas y Mexia, born at Madrid at an unknown date and dead at the Hieronymite monastery of La Sisla in 1566. He was a Spanish diplomat and ecclesiastical writer of the Council of Trent. Of an old family of the lower nobility, he studied law at Alcala, became licentiate in law, and rose to fiscal, or attorney-general, of the Council of Castile. In 1545 Charles V sent him to Trent. In 1548 he protested the council's transfer to Bologna, and in 1551 he welcomed its return to Trent.

From 1552 to 1559 he served as Spanish ambassador at Venice and negotiated at Rome in 1558 over recognising Ferdinand I as emperor and founding new dioceses in the Netherlands. From 1559 he succeeded Figueroa as ambassador to the Curia, taking an important part in electing Pius IV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fray-nicolas-:
Nicolás Armentia, a Spanish Minorite who became bishop of La Paz in 1901, spent his best years as a missionary in Bolivia's Beni region. Born in 1845, he had studied physics, astronomy, and natural science in France. He then sailed to South America under Father Rafael Sans. The entry traces a scholar-priest who cut his own paths between remote hamlets.

Among small, often hostile tribes thinned by smallpox, Armentia preached and rebuilt missions. He also gathered notes on the land, its creatures, and its peoples. His books include a diary of exploring the Madre de Dios in 1884 and 1885. He also wrote a description of the Mojos province and a Shipibo vocabulary of more than 3,800 words, still the fullest word list of its language family.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaudentius-of:
Gaudentius of Brescia, a Capuchin theologian born in 1612, ranks among the foremost voices of the Franciscan school. Sprung from the noble Bontempi house, he entered the Capuchins and served as lector of theology, visiting convents across his Brescia province and other Italian houses of study. He fell ill at Oriano while preaching a Lenten course and died there in March 1672.

His fame rests on the Palladium Theologicum, a scholastic theology built on Saint Bonaventure, praised for style, depth, and sound doctrine. His pupil Durantio published it after his death, and Louis XIV had it vetted by Sorbonne doctors before its Lyons issue in seven folio volumes in 1676. His remains now rest at the Capuchin church of Verola.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georgia:
Georgia, the largest of the original thirteen states, is surveyed here in its geography, growth, and Catholic life. Bounded by Tennessee and North Carolina north, the Savannah River and Atlantic east, and Florida and Alabama south and west, it spans 59,475 square miles. Population rose from 82,548 in 1790 to 2,216,331 in 1900, with Savannah the largest city at 54,244.

Cotton leads an unmatched variety of farm products, with 1,920,000 bales in 1907, while manufactures reached over 151 million dollars in 1905 and railroads ran 6,786 miles in 1907. Schools run from the state university at Athens, founded in 1785, to Atlanta, Clark, Emory, and Morris Brown colleges. The Diocese of Savannah, comprising the whole state and established in 1850, counted 23,000 Catholics in the 1908 census, with eighteen secular and forty-one religious priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-germanicia:
Germanicia, a titular see in Euphratensis under Antioch, is often misplaced and misnamed. An 1884 Propaganda catalogue expressly fixes it in Euphratensis, not Germaniciana in Byzacene, Africa. Le Quien names five Greek bishops, among them the Arian Eudoxius, later Bishop of Antioch and Constantinople. He adds four Jacobite bishops and at least eighteen more from the eighth to the thirteenth centuries, if Germanicia equals Marash, which remains unproven.

Müller's Ptolemy texts contradict each other so sharply that no conclusion stands, and he prefers the nearby ruins of Altun-Tash-Kale. If Germanicia is Marash, that industrial city in Aleppo's province counts 52,000 people. About 15,000 are Catholics of Melchite, Armenian, Chaldean, and Latin rites, with 22,000 Muslims and the rest schismatic Christians or Jews. Its climate is described as very healthy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-germia:
Germia, a titular see of Galatia Secunda suffragan of Pessinus, rose and vanished across seven centuries of lists. Hierocles names it in the sixth century, and about 650 it already stood as an autocephalous archdiocese directly under Constantinople. The same rank held in the ninth century, under Leo the Wise from 901 to 907, under Constantine Porphyrogenitus, and under Alexius I Comnenus after 1084.

About 1260, under Michael Palaeologus, Germia must have become an autocephalous metropolitan see, a rank it kept under Andronicus II about 1300 and Andronicus III about 1330, before soon disappearing. Lequien knows four titular bishops. From Justinian's reign it bore the name Myriangeloi for its church of Saint Michael and the Holy Angels, and Justinian took its baths in 556. Today it is Germa village, twenty-one miles southeast of Sivri-Hissar, its ancient baths and Justinian's inn still visible. It must not be confused with Germa of Cyzicus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ghardaia:
In 1901 the French Sahara gained a Prefecture Apostolic at Ghardaia, carved from the Vicariate Apostolic covering Sahara and the Soudan. Its region stretched from Morocco's prefecture and the Algerian and Tunisian dioceses to Tripoli's mission and the twentieth parallel north. About three hundred thousand people lived there, all Muslims of Arab and Berber stock. Nomadic tribes crossed the wastes, while settled folk kept the oases, including the Mozabites of the Mzab district.

Three stations carried the mission: Ghardaia, Wargla, and Elgolea. The White Fathers staffed them with twelve missionaries and three lay brothers, in a land where open preaching could not begin at once. Their task was preparation through charity, teaching, and steady friendly contact. Only slowly, the article argues, would old prejudice toward Christians soften, and a younger generation arise among whom lasting conversions could take hold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gift-of-tongu:
The gift of tongues, or glossolalia, is a supernatural grace meant to help the early Church grow outward. A Catholic Encyclopedia article treats its scriptural and historical side, leaving its theology to the article on charismata. At Pentecost, Luke relates, one hundred and twenty Galilean disciples were heard speaking in many tongues as the Holy Spirit gave them speech.

Devout Jews and proselytes from fifteen lands, gathered at Jerusalem, each heard the wonderful things of God in his own tongue. Peter explained the marvel by prophecy as a sign of the last times. The article stresses that the speech was real, clear, and intelligible, with the variety belonging to the group rather than to single speakers. Later outpourings followed at Caesarea, Ephesus, and Corinth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-anim:
Giovanni Animuccia was an Italian composer born at Florence about 1500, who died in 1571. A pupil of Claude Goudimel, he became choir-master at the Vatican and kept the post until his death. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the real predecessor of Palestrina, in office and in his search for harmonic clearness amid the counterpoint of the day.

He sought to perfect the old Flemish style with fuller harmony, more natural voice leading, and a closer fit between melody and text. His friendship with St. Philip Neri made him music-master of the saint's new society. For it he wrote the first laudi, songs of praise sung after the sermon. Those laudi, in volumes of 1566 and 1570, became the germs of the later oratorio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Beccaria was a physicist born at Mondovì in 1716, who died at Turin in 1781.
