Two great white feather fans were carried beside it, a survival of an older liturgical fan.

Coronations and solemn entries to Saint Peter's were its chief outings. The entry lingers on the coronation rite. Bundles of flax were burned before the new pope, with the warning that worldly glory passes. It also traces the carrying custom back through bishops and Roman consuls to early witnesses like Ennodius of Pavia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sedilia:
Stone seats set into the south wall of a sanctuary gave the clergy a place to sit during parts of the liturgy. This entry explains those seats, called sedilia from the Latin word for a seat. The earliest examples were single stone seats in the catacombs. Later came matching seats for deacon and subdeacon. Three became the usual number in English churches.

English sedilia grew common in the 1100s and 1200s. They were often carved as rich niches with canopies, shafts, and pinnacles. Some were joined to the piscina basin. The entry names places with four or five seats. It notes that the celebrant took the highest and easternmost seat. It contrasts England's stone niches with the movable benches used elsewhere in Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-see-of-tinin-:
Knin, a fortified town on the Kerka river in Dalmatia once called Ardula by the Romans, anchors this short diocesan entry. At the request of King Casimir IV of Croatia, a bishopric was created there in 1050. Its bishop was attached to the royal court as preacher. The entry follows the line of prelates from Mark in 1050 down to Joseph in 1755.

A Saracen invasion broke the residential succession in 1622. After Venice took the district in 1768, the bishop of Sebenico administered the see. It was joined to Sebenico in 1828. Ruins of the old cathedral of Saint John the Evangelist still stand. The entry closes with the see's standing as a titular bishopric under Kalocsa and its then bishop, Joseph Lányi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-segovia:
The diocese of Segovia in Spain, stretching across Segovia, Valladolid, Burgos, and Avila with a city of about 15,000 people, gets a full local history in this entry. A forged chronicle's claim is set aside as refuted. It had named Hierotheus, teacher of Dionysius the Areopagite, as the first bishop. The likelier story is told instead. Segovia belonged to Palencia until 527, when a disputed consecration led Toledo's metropolitan to grant the city to the new bishop for life.

From Petrus, who signed as bishop at the Third Council of Toledo in 589, the entry tracks bishops through Visigothic councils, the Moorish period, and later centuries. Notes on the cathedral and diocesan life run alongside. Readers looking for the region's monuments and church history are pointed to the standard Spanish sources the entry cites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seleucia-pier:
Seleucia Pieria was a titular metropolis of Syria Prima near the mouth of the Orontes. Seleucus Nicator founded it about 300 BC, on or near the site of an older city called Palaeopolis. This entry follows its career as the seaport and naval base of Antioch. It was captured and recaptured by Ptolemies and Seleucids. It long enjoyed freedom and the right to coin money. Its harbour was enlarged repeatedly under emperors like Diocletian.

Paul and Barnabas stopped there, the entry notes, though nothing shows they made converts. The city's church history runs from Zenobius at Nicaea in 325 through later bishops to its standing as an autocephalous archbishopric in the sixth century. Famous sons included Apollophanes, physician to Antiochus, and Firmus, who stirred Palmyra and Egypt against Rome in 272.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-selymbria:
Selymbria, a titular see in Thracia Prima suffragan to Heraclea, was a Megarian colony on the Propontis founded before Byzantium. It was the birthplace of Prodicus, a disciple of Hippocrates, and the place where Xenophon met the envoy of Seuthes. In 410 BC Alcibiades, refused entry, took money from the town, then later seized it by treachery and left a garrison.

Renamed Eudoxiopolis for the empress Eudoxia, it was pillaged by the Bulgarian king Kroum in 805 and later fortified by Michael III. Byzantine historians mention it often. Godfrey of Bouillon ravaged its country in 1096, and the Turks captured it in 1453. Now Silivri, it holds 8,000 people, mostly farmers or fishermen, Turks and Greeks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-senegambia:
Senegambia, a vicariate apostolic joined to the prefecture of Senegal in French West Africa, is the subject of this mission history. A Norman trading settlement of the 1300s died in the troubles of the Hundred Years War. Portuguese ships reached Gambia and Sierra Leone in 1432, and in 1446 came the first sale of local people in the Lagos market. English, Dutch, and French traders followed, each chasing the profits.

French settlers also planted the cross, and the entry follows the missionaries who came after them. Norman Capuchins arrived in 1637, only to be poisoned or expelled by the Dutch. Dominicans entered under French protection after Admiral d'Estrées seized the Senegal posts in 1672, and Franciscan Observants began work in 1686. Later chapters cover the vicariate's growth, its schools, and its clergy under the Holy Ghost Fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-servia-serbia:
Servia, a European kingdom in the northwest of the Balkan peninsula, is given a sweeping history in this long entry. Much of its land once belonged to the Roman provinces of Moesia and Dalmatia, where cities rose along the Danube and Morava and Christianity entered early. Martyrs appear only under Diocletian, at Singidunum, now Belgrade. Ostrogoths, Huns, and Lombards crossed the land in turn.

Southern Slav forefathers of the Serbs arrived in the seventh century and gave the country its name. The entry follows medieval princes, the Ottoman conquest of 1459, and centuries under Turkish rule, when folk songs kept national memory alive. It closes with the revolts of Karageorge in 1804 and Milosch Obrenovich in 1815, and the slow road toward a self-governing principality.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-siberia:
Siberia, the Russian possession forming the northern third of Asia, runs from the Urals to the Pacific and from the Arctic coast to about the fiftieth parallel. It covers 4,786,730 square miles and held 5,758,822 people in 1897, rising to about 7,878,500 by 1909. Russians formed the great bulk, beside Poles, Germans, Finno-Ugrians, Turko-Tatars, Buriats, Samoyedes, Tunguses, Chinese, and Koreans. Orthodox Greeks dominated in religion, with Catholics numbering near 74,000, largely exiled Poles and Ruthenians.

The Russian advance eastward followed the great rivers, from Cossack conquests and peasant settlements to Yakutsk in 1632 and Irkutsk in 1652. The Siberian eparchy dates to 1621, and the border settlement with China to 1728 and 1729. The founding of Omsk and Semipalatinsk and the scientific exploration of a region long unknown follow. Catholic missions, schools, and the hardships of exile complete the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sicca-veneria:
Sicca Veneria, a titular see in Africa Proconsularis suffragan to Carthage, was an ancient and important town in Numidia, very likely of Phoenician origin. It stood on the Bagradas river, on the road from Carthage to Hippo Regius, and took its name from a celebrated temple of Venus. After the first Punic War the Carthaginians sent their feared mercenaries there. Under Augustus it gained the title of colony, and it also bore names linking it to Cirta.

Arnobius taught rhetoric there under Diocletian. Six bishops are known, from Castus at Carthage in 255 to Candidus in 646. The town kept strategic value commanding the roads from Algeria to Tunis until the French occupation. Arabs called it Shikka Benar, but it is better known as Le Kef, chief town of a district in Tunis with 6,000 people, a railroad, two mosques, a fortress, and Roman ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-silesia:
Prussian Silesia, the largest province of Prussia, covers 15,557 square miles along the whole course of the Oder. In 1905 it held 4,942,612 people, of whom Lutherans numbered 2,120,361, Jews 46,845, and Catholics 2,765,394, with Germans at 72 per cent and Poles near 25 per cent. Farming flourished on two thirds of the land, mining of iron, lead, and coal ran large, and manufactures included hardware, glass, china, linen, and cotton goods.

Earliest Silesia was German, held by the Lygii and Silingii, then Slavonic for some eight hundred years after the migrations. Christianity came from Bohemia and Moravia through Cyril and Methodius. Its story runs through Piast divisions into eighteen principalities, Bohemian overlordship, Hussite devastation, the Reformation's rapid advance, Jesuit restoration through nine colleges, and Prussia's seizure after the three Silesian wars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sinigaglia:
Sinigaglia, also called Senigallia, is a diocese in Ancona province in Italy's Marches. The city sits on the Adriatic at the Misa's mouth, which cuts it in two. Sea trade, silk, farming, and cattle raising support the people. Santa Maria delle Grazie of 1491 outside the walls holds a Perugino Madonna with six saints.

The name recalls the Senones, Gauls who held the city before Rome's conquest, when it became the colony Sena Hadria, later Senogallia. Pompey sacked it in the civil war of 82 BC, Alaric pillaged it in 408, and under Byzantine rule it joined the Pentapolis. Lombards tried repeatedly to take it in the 500s and 600s, and shortly before its gift to the Holy See it served a Duke Arioldo, owing allegiance to King Desiderius in 772. Later it shared the March of Ancona's fortunes. The diocese, suffragan to Urbino, counts 48 parishes and 92,000 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-siunia:
Siunia is not a town but a province between Goghtcha, Araxa, and Aghovania, in the Russian districts of Chamakha, or Baku, and Elisavetpol. Its true name should be Sisacan, the Persian form, since Siunia took its name from Sisac, son of Gegham, fifth Armenian sovereign. Its first rulers, vassals of Armenian kings or Persian shahs, date to the fourth century, and about 1046 it became an independent kingdom until 1166.

The Church of Siunia arose in the fifth century or a little earlier and soon became a metropolis under the Catholicos of Armenia, counting twelve suffragan sees in 1006. The archdiocese held 1,400 villages and 28 monasteries, with its metropolitan seat fixed at Tatheo in the ninth century. In 1837 the Synod of Etchmiadzin suppressed the diocese, placing it directly under the catholicos. The entry notes the Roman Curia's use of this title is unexplained, since it appears in no Greek or Latin list of sees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-agnes-of-b:
St. Agnes of Bohemia, also called Agnes of Prague, was born in 1200 and probably died in 1281, a king's daughter who refused an emperor for the cloister. Daughter of Ottocar, King of Bohemia, and Constance of Hungary, kinswoman of St. Elizabeth, she was schooled young by Cistercians at Treinitz in a manner fitting her rank.

Betrothed to Frederick II, Emperor of Germany, she would not abandon her resolve to consecrate herself to God when the marriage day came. Frederick was furious at the failed match. Yet, on learning she had left him to become the spouse of Christ, reportedly said he could not take offence, since no mortal man had taken her from him. The entry gives a royal vocation in a few vivid strokes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alexander-:
St. Alexander was patriarch of Alexandria, dying on 17 April 326, and this entry presents him as the man whose election shut the heresiarch Arius out of the patriarchate. Arius had begun teaching his errors about 300 under Patriarch Peter, who excommunicated him, was restored by Achillas. And schemed to become bishop, until Achillas died and Alexander was chosen, after which Arius dropped all disguise.

Alexander at first tolerated Arius so mildly that his clergy nearly revolted. But at last the heresy was condemned at a council in Alexandria and then at the general Council of Nicaea, whose Acts Alexander is credited with drafting. The entry adds that during his priesthood he endured the bloody persecutions of Galerius, a steadfastness that frames his stand against Arianism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anastasia:
St. Anastasia holds a distinction unique in the Roman liturgy, a special commemoration in the second Mass of Christmas Day, and this entry explains why. That Mass was first celebrated not for Christ's birth but for this martyr. Toward the end of the fifth century her name entered the Roman canon. Yet she was not a Roman saint at all, having suffered at Sirmium and reaching Roman veneration only near the fifth century's end.

A later legend, no earlier than the sixth century, makes her a Roman and links her with Chrysogonus, likewise no Roman martyr, though he had a Roman church. In that Passio she appears as daughter of the illustrious Praetextatus, and the entry separates the legend's embroidery from the martyr's solid, early cult.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anatolia:
St. Anatolia was a virgin and martyr under Decius, put to death in a city variously called Thyrum, Thurium, or Thora, and this entry is honest about the uncertainties around her. Living in retirement with her sister when persecution raged, she was sought in marriage by a youth named Aurelius. Though the Bollandists doubt she was actually espoused, and, on the verge of yielding to her sister Victoria's urging, she was strengthened by a vision of an angel.

Banished to Thora and denounced as a Christian, she was shut by the executioner Audax into a room with a venomous serpent, which harmed her not at all. Audax himself professed the faith and died a martyr. Anatolia was then put to death by the sword, and her feast is kept on 9 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-antonio-ma:
St. Antonio Maria Zaccaria was founder of the Clerks Regular of St. Paul, commonly called the Barnabites. He was born at Cremona in Italy in 1502. He died on 5 July 1539. This entry follows a boy whose father died while he was still an infant. His mother took charge of his education, teaching him compassion for the poor and suffering by making him her almoner.

After school at Cremona he went to Padua for philosophy. In 1520 he finished that course and began medicine at the university there. At twenty-two he took his doctorate in medicine and returned to Cremona to practise. Three years later he turned to theology and was ordained in 1528. He then gave himself with fresh energy to charity and mercy, visiting the sick in hospitals and poor-prisons, while preaching and administering the sacraments bore great fruit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-apollonia:
St. Apollonia was a holy virgin martyred at Alexandria during a local uprising against Christians, just before the persecution of Decius, at the end of 248 or the start of 249. This entry follows the rising through the letter of Dionysius, then bishop of Alexandria, to Fabius of Antioch, long extracts of which Eusebius preserved. During festivities for the first millenary of the Roman Empire, heathen agitation rose to a great height.

When one of their poets prophesied calamity, the mob committed bloody outrages on Christians, whom the authorities made no effort to protect. Dionysius describes how Metras and Quinta, a Christian man and woman, were seized and put to death with cruel tortures. He also tells how the houses of several other Christians were completely pillaged, before turning to Apollonia's own sufferings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-benedict-o:
St. Benedict of Nursia was the founder of Western monasticism, born at Nursia about 480. He died at Monte Cassino in 543. This entry follows a life known only from the second book of St. Gregory's Dialogues, the sole authentic life of Benedict. It is more a character sketch than a biography, made up mostly of miraculous incidents. Those incidents illustrate his life, but give little help towards a chronology of his career.

Gregory's authorities for all he relates were Benedict's own disciples. They were Constantinus, his successor as Monte Cassino's abbot, and Honoratus, Subiaco's abbot when Gregory wrote. Benedict's father was a Roman noble of Nursia, a small town near Spoleto, and tradition accepted by Bede makes Scholastica his twin sister. His boyhood was spent in Rome, where he lived with his parents and attended school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-catherine-:
St. Catherine of Alexandria, virgin and martyr, has her feast on 25 November in the Latin Church and in the various Oriental churches. This entry follows a woman who for almost six centuries drew a very popular devotion. Of noble birth and learned in the sciences, Catherine, only eighteen, presented herself to Emperor Maximinus, who was violently persecuting the Christians.

She reproached him for his cruelty and set out to prove how iniquitous the worship of false gods was. Astounded at her audacity, but unable to vie with her in learning, the tyrant detained her in his palace and summoned numerous scholars. He commanded them to use all their skill in specious reasoning to lead Catherine to apostatize. But she won the debate. Her eloquence won over several adversaries, who declared themselves Christians and were at once put to death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cecilia:
St. Cecilia was a virgin and martyr and patroness of church music, dead at Rome. This entry follows a saint often glorified in the fine arts and in poetry, and one of the most venerated martyrs of Christian antiquity. The oldest historical account of Cecilia is found in the Martyrologium Hieronymianum. From it, her feast evidently dates to the Roman Church of the fourth century.

That martyrology lists her name under different dates. The mention under 11 August — the martyr Tiburtius's feast — is evidently a later, erroneous addition. That Tiburtius, buried on the Via Labicana, was wrongly identified with Tiburtius, Cecilia's brother-in-law in the Acts of her martyrdom. Perhaps another Roman martyr named Cecilia was also buried on the Via Labicana. Under 16 September Cecilia appears alone, with a note placing her on the Appian Way.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-colman-pat: St. Colman, one of Austria's patrons, was an Irish saint martyred near Vienna in 1012 while journeying to Jerusalem. His feast is observed on 13 October, the day of his martyrdom. He died a martyr's death on 13 October 1012. His life, written by Erchenfrid of Melk, is found in the Acta Sanctorum and the Monumenta Germaniae Historica.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cyril-of-a:
St. Cyril of Alexandria was a Doctor of the Church. This entry follows a man whose feast in the Western Church is 28 January, in the Greek Menaea 9 June, and, together with St. Athanasius, 18 January. He seems to have been of an Alexandrian family, son of Theophilus's brother, the Patriarch of Alexandria. If he is the Cyril addressed by Isidore of Pelusium, he was for a time a monk.

He went with Theophilus to Constantinople when that bishop held the Synod of the Oak in 402, deposing St. John Chrysostom. Theophilus died 15 October 412. On the 18th, Cyril succeeded his uncle as patriarch — but only after a riot between his supporters and his rival Timotheus's. Socrates bitterly complains that Cyril's first acts included plundering and shutting the Novatian churches. He also expelled Alexandria's Jews, who had formed a flourishing community there since Alexander the Great.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eustochium:
Eustochium Julia, third daughter of the Roman senator Toxotius and Paula, chose desert austerity in the heart of Rome. After her father's death about 380, mother and daughter lived as strictly as the desert fathers. When Jerome reached Rome in 382, they placed themselves under his guidance. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Bethlehem to 28 September 419 or 420.

Her uncle Hymettius and his wife Praetextata tried to lure her back to worldly pleasures, without success. About 384 she vowed perpetual virginity, and Jerome addressed her his celebrated letter on guarding virginity. A year later she followed Jerome and Paula east, sharing their Palestinian life. The entry joins noble birth, Roman asceticism, and Bethlehem exile in one devoted career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gonsalo-ga:
Gonsalo Garcia, lay brother martyr of Nagasaki, moved from Bassein schoolboy to Japan catechist, trader, and Franciscan. Born at Bassein in East India about 1556 or 1557 to a Portuguese father and Canarese mother, he was raised by Jesuits in Bassein Fort's college. At twenty-four or twenty-five he sailed with Jesuit fathers in 1580 for Japan, quickly learned the language, and served eight years as a beloved catechist. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 5 February 1597.

Leaving catechetical work, he traded at Alacao, opened branches, and on Manila visits drew toward the Franciscans, joining them as a lay brother. On 26 May 1592 he sailed from the Philippines under Petrus Baptista on an embassy from Spain's governor to Japan's emperor. The entry follows a life crossing three worlds, India, Japan, and Manila, toward martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-odilia:
Odilia, patroness of Alsace, founded the convent of Hohenburg on the Odilienberg and is pictured with two eyes on a book. Born at the end of the seventh century to the Frankish lord Adalrich and Bereswinda, she is said to have been born blind and to have gained sight at baptism. A tenth-century life preserves the story, with signs pointing to an eighth-century original.

Charlemagne granted immunity to her Hohenburg foundation, confirmed in 837 by Louis the Pious, who endowed it. A later life claimed by Vignier has been proved a forgery. Her grave lies in a chapel near the convent church, and her feast falls on 13 December. The entry weighs legend against documents for a saint of the Alsatian hills.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-rita-of-ca:
Rita of Cascia, an Augustinian nun, endured a cruel marriage, a husband's murder, and her sons' deaths before the cloister took her. Born at Rocca Porena near Spoleto in 1386 to elderly parents famed as peacemakers of Jesus Christ, she longed to be a nun. At twelve she obeyed her parents and married a harsh, bad-tempered man.

Eighteen years as wife and mother followed, lived as a model of patience. After her husband's murder, she prayed that her twin sons might die reconciled to God rather than take revenge, and they did. Refused at first as a widow, she won admission to Cascia's Augustinian convent by persistence and, as told, by divine intervention. She died there in 1456, pictured with roses and a forehead wound. Her feast falls on 22 May.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-rosalia:
Rosalia, hermitess and patroness of Palermo and all Sicily, hid in caves and was forgotten until plague-era Palermo found her bones. No account of her survives before Valerius Rossi about 1590, though churches honoured her by 1237. Her life, compiled from local traditions, paintings, and inscriptions, calls her daughter of Sinibald, lord of Quisquina, descended from Charlemagne.

Leaving home young, she hid in a cave near Bivona and later in one on Monte Pellegrino near Palermo, where she died and was buried. In 1624 her remains were found and carried to Palermo cathedral, and Urban VIII entered her name in the Roman Martyrology. Her feast falls on 4 September, with a translation feast on 15 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-silvia:
Silvia, mother of Pope Gregory the Great, raised two sons in piety and gave them an excellent education. Born about 515 or 525, her birthplace is given sometimes as Sicily and sometimes as Rome. She married Gordianus, a Roman regionarius, a man of family as distinguished as her own. Besides Gregory she had a second son.

After her husband's death she devoted herself wholly to religion in a new cell by the gate of blessed Paul. Gregory had a mosaic portrait of his parents made at St Andrew's monastery, minutely described by John the Deacon. Silvia appears seated, aged but beautiful, with large blue eyes and a gracious, lively expression. An oratory rose over her dwelling in the ninth century, and Clement VIII entered her name on 3 November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stefano-borgi:
Stefano Borgia, cardinal, theologian, antiquarian, and historian, built a museum of coins and manuscripts at Velletri. Born there on 3 December 1731 to a well known local family, not to be confused with the Spanish Borgias, his early education was guided by his uncle Alessandro, archbishop of Fermo. From youth he showed aptitude for historical research and an extraordinary taste for relics of ancient civilisations.

At nineteen he entered Cortona's Academy. He founded his Velletri museum, gathering coins and manuscripts, especially Coptic, through his whole life, counting it his greatest undertaking. His passion ran so high that he sold jewels and precious earthenware to secure treasures and print their descriptions. In his scientific career he showed great distinction, later serving as cardinal and prefect of Propaganda. He died at Lyons in 1804.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-chrysanth:
Chrysanthus and Daria were Roman martyrs buried on the Via Salaria Nova, and this entry separates solid fact from fifth-century legend. Their tombs were publicly honoured in the fourth century, and their names appear in the early Martyrologium Hieronymianum, which proves a real cult even though the surviving Acts hold no historical value.

Legend makes Chrysanthus the son of a noble Alexandrian, converted by a priest, and Daria a learned Vestal who embraced the faith and joined him in a virginal marriage. Converts followed, including the tribune Claudius and his household, until both saints were condemned and stoned in a disused sandpit. Their feast stands on 25 October in the Roman Martyrology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-vitus-mod:
Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia, kept on 15 June, are historical martyrs known only through legend. This entry proves the first point from the Martyrologium Hieronymianum, whose fifth-century exemplar already records their public veneration in Sicily and Lucania. No historical account of their deaths survives.

A legend of the sixth and seventh centuries, built on other legends and decked with wonders, fills the gap. Vitus, a boy of seven or twelve and son of a pagan senator, holds firm against his father's tortures. He flees by boat with his tutor Modestus, and is taken to Rome to free a demon-possessed son of Diocletian. Torture follows for all three, and the entry leaves the tale plainly marked as legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-styria:
Styria, in German Steiermark, was a duchy and Austrian crownland split by the River Mur into Upper and Lower Styria. Rich in iron ore and brown coal, it covered 8,980 square miles and counted 1,441,604 people in 1910. Of those people, 68 per cent were Germans and 32 per cent Slovenes, and 98 per cent were Catholics. Its capital was Graz, with 152,000 inhabitants.

Roman Noricum in ancient times, the land passed through migrations and Slav settlement about 600, then came under Charlemagne as part of Karantania. Bavarian settlers and Salzburg missionaries made it Christian, with Bishop Virgilius, called Apostle of Karantania, leading the work. The margraves took their title from Steier castle, and Barbarossa raised Styria to a duchy in 1180. A long source list closes the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synod-of-pist:
The Synod of Pistoia met from 18 to 28 September 1786 under Scipio de' Ricci, bishop of Pistoia and Prato. It was the boldest attempt to plant Jansenism in Italy. Grand Duke Peter Leopold of Tuscany copied his brother Joseph II and sought to control religious affairs. In 1785 and 1786 he sent Tuscan bishops fifty-seven points for reform. He ordered diocesan synods every two years to restore bishops' rights allegedly seized by Rome.

Of eighteen bishops only three called synods, and only Ricci was the duke's partisan. Born in 1714 and made bishop in 1780, Ricci pursued real reform with reckless zeal. He condemned Sacred Heart devotion, discouraged relics and images, slighted indulgences, improvised liturgy, and founded a Jansenist press. A full source list, including Vatican archive work, closes the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syria:
Syria, in modern usage, is a Western Asian country. It is bounded by the Taurus highlands, Egypt, Mesopotamia with the Arabian desert, and the Mediterranean. It thus takes in Aram, parts of Hittite and Mitanni lands, Phoenicia, Canaan or Palestine, and a slice of Sinai. In the stricter biblical and classical sense, Syria proper is narrower, bounded by Asia Minor, Palestine, the Euphrates and desert, and the sea.

Its north is high, its east level toward the desert, and Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon run parallel above Palestine, enclosing the long valley of Coele-Syria. The Litany, Orontes, and Barada water that fertile corridor, always a highway between Mesopotamia, the coast, Arabia, and Egypt. About 250 miles long and 130 wide, Syria covers some 32,500 square miles, and the vast entry then covers history, peoples, and missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tabae-caria:
Tabae in Caria was a titular see, suffragan of Stauropolis, lying in a Phrygian plain on Caria's border according to Strabo. Stephanus of Byzantium knows two cities of the name, one in Lydia and one in Caria, while Livy places this one on the Pisidian frontier toward the Pamphylian Gulf. Its coins survive, and its name is traced either to a founder Tabus, to a Semitic word for good, or to a native word for rock.

In 189 BC the consul Manlius Vulso, having beaten natives who blocked his march, fined Tabae twenty-five talents and 10,000 measures of wheat. Three bishops are known, from Ephesus in 431, Constantinople in 553, and Nicaea in 787, and the see appears among Stauropolis's suffragans until the thirteenth century. Today it is the village of Davas, rich in inscriptions and ancient remains.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-church-of:
Egypt's mother church, founded by tradition on Mark the Evangelist, is the patriarchate surveyed here. From Alexandria Christianity spread through all Egypt, and the patriarchate at its height held some 108 bishops across six provinces: Upper and Lower Libya, the Thebaid, Egypt, Arcadia or Heptapolis, and Augustamnica. Mark's successor at first stood alone as metropolitan of the whole land.

As Christians grew and new metropolitans rose, he became arch-metropolitan, and patriarch as a title came only in the fifth century. Till the second ecumenical council in 381 Alexandria ranked next to Rome. Schools, heresies, monks, and schisms follow, with election disputes over Mark's earliest successors noted for readers who seek the roots of Egyptian Christianity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-kingdom-o:
Germany's second state, ruled by the Wittelsbach dynasty, is surveyed here in constitution, land, and people. Since 1871 Bavaria stood as a constituent kingdom of the German Empire with special rights, its head in 1907 being Prince-Regent Luitpold. In peace the king commanded the army; in war the emperor took control by agreement. Six seats in the Federal Council and forty-eight in the Reichstag marked its weight.

Two separated territories, either side of the Rhine, covered 29,283 square miles. The census of 1 December 1905 counted 6,254,372 people, of whom 4,608,469, or 70 per cent, professed the Catholic faith. Dioceses, schools, and religious orders complete a portrait of a deeply Catholic kingdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-religion-:
Russian Christianity's origins divide scholars, and this long entry opens with the dispute. One theory holds Russia Catholic from conversion until the twelfth century, argued by Vizzardelli in 1826 and more fully by Verdière in 1856. The other holds Russia always Orthodox, an adherent of the Greek schism from the first missions across her frontiers. Orthodox writers unanimously reject Verdière's theses as foundationless.

History proper starts in the ninth century, though Kievan merchants trading with Constantinople knew Christianity earlier. Conversion, princes, monks, and metropolitans carry the story through schism, Mongol rule, and empire. Rites, sects, and the modern church close a survey that treats Russia's faith as a field of live controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-of-m:
Bishop Theodore of Mopsuestia, a bright but disputed Bible scholar, stands at the heart of this entry. Born at Antioch about 350 to rich and well-known parents, he died in 428. Syrian sources call him cousin to the younger Nestorius, and his brother Polychromius later became Bishop of Apamea. Libanius taught him Greek letters, thought, and speech, side by side with John Chrysostom and Maximus.

Near eighteen he gave up a worldly career and joined the strict school of Diodorus and Carterius near Antioch. Young zeal cooled when thoughts of Hermione, the girl he meant to wed, pulled him back, but he came back to discipline in time. As bishop he wrote notes on Scripture and tracts that later councils judged unsound, sowing seeds of the Nestorian row.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thuringia:
Thuringia is a large region of central Germany. It is bounded by the Werra in the west, the Saale in the east, the Harz Mountains in the north and the Thuringian Forest in the south. Its early people, the Hermunduri, became known as Thuringians about 420, and their powerful kingdom, reaching to the Danube, fell to the Franks in 531. The region later held the duchies of Saxe-Weimar, Coburg-Gotha, Altenburg and Meiningen, with parts of Prussia.

Kilian, Willibrord and others preached there with little success, and the real apostle of Thuringia was St. Boniface, who made Erfurt a see in 742. Monasteries at Fulda and Hersfeld spread the faith. In the sixteenth century the Reformation swept the region, Catholic worship survived mainly in Eichsfeld under Mainz, and the Peasants' War of 1525 wrecked many churches and monasteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ticelia:
Ticelia is a shadowy titular see, subject to Cyrene in the Libya Pentapolis, whose very name is in doubt. It appears in no list of bishoprics and no sacred or profane geography. Yet at the Robber Synod of Ephesus in 449 a Theodulus, Bishop of Ticelia in Libya, is named, though the Greek text corrupts the city's name. A list published by Gelzer gives instead the see of Sicelia, evidently the same place.

Which name is right cannot now be said. At Ephesus in 431 a Sosipater, Bishop of Septimiace, a town otherwise unknown but seemingly also in Libya, subscribed the acts. Whether Ticelia, Sicelia and Septimiace are one city or three, and what the diocese was truly called, remains open. The entry is valuable precisely because it refuses to settle a question the evidence cannot settle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-titular-see-o:
Philadelphia, in Lydia, was a titular see subject to Sardes, founded by Philadelphus, King of Pergamon, near Callatebus on the Cogamus River. Its site suited trade and defence, and in 133 BC it became Roman. Earthquakes nearly ruined it under Augustus, but it recovered and stayed commercially important into Byzantine times, famed for its wines and for coins bearing Bacchus.

Christianity reached Philadelphia in apostolic times, and its first bishop, Demetrius, is said to have been appointed by St. John. The city changed hands between Turks and Christians for centuries until Bajazet took it finally in 1390. In the seventeenth century it held 8,000 people, 2,000 of them Christians, and today, as Ala Sheir, it counts about 15,000, with ruins, a theatre, a stadium and mineral springs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tommaso-badia:
Tommaso Badia, cardinal, author and papal legate, was born at Modena in 1483 and died at Rome in 1547. He joined the Dominicans in his native city, outshone his brethren in learning, and taught theology at Ferrara, Venice and Rome. When Sylvester de Prierias left on a mission to the princes of Italy, Badia filled the office of Master of the Sacred Palace, first temporarily and then permanently, probably from 1523.

He sat on the commission that listed abuses for reform at Trent, and at the Diet of Worms in 1540 he acted as disputant and as theologian to Cardinal Contarini. Paul III made him cardinal on his return, and though chosen as a legate to preside at Trent, he stayed in Rome to vet the council's doctrinal papers. On his favourable report Paul III confirmed the Society of Jesus, and at his wish Badia was buried in the Minerva beside Cajetan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-toribio-de-be:
Toribio de Benavente, called Motolinia, was a Franciscan missionary born at Benavente, Spain, late in the fifteenth century, who died at Mexico City in 1568. One of the first band of Franciscans sent to Mexico with Martin de Valencia, he outlived all his companions. Born Paredes, he took the name Benavente on entering religion, following his order's custom.

Passing through Tlaxcala, he heard the people repeat motolinia, the Mexican word for poor, and took it as his own name. Barefoot and ragged, he gave away all he received, and the people loved him for it. He said the first Mass at Puebla in April 1530 and recorded 400,000 baptisms by his own hand. His 1555 letter to Charles V savagely attacked Las Casas, and his Historia de los Indios aided later historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-transylvania:
A diocese in Hungary, suffragan of Kalocsa-Bács, with its residence at Gyula-Fehérvar, also called Alba Julia. Its foundation is credited to King St. Stephen, though the entry judges King St. Ladislaus, patron of Transylvania, the likelier founder, with Simon, bishop from 1103 to 1113, as its first bishop.

The see grew rich on gifts from Béla IV, Charles Robert, Louis I and Sigismund, but suffered under the Tatar invasion and later civil strife. Decay set in with the spread of Lutheranism in the sixteenth century, and the see was secularized in 1556. Prince Stephen Báthory restored it, and the Catholic faith revived with the Jesuits while the Báthory house ruled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tricomia:
A titular see, suffragan of Caesarea in Palaestina Prima, whose place in southern Palestine is fixed by its neighbours in George of Cyprus's description. Malalas tells an old legend of the town, which he calls Nyssa and confuses with Scythopolis. His account makes the town home to a celebrated temple of Artemis.

No Greek bishop ever held the see, so Le Quien's complaint at finding none misses the mark. The Roman Curia, reading George's civil list as an episcopal list, made Tricomia a titular see. It is now the Muslim village of Terkoumieh, on a high hill between Hebron and Bet-Djibrin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-triest-capo-d:
A suffragan diocese of Görz-Gradiska, existing as a triple see since 1821, when Cittanova and Capodistria were united to Triest. St. Frugifer, consecrated in 524, was the first Bishop of Triest, and the line since then runs to eighty-seven bishops, few of whom reached eminence in so small a diocese.

Foremost among them is Enea Silvio de' Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, and Petrus Bonomo, bishop from 1502, known as father of the council at the Fifth Lateran Council. Joseph II abolished the see in 1788, Leopold II restored it in 1791, and after an eighteen-year vacancy under Napoleon, Emperor Franz appointed Leonardi bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Pavia was a literary centre even in Roman times, and as capital of the Lombard kingdom it held grammar schools. Emperor Lothair raised a central school there in 825. In the tenth and twelfth centuries professors of dialectic, law, and literature taught at Pavia, and though Bologna's authority then stood unchallenged, the views of the Papienses won respect. One of them was a certain Lanfranco, and another Lanfranco, who died bishop of the city, had taught arts and theology.

Until 1361 Pavia had no Studium Generale, and seekers of legal honours went to Bologna. Other schools existed early in the fourteenth century, but in 1361 Galeazzo II obtained from Charles IV a studium generale with the privileges of the most renowned universities. The entry follows its faculties, its law school, and its later fortunes, a compact history of a Lombard city that kept learning alive between empires.

Perugia counts among Italy's free universities, raised to a studium generale on 8 September 1308 by Clement V's bull Super specula. A school of arts already existed about 1200, teaching medicine and law, and several student associations formed before 1300. The famed civil jurist Jacobus de Belviso taught there from 1316 to 1321. John XXII granted degree rights in civil and canon law in 1318, and in medicine and arts in 1321.

On 19 May 1355 Emperor Charles IV confirmed the papal erection and lifted Perugia to imperial university rank. That rare favour aimed to aid the city after the plague years of 1348 and 1349. In 1362 Cardinal Niccolò Capocci founded the Collegium Gregorianum, later the Sapienza vecchia, for poor students. The entry follows the university's colleges, faculties, and scholars through later centuries.

Valencia's university studies began when Innocent IV, at the request of Jaime I the Conqueror, authorized estudios generales there by a bull in 1246. Under that bull some university courses ran at Valencia, but the university itself was not founded until 1411. Its founding owed much to the zeal of St Vincent Ferrer and to a building donated by Mosen Pedro Vilaragut. Only meagre accounts survive of its early workings.

From the start its courses covered Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, philosophy, mathematics, physics, theology, canon law, and medicine. The late seventeenth and whole eighteenth centuries brought its most prosperous era, with Greek, Latin, mathematics, and medicine specially cultivated. The entry lists its notable professors and follows its fortunes into the modern age, a Mediterranean university of long standing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-upper-and-low:
Nigeria, as this entry presents it, was a British colony stretching from the Gulf of Guinea to Lake Chad, between French Sudan, Lagos, the Atlantic, and German Kamerun. It took its name from the River Niger, which enters the colony above Ilo and gathers the Sokoto at Gomba and the Benue at Lokoja, its chief tributaries in English territory. English settlement dated only from 1879, though explorers had long reconnoitred the river.

Among the famed explorers were Mungo Park, Clapperton, René Caillié, Lander, and Barth, whose journeys mapped the Niger's course. The entry then describes the colony's peoples, trade, and administration, and the Catholic missions at work there, with their stations and schools. It offers a compact survey of a vast river colony at the height of British rule in West Africa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-utopia:
Utopia, from Greek words meaning no place, names a visionary or ideally perfect state of society. Sir Thomas More coined the term in his work De optimo reipublicae statu deque nova insula Utopia, printed at Louvain in 1516. It has since served as a generic name for political romances. More owed much to Plato's Republic, where guardians and auxiliaries, though not producers, live communally.

Plato kept their quality by selective breeding and state control of child-rearing, seeking political rather than economic ends. More, by contrast, ranged more widely, picturing laws, labour, religion, and daily life on his island. The entry follows the utopian romance from Plato through More to later writers, weighing the genre's hopes and its warnings about perfect states.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valencia:
Valencia's archdiocese in Spain covers the civil provinces of Valencia, Alicante, and Castellón. The city stands in the ancient region of Edetania and counts 173,000 inhabitants. Florus says Junius Brutus, conqueror of Viriathus, settled there in 140 before Christ the soldiers who had fought under Viriathus. Later it became a Roman military colony, was destroyed by Pompey for backing Sertorius, and was rebuilt to rank among Hispania Tarraconensis's leading cities.

Nothing certain is known of Christianity's arrival. Yet early in the fourth century, when Dacianus brought the martyrs Valerius of Saragossa and his deacon Vincent of Huesca to Valencia, Christians already seem settled there. The entry follows the see through Visigoths, Moors, and reconquest to its modern archdiocese, with its parishes, clergy, and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-veglia:
Veglia, with Arbe, was a diocese in Austria, suffragan of Görz-Gradisca. Parallel to the Dinaric Alps runs a chain of rocky islands, cut from the mainland by a deep though narrow strait. The largest is Veglia, which by the year 1000 had a bishop, Vitalis, present at a synod held in Spoleto. Eugene III made it a suffragan of Zara, though since 1828 it has answered to Görz.

Bartholomaus Bozarich attended the bishops' assembly of 1849, and his successor sat in the Vatican Council. Still older is the See of Ossero, whose bishop received a letter from Pope John VIII in 870. Its fifty-fifth bishop, Raccamarich, moved to Cattaro in 1818, and Ossero joined Veglia. Arbe's see is older still, its first known bishop attending a council at Salona in 530. The entry untangles three island sees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-louis-of-:
Louis of Casoria was a Friar Minor and founder of the Frati Bigi, born at Casoria near Naples on 11 March 1814, who died at Pausilippo on 30 March 1885. His worldly name was Archangelo Palmentieri. On 1 July 1832 he entered the Friars Minor, and shortly after his year's novitiate he was put to teach philosophy and mathematics in the Franciscan convent of San Pietro in Naples.

On his superiors' advice, he set up a branch of the Third Order at San Pietro. From its members he later formed a religious institute commonly called the Frati Bigi, from the greyish or ashen colour of their habits. Louis also founded a congregation of religious women, the Suore Bigie, under St Elizabeth of Hungary's protection. About 1852 he opened a school for the education of African children ransomed from slavery, the entry notes, among his many charities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ventimiglia:
Ventimiglia is a northern Italian diocese on the Gulf of Genoa, at the mouth of the Roia, with a small harbour, a fine cathedral with a fifth-century baptistery. A church of St Michael raised on a pagan temple's foundations. Ancient Albium Intemelium, capital of the Ligurian Intemelii, it resisted Rome until forced to submit in 115 BC.

Its later story is one of sack and siege: plundered in the civil wars of AD 69. Beset by Byzantines and Goths, raided by Lombards and tenth-century Saracens, then fought over by Genoa, Savoy, and Naples. The counts of Ventimiglia held the city as Genoese vassals after 1139, rebelling more than once. Christian tradition traces preaching there to the fourth century, with a bishop probably from the fifth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
Arabia's mission history is a story of separation, reunion, and frustrated hopes. Formerly part of the African mission of Galla, it became a separate prefecture under Pius IX in 1875, rejoined Galla. Then was erected a vicariate apostolic by Leo XIII in 1888 under Mgr Lasserre, with Capuchins long in charge of Aden and Somaliland.

The first vicar apostolic brought French Franciscan sisters to Aden. British authorities entrusted them with a hundred Galla children rescued from Arab slave ships, in hopes of founding a Catholic colony inland. By 1906 that hope, and other attempts to carry the faith into Arabia's interior, had been frustrated. The vicariate held some twelve million inhabitants, about 15,000 Catholics, eleven missions, and four churches or chapels.

Central Oceania's vicariate grew out of a Pacific mission first entrusted as a whole to the Society of the Sacred Hearts in 1825. The west went to the Marists in 1836, and in 1842 Rome created Central Oceania from New Caledonia, Tonga, Samoa, and Fiji, later narrowed to Tonga, Wallis, Futuna, and Niué.

Those archipelagos, divided among the kingdoms of Tonga, Niué, Wallis, and two Futuna kingdoms, lived under British protectorate in Tonga and Niué and French in Wallis and Futuna. Freedom of worship held everywhere except exclusively Protestant Niué, while Wallis and Futuna were entirely Catholic. Of 34,000 people, 9,200 were Catholics, served by thirty-five churches, twenty-one European and one native Marist priest.

Ernakulam is a Syro-Malabar vicariate on India's Malabar Coast, born from a plea for bishops of the people's own race and rite. In 1887 Leo XIII separated Malabar's Syrian-rite churches from the Latin rite into Trichur and Kottayam under European prelates.

In 1896 his brief Quae Rei Sacrae divided them anew into Trichur, Changanacherry, and Ernakulam. Ernakulam covers Syrian-rite churches between the Chalakudy River and Lake Vempanatu, apart from Suddhist churches later restored to Kottayam in 1911. It held about 814,000 inhabitants, 101,400 Catholics speaking Malayalam, under Mgr Aloysius Pareparambil, first vicar apostolic in 1896. With eighty-one parish churches, 112 secular priests, seminarians at Puthenpally and Kandy, and 116 native Carmelite tertiary nuns.

Kenia, now Kenya, is a vicariate coextensive with the civil province of that name in British East Africa, plus the station of Limuru. Stretching to the Tana and Seca rivers, the Aberdare mountains, and the Guaso-Ugiro, with its northern limits still indeterminate. Originally part of Northern Zanzibar, it was entered by priests of Turin's Consolata Institute, erected an independent mission in 1905.

A vicariate in 1909 under Father Philippus Perlo, titular Bishop of Maronia. The climate is mostly temperate and healthy, the languages chiefly Kikuyu and Swahili. The population, estimated at two to three million, is described in the entry's period language as given to fetishism and nature worship, with conversions gradually being made. The vicariate counted seventeen Consolata priests, eighty chapels, schools at its stations, an orphanage, and houses of Consolata religious and Cottolengo sisters.

Lower California, Baja California, is a Mexican vicariate covering a peninsula 770 miles long and 30 to 120 miles broad. Crossed lengthwise by mountain chains, abrupt toward the gulf and gentler toward the Pacific. Running water is scarce among granitic and volcanic hills, so irrigation depends on short, violent showers that flood the country; the north is hot and dry, the south more temperate.

Created in January 1874 and first confided to the Bishop of Sonora, the vicariate came directly under Propaganda, which from 1895 entrusted it to Rome's Missionary College of Sts Peter and Paul. In 1900 its Spanish-speaking population of about 47,000 was nearly all Catholic, served by six churches with resident priests, ten without, twenty chapels. As many stations, with the vicar apostolic resident at La Paz.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-victoria:
Victoria is a diocese in southwestern British Columbia, the province's mother diocese, first known as Vancouver. Established in 1847, it once covered the mainland and all coastal islands including the Queen Charlotte group. In 1863 the mainland became a vicariate and later New Westminster diocese, leaving Vancouver restricted to Vancouver Island and nearby islands, with Alaska attached until it became a prefecture in 1894.

Franciscan missionaries reached Nootka as early as 1778, settlers later gathered at Fort Camosun, renamed Victoria for the reigning queen, and in 1843 Father Bolduc volunteered to serve those pioneers. In 1847 Modeste Demers, a missionary of Oregon, was called to the new see. The title became an archdiocese in 1904 and the Diocese of Victoria in 1909, when the Vancouver archdiocese moved to Vancouver city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-virginia:
Virginia, surnamed the Old Dominion and Mother of States and of Statesmen, is one of the thirteen original states. The southernmost of the Middle Atlantic division, 42,627 square miles between West Virginia, Maryland, the Atlantic, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Kentucky, with a hundred counties. In 1910 its population was 2,061,612, with Richmond, 127,628, as capital and former capital of the Confederacy.

Beyond geography and population the entry, like other state articles, surveys government, laws, and institutions, including liquor policy. Local option prevailed: by January 1912 sixty-six counties and eight cities held no liquor licence. It also sets out the law of wills, under which no person of unsound mind or under twenty-one may make a will. Except that minors eighteen and over may dispose of personal estate, and a valid will must be signed by the testator or by another in his presence and by his direction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vitoria:
Vitoria is a Spanish diocese, suffragan to Burgos, bounded by the Bay of Biscay, Guipúzcoa, Navarre, Logroño. Burgos, comprising the Basque provinces and most of Álava, its chief city numbering over 27,000. Before the tenth century the city was called Gazteiz, a Basque word meaning height of the fray, belonging to the ancient federation of Arriaga.

Occupying the upper town now called Villa de Suso. King Sancho the Wise of Navarre took the region in 1181, renamed it Victoria. Later Vitoria by local phonetics, conferred town privileges, built two castles, walled the town, and granted it Logroño's charter. Alfonso VIII won it for Castile and added further charters, confirmed by Ferdinand III and Alfonso X, and John II gave it a city charter in 1431. Isabella the Catholic later obtained from Alexander VI the transfer of Armentia's collegiate church to the parish church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-west-virginia:
West Virginia is an American state bounded by Pennsylvania, Maryland, Ohio, Virginia. Kentucky, between latitudes 37°36' and 40°38' north, covering 24,780 square miles, 24,645 of land, with a 1910 population of 1,221,119. Its chief cities were Wheeling, 41,641, Huntington, 31,161, Parkersburg, 17,742, Charleston, 22,926, and Clarksburg, 9,201.

Runs 300 miles along the state, linking it to Mississippi Valley, Gulf, and far western trade. The Allegheny Ridge divides Atlantic from Mississippi watersheds, with parallel ridges westward. Later sections cover its Catholic life. Visitation academies for young ladies stood at Mount de Chantal near Wheeling and Parkersburg, and St Joseph academies at Clarksburg and Wheeling. A Xaverian high school for boys stood at Wheeling, St Edward's preparatory school at Huntington opened in 1909, and fourteen parochial schools held 1,975 pupils. Wheeling Hospital, incorporated in 1850 under the Sisters of St Joseph, was the state's oldest Catholic charity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-westphalia:
Westphalia is a Prussian province between the Rhine and Weser, bounded by the Netherlands, Hanover, Schaumburg-Lippe, Lippe-Detmold, Brunswick, Hesse-Nassau, Waldeck, and the Rhine province. Tenth in size and third in population among Prussian provinces, it covers 7,804 square miles with 4,125,096 inhabitants, 2,121,534 Catholics and 1,947,672 Evangelicals, in 107 cities and 1,468 village communities. Mountainous in the south and northeast and level elsewhere, its chief industries are agriculture, cattle breeding, mining, and manufactures.

The Ruhr industrial district holds Germany's most productive coal beds and most valuable iron mines, seat of extensive mining, great iron forges. Innumerable machinery and iron factories, with some twenty towns over 20,000 people and 750,000 souls in a relatively small 386-square-mile district. Overall, 53. 4 per cent lived by mining and manufacturing, 26. 2 per cent by agriculture, and 10 per cent by commerce and traffic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilcannia:
Wilcannia is a diocese in New South Wales, one of Sydney's six suffragan sees, formed mostly from western portions of Bathurst, Armidale. Goulburn, covering nearly half the state at 150,000 square miles. Its thinly scattered people work chiefly in pastoral pursuits, though important mining centres have lately arisen. At its formation in 1887 its Catholic population was estimated at about seven thousand, with eight priests and an average of eight hundred children in Catholic schools.

Official returns for 1912 show nineteen thousand Catholics, nineteen secular priests, and 2,960 children in Catholic schools under 146 religious teachers. Material progress fell short of expectations at its founding, owing to dry climate, land tenure favouring vast pastoral holdings or squattages, and mining's uncertainty, but railways, scientific wheat growing. Irrigation along the western plains' great rivers promise great development, and valuable mineral deposits await settlement, above all Broken Hill's famous silver and lead mines and Cobar's mines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelm-v-duk:
Wilhelm V, called the Pious, ruled Bavaria from 1579 until he handed power to his son Maximilian in 1597. Born at Munich in 1548, he died at Schleissheim in 1626. He studied at Ingolstadt, kept a lifelong love of learning and art, and shaped his court around daily Mass, long prayer, weekly sacraments, pilgrimages, and public devotions. Visitors joked that his court resembled a monastery and his capital a German Rome.

Jesuit guidance marked his reign, and he poured funds into Jesuit houses, above all Saint Michael at Munich, plus missions in China and Japan. He fought hard to hold Cologne for Catholicism by backing his brother Ernst as archbishop, and he pressed the Counter-Reformation across Bavaria and the empire. Critics note that he showered church posts on kin: Ernst held five dioceses, and his son Ferdinand as many.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zulia:
Zulia is the Venezuelan diocese comprising the State of Zulia, erected by Leo XIII on 28 July 1897 from territory detached from Mérida. Francesco Marvez, the first bishop, was elected on 17 May 1897 and consecrated on 16 January 1898. At his death the see stayed vacant from 17 December 1904 to 16 August 1910, administered meanwhile by capitular vicar Felipe S. Jimènez. Arturo Celestino Alvares, consecrated on 6 November 1910, is the present bishop. Zulia is suffragan of Santiago de Venezuela, with the episcopal residence at Maracaibo.

Its notable buildings are the cathedral, the churches of the Immaculate Conception and Our Lady of Chiquinquira, the poor-house, and the insane asylum. The diocese holds a preparatory seminary, the Colegio Don Bosco run by Salesian Fathers for boys, and an academy run by Sisters of Charity of Saint Anne for girls. Other Catholic schools also serve the diocese. Several Catholic periodicals appear in the diocese.
cecilia:
Frances Burney's long novel of 1782 carries the subtitle Memoirs of an Heiress, and its heroine's fortune drives everything. Ten books of short, titled chapters move Cecilia through London high life. A Journey, An Assembly, A Masquerade, and A Miser's Mansion are among the chapter names. Wealth, family pride, and fashion set the terms of every meeting.

Guardians, suitors, gamesters, and fashionable friends press on her from all sides. Mortimer Delvile, proud and reserved, becomes the emotional centre, tested by storms, partings, and misunderstandings. Burney fills assembly rooms and opera rehearsals with sharp talk about money and rank. Cecilia's good sense must survive a world that prices her before it knows her.
czaplicka-turks-central-asia:
Maria Czaplicka published The Turks of Central Asia in 1918 at Oxford. The Polish scholar wrote the classic English survey of her subject. Turkic peoples stand viewed in their past and in her present day.

She drew on Russian research few Western readers could reach then. From Siberia to Samarkand, khans and nomads fill her swift survey. War raged in Europe as she wrote, yet her tone stays clear. Her book pairs with Aboriginal Siberia elsewhere in the catalog here. Many still call it the best first guide to the Turkic world in English. Czaplicka died young, and this survey keeps her name alive.

doe-osti-3393466-aluminum-critical-miner: Old landfills are full of aluminum the world now calls critical. This study asks whether mining landfills for aluminum makes sense — environmentally, technically, and for the surrounding community. The feasibility verdict could turn yesterday's trash into tomorrow's supply chain.
