egeria-pilgrimage-etheria:
Egeria was a woman from the western Roman world who traveled to the Holy Land around 381 to 384. Her account, in McClure's English version, is the earliest Christian pilgrim diary that survives. It is also the oldest known travel writing by a woman.

Egeria visits Jerusalem, Sinai, and Egypt, describing churches, monks, and feast days. She explains how services were held at each holy site, in careful detail. Her Latin is plain and eager, full of questions for local guides. Historians prize the text for its window on early Christian worship. The text breaks off in the middle, yet what survives runs to many sites.
eurasia:
Christopher Evans imagined Eurasia as an ideal republic and sent a shipwrecked American sailor ashore to inspect it, department by department. Evans, a Vermont-born Civil War cavalryman who later fought in the West, gives his narrator a guided tour: departments of justice, education, mines, railways, health, and foreign affairs each explain themselves. A visit to a state prison and a talk with the minister of state frame the survey.

In Eurasia women share full responsibility, children learn trades and swimming, the idle build roads and canals, and workers receive a fairer share of what they make. The preface calls it a readable answer to the problems confronting America. It belongs to the utopian shelf beside Bellamy, practical rather than dreamy.
fountains-in-the-sand-rambles-among-the-:
Douglas rambles among the oases of southern Tunisia, from Gafsa and its Roman stones to Tozeur and Nefta. The chapters mix travel notes with phosphate mines, the Seldja gorge, and gardens at the head of the waters. Hadrian's inscription and the Roman wall stand among the illustrations.

One long conversation stays with him: a stranger unburdening himself with imperious need to a chance acquaintance. Douglas hears two different individuals in the man's voice and finds him mentally disorganized. He sets that rambling emotionalism against the diamond-like logic of a mining engineer. Norman Douglas keeps the traveler's eye dry and amused throughout.
franco-gallia:
Hotman's Franco-Gallia argues that France was once a free state, and most of Europe with it. Written in Latin in 1574, it reached English readers in this translation, printed here in a second edition of 1721. The translator was the author of the Account of Denmark.

Its evidence comes from the oldest Frankish laws. One chapter of the Salic law, title sixty-two, rules that no part of the Salic land passes to a female. Hotman insists such articles governed private right between man and man. François Hotman built from them a case about the public right of the kingdom itself.
from-aldershot-to-pretoria:
Sellers follows Christian work among British troops in the South African War. His story starts at Aldershot, the great army camp at home. It sails with the soldiers to the front. Chapters track the advance under Lord Methuen and Lord Roberts. Magersfontein, Kimberley, and Bloemfontein mark the route. The book ends on the road to Pretoria and at Ladysmith.

The focus stays on the men's spiritual welfare. Sellers describes soldiers' homes, parade services, and hospital visits. Chaplains and mission workers appear throughout the fighting. Letters and deathbed scenes carry the emotional weight. The book mixes war reporting with revivalist appeal. It shows the war through the eyes of those who ministered to the ranks.
frus-1919Russia:
The 1919 Russia volume opens with a conference that never met. Allies proposed talks at Prinkipo with every Russian faction. The Bullitt mission then carried terms to Moscow. Nansen proposed feeding Russia under neutral watch. America refused further dealings with Soviet power. The Soviet agent Martens won no recognition either. Trade bars and a ruble traffic ban follow. Detained Americans fill the chapter's last long file.

Siberia takes chapter two. Kolchak's armies win, then fall for good. The Allies agree to supervise Siberia's railways. Czech forces win a promise of evacuation home. A mid-volume note states General Graves's orders. He must not meddle in Russian affairs. He backs the railway chief Stevens instead. The volume is refusal as policy.
gentle-julia:
Booth Tarkington's 1922 novel turns on Julia Atwater, the adored young aunt of a Midwestern family. Her beauty draws a crowd of suitors to the house, each sure he will win her. Two children of the family, Florence and her cousin Herbert, watch the courtship from the stairs and the yard. Their schemes and spying drive much of the fun.

Among the suitors, shy Noble Dill loves Julia with a plain, dogged heart. Rivals with more polish cut in, and mix-ups pile up at dances and calls. Tarkington treats the whole chase with warmth and gentle mockery. The book is a light comedy of small-town courtship, told with a sharp eye for how children see grown-up love.
govdocs-archive_org-OswaldTheCIAAndMexic:
The Lopez Report is the House Select Committee on Assassinations staff study of CIA files on Lee Harvey Oswald's trip to Mexico City in the fall of 1963. Staff members Dan Hardway and Edwin Lopez wrote it in the late 1970s. The CIA released it in 1993, with redactions the JFK review board checked in 1995 and 1996.

Oswald visited the Cuban and Soviet embassies in Mexico City weeks before President Kennedy's murder, and the CIA had him under watch. Lopez and Hardway test what the agency recorded, what it hid from investigators, and where its files fail. The report remains a core document of assassination research, from inside the official inquiry.
govdocs-archive_org-denImplantsInAmerica:
Wilson Bryan Key followed his bestseller Subliminal Seduction with Media Sexploitation, a second attack on hidden persuasion in American media. Key argued that advertisers and broadcasters buried secret messages in images and sound, steering buyers without their knowledge.

He points to shapes, words, and symbols he claims to find hidden in advertisements, photographs, and television, and he treats them as deliberate implants. Critics dismissed his readings as patterns that were not there, but his books sold widely in the 1970s. The work survives as a time capsule of that decade's suspicion of mass media.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DeuelPatricia_D:
An FBI document later numbered Commission Document 513 recounts the surveillance of a woman named Patricia Deuel. In 1943, during a conversation at the Statler Hotel, Deuel was reported as terribly anti-American. That report was enough to put her in an FBI file.

The excerpt shows wartime counterintelligence at the level of one overheard conversation. A remark in a hotel became a recorded judgment, kept and later passed to a presidential commission. Files like Deuel's reveal how wide the Bureau's net was cast in 1943, and how little it sometimes took to be watched.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HunterReportCIA:
An FBI memorandum dated November 26, 1963 deals with something called the Hunter Report. Its subject is Lee Harvey Oswald's possession of a membership card. The card was for the New Orleans chapter of the Fair Play for Cuba Committee, the pro-Castro group Oswald had represented that summer.

The card mattered because it tied Oswald, in writing, to a Castro support organization days after he was accused of killing the president. Investigators chased every document in his pockets and rooms. The memo, written four days after the assassination, preserves the Bureau working that paper trail at the start.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KimseyHermanCIA: Memorandum of Call (Blank Form): the blank government memorandum-of-call form - no call information is filled in. A form, empty, kept, complete. An obscure item, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of ephemera.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LawrenceVintCIA: A profile titled 'From the CIA to the Drawing Board' follows Vint Lawrence from intelligence work to art. Lawrence served as a CIA officer, and the headline traces his second career at the drawing board. The file gives the title and the subject but no author, date, or further detail, so the profile's specific claims cannot be summarized from the evidence preserved here.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PeetTomGeorgia_: Tom and Georgia Peet of Gahanna, Ohio, sent this Christmas card to Mr. and Mrs. Harold Weisberg of Frederick, Maryland. Holiday cards survive in a researcher's files because they were kept with the year's correspondence. This one records a friendship maintained by mail between Ohio and Maryland. Beyond the names, the two addresses, and the season, a greeting card carries no further evidence, and none is claimed for it here.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PostalJulia_Pos:
Julia Postal worked the box office of the Texas Theatre in Dallas. On the afternoon of November 22, 1963, a man slipped into the theater without paying, and police arrested Lee Harvey Oswald inside. This file summarizes Postal's Warren Commission deposition of April 2, 1964, her account of that afternoon.

Postal's testimony fixed the arrest story's first minutes: the breathless man at her window, the call to police, the officers filling the theater. The summary form matters too. Researchers often worked from summaries rather than full transcripts, and summaries choose what to keep. This one preserves the deposition's substance as a reader of the file received it, the cashier's evidence in brief.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PurdomAlicia_Pu:
Harry Altshuler wrote this tabloid article under the headline 'Johnson Suspected CIA Was Involved in Kennedy Murder.' Altshuler claims that newly disclosed papers show Lyndon Johnson suspected CIA involvement in the killing. He also claims Robert Kennedy paid 500,000 dollars to hush up a Kennedy love scandal. The publication is not identified.

Tabloid treatment is part of the assassination story's history. Claims that would need documents in a court record ran here as headlines, sourced to papers no reader could inspect. The article preserves two such claims in their printed form. It is evidence of what the supermarket press sold about Dallas, and of the market that kept suspicion about Johnson and the CIA in circulation.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SecurityAssocia: nsia-SecurityAssociates Security Associates: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-StapletonCIA_St: All that survives here is a fragment: a short note asserting that someone is still with the Agency, meaning the CIA. The note is cataloged under the name Stapleton, but its author is unknown and the rest of the record is missing. Kept as a scrap, it shows the kind of loose paper that gathers in intelligence research files, where one line can point to a story no longer attached.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SwedenCIA_Swede: Parade magazine's intelligence column took a reader's question on May 9, 1976: what was the CIA doing in Sweden? The short question-and-answer format was how many Americans got news about secret agencies in the 1970s. The column answers in brief, for a general audience. It survives as a sample of popular reporting on intelligence work during the years when Congress was also probing the CIA.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
Colombia was a quiet Cold War battleground, and Michael Evans edited this briefing book, number 902, on the spying there between 1963 and 1972. It was published in September 2025 and draws on new revelations from the JFK assassination records.

One 1968 CIA operation gathered intelligence on the entire clandestine leadership of Colombia's Communist Party and the FARC. Agents planted information about a Soviet agent in the Colombian press. A high-level Cuban defector, a Bay of Pigs veteran, ran a CIA listening post in Bogotá. The agency also secretly funded a civilian anti-communist group, a full toolkit in one country.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia:
On July 4, 1966, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Freedom of Information Act at his Texas ranch. Fifty years later, in July 2016, the National Security Archive marked the anniversary with this briefing book. FOIA became the main legal tool for forcing United States secrets into the open.

Nearly every briefing book in the Archive's collection exists because of that law. The anniversary posting is therefore partly a birthday card to its own method. It also gives readers a short history of the act that researchers, journalists, and citizens now use to pry loose government records of every kind.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nato-rus: The Short-lived NATO-Russia Honeymoon: the National Security Archive Electronic Briefing Book publishing made public records. The archivists publish, complete. A single briefing. Dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Eight former American ambassadors to Russia had already given interview transcripts to the National Security Archive when this update added three more. The new voices are Jack Matlock, Thomas Pickering, and James Collins. All three rank among the most experienced diplomats the United States sent to Moscow, in the late Cold War and the years right after it.

Ambassadors speak with a freedom that cables and memos rarely allow, judging leaders and mistakes in plain terms. Matlock served under Reagan and Bush as the Soviet Union changed and fell. Pickering and Collins dealt with the hard years of building ties with Yeltsin's Russia. Together, the interviews give readers firsthand judgment from the people who carried American policy into the Kremlin across three decades.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia-intelligence:
Gina Haspel ran a CIA black site prison in Thailand in 2002, and years later President Trump nominated her to direct the agency. In June 2022, the National Security Archive reported testimony given at a military tribunal at Guantanamo Bay. A witness said Haspel personally oversaw the waterboarding of Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, the man accused of bombing the USS Cole.

The posting, edited by Lauren Harper, came fifteen years after the events and four years after the Senate confirmed Haspel despite the controversy. Eyewitness testimony at a tribunal carries a different weight from memos and timelines, and the account placed the director herself in the room during a technique many officials call torture. Readers get a short, sourced piece that ties a senior official's past directly to the black site program's hardest questions.
guy-rivers-a-tale-of-georgia:
William Gilmore Simms, the South's most prolific romancer, published Guy Rivers as A Tale of Georgia. This revised edition is of 1890. The scene lies in the upper part of Georgia, in Cherokee territory, a region fruitful of dispute when the tale opens. A lonely traveler crosses a sterile prospect in the first chapter. The country was then a gold frontier, where law sat lightly and strangers were watched.

Guy Rivers is the frontier's dark genius: a lawyer turned outlaw chief, who runs a band of rogues from a wild settlement. Against him stand young men of honor drawn into his toils. Simms mixes gold fever, Indian treaty politics, and bandit war into a long, dense romance. The tale shows the border as he loved to paint it: raw, violent, and full of men whom the states had not yet tamed.
halma-nicolas-catholic-encyclopedia:
William Fox wrote the Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Nicolas Halma, a French scholar and priest. Halma lived from 1755 to 1828 and worked on old astronomy. He is best known for editing Ptolemy's Almagest in French.

Fox gives a brief, factual life with a list of works. Halma taught, translated Greek science, and served the church. The entry is short, as fits an obscure figure. It preserves basic facts a researcher may need. Readers of science history will value it as a pointer to a man who kept ancient star lore alive.
heart-s-desire-the-story-of-a-contented-:
Emerson Hough, author of The Mississippi Bubble, published Heart's Desire in 1905, calling it the story of a contented town, certain peculiar citizens, and two fortunate lovers. The frontispiece shows a man looking up to see her standing at his door. The town of Heart's Desire lies in the West Hough knew, a place that has chosen content over progress and means to keep the railroad, and the century, out.

Strangers who stray in are gently converted or gently expelled, while the two lovers of the subtitle find their way. Hough writes with humor and a real love of the old, slow West that was passing as he wrote. The book was a popular success in its day. It reads now as a fable of resistance to hustle, told by a man who had seen both worlds and picked his side.
history-of-california:
Helen Elliot Bandini wrote this history of California with young readers in mind. Her preface says she aimed at a tale children could read with pleasure. She drew, she notes, almost wholly on source material. Her ties to old Spanish families opened records few writers could reach.

The story runs from Indian occupancy through Spanish and mission days. Gold discovery, statehood, and the latest events of her day follow. Whole chapters treat the growth of the state's great industries. Tourists and older readers were also in her mind. The result is a warm, clear one-volume history of the state.
history-of-phoenicia:
George Rawlinson, Oxford's Camden Professor of ancient history, published his History of Phoenicia in 1889 as his last professorial work. Rawlinson pulls together what classical writers, travelers, and excavators had established about the Phoenicians, the sea traders of Tyre and Sidon. Earlier histories by Movers and Kenrick had stood for nearly half a century; new digging in Phoenicia and Cyprus, much of it by Renan and the Di Cesnolas, demanded a fresh account.

Chapters cover the land, the people, their religion, art, industry, colonies, and wars, down to absorption into later empires. Rawlinson writes careful Victorian synthesis, weighing inscriptions against Greek and Hebrew testimony. His Phoenicians emerge as the ancient world's carriers: of goods, of crafts, and of the alphabet itself.
in-clive-s-command-a-story-of-the-fight-:
Herbert Strang wrote In Clive's Command as a story of the fight for India. The tale opens in Market Drayton in 1754, where Colonel Robert Clive is honored. A cart brings the hero into a crowded market town at sunset. His father served as Captain Richard Burke in the Company's service.

Sea fights, escapes, and service under Clive drive the adventure. In one scene a commander greets the young Burke as a chip of the old block. He is sent ashore to see the governor after a bold escape. Boys get a fast tale of India in Clive's time.
in-times-of-peril-a-tale-of-india:
G. A. Henty's In Times of Peril is a tale of India during the Mutiny of 1857, opening in the bright, pretty cantonments of Sandynugghur in early spring. British garrisons stood apart from the Indian towns, forming suburbs of their own, and Henty sets his young heroes among them.

Chapters follow the outbreak, the flight, the defence of Delhi and Lucknow, a tiger's intervention, treachery, and the relief of Lucknow. The storming of Delhi, a riot at Cawnpore and the last capture of Lucknow carry the action to its close. Boys who enjoy Henty's imperial adventures will find this one of his most exciting Indian tales.
ismailia:
Samuel White Baker commanded an Egyptian expedition into Central Africa, and Ismailia tells that campaign as a full narrative. Ismail, Khedive of Egypt, organized the force to suppress the slave trade on the upper Nile. Baker, an English explorer and big-game hunter, had already seen slaving raids on earlier journeys. He writes as commander, not as a passing traveler.

Chapters follow his English officers, a hard retreat, and a camp at Tewfikeeyah on the river. Steamers probe the old White Nile channel before the party pushes on to Gondokoro. Baker describes setting up government in the Equatorial Nile Basin, fighting hostile traders, and moving men and stores through swamp and heat. River craft, local peoples, ivory traders, and armed resistance fill the record. Historians of Africa read it as a commander's own account of Egypt's southward push and the war against the slave caravans.
john-l-stoddard-s-lectures-vol-10-of-10-:
Volume ten of John L. Stoddard's Lectures gathers three travel talks: Southern California, the Grand Cañon of the Colorado River, and Yellowstone National Park. Stoddard delivered these discourses over eighteen years under the Stoddard Lectures title. The volume is filled with views of famous places and people. The California lecture opens with nature standing guard over the land.

Ten thousand miles of ocean guard Southern California from the west, Stoddard says. Dreary deserts hedge it from the east and forbid approach. The westbound tourist passes Flagstaff before the desert turns truly dreadful. For fifty miles at a stretch he may see neither man nor beast. Stoddard's lectures brought such scenery, in words and pictures, to audiences who might never travel.
journals-of-expeditions-of-discovery-int:
Edward John Eyre's Journals of Expeditions of Discovery into Central Australia tell of his 1840-41 journeys. Volume one opens a work sent out by the colonists of South Australia with government support. Eyre dedicates it to Governor George Gawler, under whom the expeditions were undertaken. The full title promises an account of Aboriginal manners, customs, and relations with Europeans.

Eyre's preface explains why the book appeared late. After the expeditions, the governor asked him to stay and rebuild peace with the Murray River tribes. That work held him from September 1841 to December 1844. His personal knowledge of Aboriginal people, he hoped, would serve the task. The journals themselves record hard travel from Adelaide toward King George's Sound.
kinship-organisations-and-group-marriage:
Northcote Whitridge Thomas wrote this study of kinship and group marriage in Australia. It appeared in the Cambridge Archaeological and Ethnological Series. Editors at Cambridge, including William Ridgeway and A. C. Haddon, supervised that series.

The book examines how Aboriginal groups organized family ties and marriage classes. Tables set out systems such as the Arunta eight-class table. Thomas uses those tables to compare one group's rules with another's. Students of early anthropology still use it as a record of how the subject was first studied. Thomas writes in the formal style of early Cambridge scholarship. His terms can be dense, yet the tables keep the systems clear.
lamia:
John Keats wrote Lamia, a long poem in two parts. It begins long ago, before fairies drove nymphs and satyrs from the woods. Hermes leaves his golden throne on a quest of love.

Hermes steals down to a forest on the shores of Crete. He seeks a nymph who has caught his desire. That search leads him to Lamia, a serpent in lovely shape. Keats weaves their bargain into a tale of love and illusion. Rich images and swift couplets carry one of his most colorful poems. The poem's second part moves the tale to Corinth. Love, philosophy, and illusion collide there with tragic force.
london-to-ladysmith-via-pretoria:
Winston Spencer Churchill published these war letters in 1900. Longmans, Green issued the volume in London and New York. He dedicates it to the Natal Government Railway staff. Their courage amid war's perils, he writes, made them conspicuous.

The book records his adventures during the African War's first months. It also follows Buller's operations for the relief of Ladysmith. The Morning Post first printed the correspondence from the field. Churchill warns that camp tumult forbids calm, sustained thought. An essential part of one story stays omitted for discretion. A man's life depended on that silence, Churchill explains.
modern-india:
William Eleroy Curtis wrote these letters for the Chicago Record-Herald during the winter of 1903 and 1904. He dedicated the book to Lady Curzon, wife of India's viceroy. The journey opens with Bombay, its servants, hotels, and cave temples. Chapters then explain the empire of India and how India is governed.

Curtis attends two Hindu weddings and surveys the religions of India. He rides the railways, visits Ahmedabad and Jaipur, and writes about snakes and tigers. Mogul architecture, Delhi, famines, caste, and women's lives all get chapters. The series closes at Benares, the sacred city, giving American newspaper readers a full tour.
more-songs-from-vagabondia:
Bliss Carman and Richard Hovey published this second book of vagabond songs in 1896. Copeland and Day of Boston issued it, with designs by Tom B. Meteyard. The poets dedicate it to M. G. M., who lightened their cares. They call themselves, in the dedication, simply the boys.

The contents open with Jongleurs and Earth's Lyric. A wood-god, a faun's song, and a mocking-bird follow. Poems named Karlene and Kavin recur like traveling companions, beside a sea gypsy and the first julep. These lyrics celebrate roads, inns, and open air, the shared mythology of two young poets who made vagabondage a literary fashion.
moulton-early-religious-poetry-persia:
Moulton's Early Religious Poetry of Persia appeared in 1911, ahead of his larger work. Sacred verse of ancient Iran stands at the center of these lectures. The Gathas, Zoroaster's own hymns, form the oldest layer he treats.

Moulton sets the hymns inside their hard, early historical world. He shows herdsmen, priests, and converts in the prophet's first circle. Later Persian verse that keeps the old faith's fire also earns place. His Hibbert Lectures wear deep learning with rare lightness of touch. Readers meet Iran's first religious poetry as living song, not mere relic here. Moulton's ear for verse keeps the old hymns warm and human.
mr-isaacs-a-tale-of-modern-india:
F. Marion Crawford published Mr. Isaacs in 1882, subtitled a tale of modern India. The novel opens with wide claims about freedom, power, and men who rise by will or flattery. Crawford sets that talk against the East, where old rule still shapes daily life. His hero is the Isaacs of the title.

From that broad start the book moves into a story of adventure and character in India. Crawford asks how far drive and charm can carry a man. He also shows the cost when ambition meets custom and faith. The novel made Crawford's name with readers on both sides of the Atlantic. It mixes romance, travel, and sharp social talk.
myths-of-babylonia-and-assyria:
Donald A. Mackenzie surveys the myths of Babylon and Assyria here. The sample opens deep in the creation tale of Merodach. He split the dragon Tiamat like a flat fish in two. One half made the heavens, and one half made the earth.

Mackenzie quotes L. W. King's Seven Tablets of Creation for these lines. He notes old tales where heroes eat a dragon's heart for wisdom. Siegfried of the Nibelungenlied gained such gifts in German lore. The book compares dragon tales across lands and ages. Its last chapters trace the final days of both empires, in a rich, learned tour.
napoleon-and-the-queen-of-prussia:
Luise Mühlbach wrote this historical novel, Englished by F. Jordan. Appleton issued it in New York, with rights dating to 1867. Book one opens with Ferdinand von Schill and a German song. An oath of vengeance follows in chapter three.

Later chapters show the queen's flight and Napoleon in Potsdam. He enters Berlin in triumph and faces suppliant princes. The Victoria of the Brandenburg Gate changes hands in the tale. Book two carries the war and its sorrows forward. Mühlbach makes Queen Louise a symbol of Prussia's pride, crushed by Napoleon yet unbowed in spirit.
nasa-tm-19680010001-spectroscopic-study-:
Warren Winovich and Paul A. Croce, at Ames Research Center in California, explain how to read the air of Mars from a plunging probe. A fast probe heats the gas ahead of it into a glowing cap. Light from that cap, split into a spectrum, reveals what the gas is made of.

Close-range spectra could also reveal the mixture's proportions. That knowledge would aid every other experiment on future Mars missions. The authors note what was then known: Mariner IV results suggested the Martian air is at least a third carbon dioxide. Nitrogen and argon were suspected for the rest, though neither had been detected.
nasa-tm-19710003465-effect-of-facility-b:
Robert T. Bechtel, Bruce A. Banks, and Thaine W. Reynolds of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a January 1971 meeting in New York. It studies a testing problem with Kaufman ion thrusters. Material sputtered inside the test chamber settled back onto the thruster grids.

The grids carry a glass coating and steer the ion beam. Tests showed thin conductive films of chamber material on the glass faces. Those films could distort how the thruster truly behaves in space. The team ran tests in two vacuum tanks to size the effect. Ground testing that lies about flight gear can mislead a whole program.
nasa-tm-19710013147-results-and-analysis:
Godfrey Anzic and Charlene May of the Lewis Research Center reported this radio noise survey in April 1971, as NASA TM X-2244. Their team measured ultrahigh frequency noise over Phoenix, Arizona, from both the air and the ground. Man made radio noise can disturb communications and navigation. The survey checked whether aircraft alone could map the worst city noise zones.

Crews recorded noise at three frequencies while ground teams measured at the same time. Air and ground readings matched well when taken together. High urban noise areas could indeed be spotted from aerial data. The method offered a faster way to chart interference across a whole city.
old-calabria:
Norman Douglas wrote this travel book about Calabria in southern Italy. The contents list forty chapters of places and people. He visits Lucera, Venosa, Taranto, and the Sila hills. He writes about saints, brigands, Albanians, and ancient Greeks. Old ruins and wild mountains shape the whole route.

Douglas mixes sharp humor with deep learning about the past. He recalls Horace, Milton, and writer George Gissing. Chapters treat malaria, cave worship, and mountain festivals. Few travel books cover so much with such ease. Heads also name cave worship, the Bandusian Fount, and tillers of soil. A flying monk, dragons, and a sage of Croton follow.
old-kaskaskia:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood published this historical novel in 1893. Houghton Mifflin printed it in Boston and New York. Kaskaskia was an old French town in Illinois country. The contents divide the tale into named parts. Part one is called The Bonfire of Saint John.

Catherwood had written other French colonial romances before. Titles named include The Lady of Fort Saint John. Part two is called A Field Day. The sample preserves only opening contents and title pages. Readers can confirm author, date, and publisher from it. The novel belongs to her frontier history series.
old-mission-stories-of-california:
Charles Franklin Carter published these mission tales in San Francisco in 1917. The book holds seven stories set in old Spanish California. The foreword says six rest on real history, large or small. Only the tale of Juana is wholly invented, he notes. The first story introduces the mission tales proper.

Tales name Padre Peyri, Father Zalvidea, and Father Uria. An Indian sibyl and a figure called Pomponio also appear. Carter aims to picture life among Indians and Spaniards. The setting is Nueva California in the early 1800s. Carter also wrote on the missions of Nueva California, he notes. The first tale opens on a low Mojave Desert hill.
olivia-in-india:
O. Douglas wrote this cheerful book of letters from India. The sample opens with praise from the Star newspaper. Critic James Douglas calls Olivia a happy book. He urges readers to tell friends about it. The Glasgow Herald praises the author's likeable personality.

Olivia writes fascinating letters home from her Indian stay. Her humor and warmth charm the reviewers quoted here. The sample mostly preserves praise for her other books. Penny Plain and The Setons receive notices and summaries. Readers learn her style is light, kind, and witty. The book suits fans of gentle travel letters.
patricia:
Patricia was published in 1910 under the name Emilia Elliott, and a note from the publishers says the author did not live to see her book in print. The heroine is a small girl who lives with her father and her Aunt Julia. The story opens with Patricia perched on a back fence with a forlorn stray dog she has just brought home.

Aunt Julia has refused the dog, and Patricia thinks her father far more "convincible," though he never goes back on Aunt Julia. The contents promise a gingham apron party and a Christmas family. It is a gentle child's story about a warm-hearted girl and the household she keeps unsettling.
paul-and-virginia:
Bernardin de Saint-Pierre's Paul and Virginia was the most beloved French romance of its age. This edition's preface calls it the author's masterpiece and a philosophical tale, not a mere story for children. The publishers boast that earlier editions were cut and padded, while theirs gives the entire work, with a memoir of the author.

Two children grow up together on the island of Mauritius, in love as innocent as the nature around them. Fate and a voyage to France part them, with tragic results. The tale praises virtue and simple living, and its tender sorrow made it a classic across Europe.
personal-recollections-of-early-melbourn: The sample we host shows only the front matter of Personal Recollections of Early Melbourne and Victoria, the title pages, plates of Edward Henty and John Pascoe Fawkner, and verses about Australia. No chapter text is visible. The title page names William Westgarth as the author. The plates honour two founders of the colony, and the quoted poems promise a story of mount and plain, lake, river, and sea.
peter-parley-s-tales-about-america-and-a: The hosted sample stops at the front matter of Peter Parley's Tales About America and Australia, the title pages and the start of the contents, with no tales visible. The title page gives the author as Peter Parley, the pen name of Samuel Griswold Goodrich, in a new edition brought down to the present time and revised by the Reverend T. Wilson. Darton and Hodge published it in London in 1862, with illustrations by S. Williams, and the contents begin with Parley telling how America was discovered.
philistia: The hosted sample shows only the front matter of Philistia, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Grant Allen. The thirty-seven chapter titles borrow the language of the Bible's Philistines. They include Children of Light, Magdalen Quad, Askelon Villa at Gath, In the Camp of the Philistines, and Out of the Hand of the Philistines. The naming sets the novel's fight between earnest reformers, its children of light, and the comfortable world it calls Philistia.
philo-jud-us-of-alexandria: The sample provided here shows only the front matter of Philo-Judaeus of Alexandria, the title page, copyright page, dedication, and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Norman Bentwich, sometime scholar of Trinity College, Cambridge, and the Jewish Publication Society of America, Philadelphia, 1910, as publisher. The contents promise the Jewish community at Alexandria, Philo's life and times, his works and method, his theology and philosophy, and his influence.
philo-judaeus-catholic-encyclopedia:
Emile Brehier wrote the Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Philo Judaeus of Alexandria. Philo was a Jewish thinker who joined Greek philosophy with the Torah. He lived in the age of Jesus and the early church.

Brehier explains Philo's idea of the Logos, God's word and reason. He shows how Philo read scripture as allegory, full of hidden sense. That method later shaped Christian thought in deep ways. The entry is brief but learned. It gives students a clear first map of a thinker who bridged two worlds of faith. Few short entries cover so much ground.
phyllis-of-philistia:
Frank Frankfort Moore's Phyllis of Philistia opens with a chapter called An Astronomer Without a Telescope. Phyllis Ayrton is in grief, and her father, a connoisseur of phrases, tries one out on her: marriage means all your eggs in one basket. She is unmoved. Her sorrow is for George Holland, a clergyman who has turned from truth to falsehood.

Holland has concluded that Abraham's morals were shaky and Samson a libertine, and risks his living for saying so. Phyllis broke with him for it. Her father calls him a fool for running into a hornets' nest. The novel plays faith, doubt, and society comedy against each other.
queen-lucia:
Queen Lucia is a comic novel by E. F. Benson, set in the village of Riseholme, where Mrs. Lucas, called Lucia, rules the local world of art and society. The opening chapter brings her home by train on a hot July morning, to the house called The Hurst and a husband waiting for her.

Rather than ride in the fly with her maid and luggage, Lucia walks the half mile from the station. She knows the whole street will see the carriage arrive without her. Everyone will wonder why. Benson plays out what each friend will guess. Daisy Quantock, deep in Christian Science, will picture illness. Georgie Pillson will place her among the Italian pictures. He will put her at the National Gallery.
queen-victoria:
Queen Victoria, by Lytton Strachey, was published in New York by Harcourt, Brace and Company in 1921. It tells the Queen's life in ten chapters. They run from Antecedents and Childhood through Lord Melbourne, Marriage, and Lord Palmerston. They end with Widowhood, Old Age, and The End. A bibliography closes the book.

Chapter one opens with a death: on November 6, 1817, the Princess Charlotte, only child of the Prince Regent and heir to the crown, died young. Strachey sketches her unhappy, impulsive life, her broken engagement to the Prince of Orange, her love for Prince Augustus of Prussia, and the arrival of Prince Leopold of Saxe-Coburg in London.
ranching-for-sylvia: Ranching for Sylvia, by Harold Bindloss, published in New York by A. L. Burt Company in 1913 and issued in England under the title The Trustee, is shown here by its title page and contents. Thirty chapters follow George to the prairie. A Strong Appeal opens the list. George Gets to Work and A Cattle Drive follow. Constable Flett's Suspicions and The Liquor-Runners appear. George Turns Reformer comes later. A blizzard strikes. Grant comes to the rescue. A climax brings Flora's enlightenment and an escape.
rasselas-prince-of-abyssinia:
Rasselas, Prince of Abyssinia, by Samuel Johnson, appears here in the Cassell and Company edition of 1889, in Cassell's National Library. An introduction tells the famous story of its making. Johnson wrote it in 1759, at the age of fifty. He wrote to pay the little debts of his mother. He wrote to pay her burial costs too. She had just died poor at ninety.

The tale was written in the evenings of one week and sent to press while being written, and it earned him a hundred pounds, with twenty-five more for a second edition. Johnson, the introduction adds, never read it again until more than twenty years later, when he took it up in a chaise with Boswell and read eagerly.
running-a-thousand-miles-for-freedom-or-: Running a Thousand Miles for Freedom is named in its front pages as a work by William and Ellen Craft. The pages shown here are chiefly Project Gutenberg header matter, dated July 4, 1996, with notes on copyright law, on keeping the file for the next readers. Other notes cover how corrected editions get a new number. The header also names Judith Boss of Omaha, Nebraska, as the person who created the electronic text. No chapter, preface, or narrative passage appears in the portion shown here.
russia: Donald Mackenzie Wallace wrote Russia, under a copyright of 1905. The contents pair each chapter title with a long string of sub-heads. Chapter I, Travelling in Russia, covers railways, state meddling, river routes, the Volga, Kazan, the Don, hotels and their odd customs, roads, bridges, posting, a tarantass carriage, and travel in winter. Chapter II, In the Northern Forests, promises a bird's-eye view of Russia, a village, a peasant's house, and vapour-baths.
scotus-reportata-parisiensia:
The Reportata Parisiensia preserve Scotus's Paris lectures on the Sentences as his students heard and wrote them down. A reportatio was a student's fair copy of a master's spoken teaching, checked against the lecture hall's noise and speed. This text appears in the 1891 Vives edition of Scotus's works, reprinting Wadding's collection.

Scotus taught at Paris in the first years of the 1300s, and the Reportata carry his theology in classroom form, closer to speech than the polished Ordinatio. Questions are posed, objections heard, and answers built in the open, day by day. Scholars compare the two versions to watch a doctrine change under pressure. The medieval university comes alive in these pages: the master thinking aloud, the students racing to keep the record straight.
songs-from-vagabondia: Bliss Carman and Richard Hovey wrote Songs from Vagabondia, with designs by Tom B. Meteyard. Copeland and Day at Boston and Elkin Mathews and John Lane at London printed the book in MDCCCXCIV, that is, 1894, under a copyright of that year. The pair give the book to H. F. W., for debts of love unpaid. Contents heads name Vagabondia, A Waif, The Joys of the Road, and Evening on the Potomac, then a faun, a rover's song, and Down the Songo.
starr-king-in-california: William Day Simonds wrote Starr King in California. He gives the book to the memory of Horace Davis. Davis was of San Francisco. Up to Starr King's death, folk widely held one view. King, more than any other man, had kept California from disunion. The whole Pacific Coast owed its keeping to him. Abraham Lincoln held that view, Simonds says. Edwin Percy Whipple is quoted to the same effect. The contents sort the life in five parts. Old New England comes first. California in 1860 and its hour of decision follow.
stories-of-california:
Ella M. Sexton wrote Stories of California, published at New York by the Macmillan Company in 1903, with the text set up and first issued in September 1902. The book tells the state's past as a chain of stories made for general readers.

The contents begin with California's name and early history, then the missions and Father Serra, and life before the Americans came. They move to the Bear-Flag Republic, the days of gold and the Argonauts of forty-nine, and mining tales. A girl's trip across the plains, the building of the overland railroad, and the story of the wheat fields close the sweep from Spanish days to farming wealth.
tales-from-bohemia:
Tales from Bohemia, by Robert Neilson Stephens, is prefaced by a memorial essay from a fellow newspaperman who knew Stephens at the start of his career. The writer climbs back in memory to a crisp evening early in March 1887, and the three flights of rickety stairs to the fourth floor of the old Press building.

There he worked the news desk on his second night as an editor. The desk was a crude piece of carpentry. The staff called it the shelf. There he met a youth with a pale face and serene smile. The youth was Mr Stephens, then a private secretary. The tales that follow, of artists, actors, and Bohemians, are offered under the shadow of that early death.
tales-of-the-punjab-folklore-of-india: Flora Annie Steel's Tales of the Punjab bears the subtitle Folklore of India. A preface and a note to the young reader come first. More than thirty folk tales then follow. Named tales include Sir Buzz, The Rat's Wedding, and The Faithful Prince. Others are The Tiger, the Brahman, and the Jackal, and The Wonderful Ring. A run of tales at the end tells how Raja Rasalu was born. They also tell how he went out into the world.
the-beautiful-eyes-of-ysidria:
Charles A. Gunnison printed a short Californian story in San Francisco and dedicated it at Palo Alto on Christmas 1894. He gives it to Madame Emma Baudouin of Luebeck in thanks for kindness. The narrator begins by praising the slope of Mount Tamalpais above the bay.

One man lives beneath that mountain yet cannot see it, though he calls it his god and giver of all good. The narrator walks miles with his son Quito, speaking of unseen things while the boy speaks of unheard things. He then turns back to his youth in California, before gold changed the land he loved.
the-black-death-and-the-dancing-mania:
J. F. C. Hecker's medical history, translated from German by B. G. Babington, was issued by Cassell in 1888. An introduction traces three generations of medicine professors. Hecker, born at Erfurt in January 1795, moved to Berlin at ten with his father.

At eighteen Hecker left study to volunteer against Napoleon, then took a medical degree in 1817. His taste ran to the historical side of medicine, and a history of medicine in 1822 won him a Berlin chair in that field. He is regarded, the introduction says, as founder of historical pathology, studying disease against the history of mankind itself.
the-boy-allies-with-haig-in-flanders-or-:
Clair W. Hayes wrote The Boy Allies with Haig in Flanders, or The Fighting Canadians of Vimy Ridge. The first chapter bears the odd head A New Use for a Dictaphone. It opens on a great field of war in a downpour of rain. In pitch dark, Hal Paine and Chester Crawford creep out of their trenches.

The trenches seem still, as if their men were dead or asleep. In truth most men sleep on their arms, ready to wake at a raid, while watchful guards stand post. The boys slip past their own guards with care, for a false step could get them shot. Past the wall of earth they move swift and mute toward the German lines, less than a hundred feet off. Both are lieutenants in the first American force in France. Years of war have made them bold, and their ranks were won on the field.
the-boy-scouts-in-russia: Captain John Blaine wrote The Boy Scouts in Russia, with art by E. A. Furman. The Saalfield Publishing Company of Chicago, Akron, and New York put it out, with rights dated 1916. The chapters start at The Border, then pass Under Arrest to A Strange Meeting. Cousins, The Germans, and The Tunnel come next. A Daring Ruse takes the boys Within the Enemy's Lines, to Sentenced and The Cossacks.
the-captivi-and-the-mostellaria:
The Captivi and the Mostellaria of Plautus are here literally translated, with notes, by Henry Thomas Riley. The Captivi's cast is headed by Hegio, an Aetolian gentleman. With him stand the captives Philocrates and Tyndarus. The parasite Ergasilus and the slave Stalagamus complete the heads named. The scene is Aetolia. An acrostic argument lays out the plot before the play begins.

The prologue then points to the two captives standing on stage. It starts the story of a father who has bought prisoners of war. He hopes one of them is his lost son. The literal translation keeps the Roman machinery intact: argument, prologue, and dramatis personae all instruct the audience before a line of dialogue is spoken.
the-case-for-india:
The Case for India is the presidential address delivered by Annie Besant at the thirty-second Indian National Congress, held at Calcutta on the 26th of December, 1917. She begins with thanks that go beyond ceremony. For the first time in Congress history, the delegates had chosen a president who lay interned. When chosen, she was under government displeasure. She was held as a person dangerous to public safety.

While she was silenced, she says, they defended her and won her release; humiliated, she was crowned with honour. Having no words fit to repay the debt, she turns the gift into service. She consecrates her life anew on the altar of the Mother. The opening closes with the cry of Vande Mataram. The address starts, that is, as a debt of gratitude turned into a pledge.
the-confutatio-pontificia:
Dated August 3, 1530, and edited by J. M. Reu, the Confutatio Pontificia is the Catholic reply to the confession of faith laid before the emperor by the Elector of Saxony, several princes, and two cities. No author is named. The emperor, it says, read the confession himself and then handed it to learned men of several nations for close study.

Those men were told to praise what matched Catholic teaching and to mark where the confession strayed from it. Their written reply was read by the emperor and passed to the other electors, princes, and estates, who approved it as sound and in line with the Gospel. The reply then takes up the confession topic by topic, starting with Part I.
the-crisis-in-russia:
Arthur Ransome dedicated The Crisis in Russia to William Peters of Aberdeen. In his introduction Ransome explains that change runs faster in a revolutionary country, though it slows as the revolution recedes. Russia, he says, is no longer the dizzying kaleidoscope of 1917, nor does it shift week by week as in 1918.

A clear view of its direction now needs visits spaced six months apart. His earlier journal of Russia in 1919 pictured February and March of that year fairly, he believes, but a very different stage from today's. Long crisis under foreign war, he argues, has rallied even foes behind the ruling party while exposing naked methods of rule, justified by need, much as in other warring lands.
the-doomswoman-an-historical-romance-of-:
Gertrude Atherton's The Doomswoman, an historical romance of old California dated 1900, begins at Governor Alvarado's house in Monterey. Chonita comes to stand godmother at a christening and learns, too late, that Diego Estenega will stand godfather. Her friend, the narrator, knows the feud between their houses too well to have warned her in time.

Chonita and Diego meet under a roof full of guests and old hate. Love grows where family honour forbids it. Atherton fills the tale with ranch life, Spanish custom, and a woman whose will shapes all fates.
the-duke-of-gandia: Algernon Charles Swinburne's play The Duke of Gandia, printed by Chatto and Windus in 1908, is present here only as title matter and a cast list. Pope Alexander VI heads the cast. His sons Francesco Borgia, Duke of Gandia, and Caesar Borgia stand below him. Michelotto, two assassins, Vannozza, and Lucrezia Borgia fill the roll. The scene is Rome in 1497. No play text appears.
the-emperor-of-portugallia:
Selma Lagerlöf's The Emperor of Portugallia, rendered from the Swedish by Velma Swanston Howard, tells of Jan of Rufflard Croft and his girl Glory Goldie. Book one's heads trace her growth: the christening, the vaccination bee, birthdays, school tests, and forbidden fruit. Book two turns on her leaving, a letter, and the dream that begins.

Waiting twists Jan's mind till he holds himself an emperor and his girl an empress. Book three brings his song, a funeral, and a dying heart. Lagerlöf writes of love and madness with deep, plain pity.
the-euahlayi-tribe-a-study-of-aboriginal:
K. Langloh Parker's The Euahlayi Tribe studies Aboriginal life in Australia, from her years on a New South Wales station. Contents name Byamee the All Father, relationships and totems, medicine men and leechcraft, a witch woman, and a girl's path from infancy to womanhood. Later chapters cover the boorah rite, funerals, stars and legends, trapping, cooking, dress, and games.

Parker learned the Euahlayi tongue and set down tales from the people's own mouths. Her book guards lore that might else have been lost. A native artist's drawings are noted, though left out of this text.
the-famous-missions-of-california:
William Henry Hudson, once a professor of English at Stanford, wrote The Famous Missions of California, a short history of the Spanish missions. He signed the dedication from London, England, in 1901.

The tale starts with Junipero Serra and the plan to settle Alta California, then follows the party that reached San Diego Bay on July 1, 1769. Mission after mission rises: San Carlos, San Gabriel, San Juan Capistrano, Santa Barbara, and more. Hudson tells of Serra's death, the fall of the mission system, and daily life inside the walls, weighing what the chain of missions left behind.
the-gold-hunters-adventures-or-life-in-a:
William H. Thomes wrote The Gold Hunter's Adventures. Its subtitle is Or, Life in Australia. Thomes calls himself a returned Australian. Lee and Shepard printed it in Boston. Pictures are by Champney. A contents summary traces the arc. It runs from first thoughts of going, to the ship from California. It reaches Williamstown, Melbourne, and a convict's hut.

The tale opens on a hot afternoon in California. Two big, hard-handed men lie in a small tent on the banks of the American Fork. One reads a newspaper. The other tries to sleep. From that worn camp the book follows gold seekers. They leave California for the newer fields of Australia. The move carries all the risk and hope of such a jump.
the-haskalah-movement-in-russia: Jacob S. Raisin, Ph.D., D.D., wrote The Haskalah Movement in Russia, published in Philadelphia by The Jewish Publication Society of America in 1913. Raisin is named as the author of Sect, Creed and Custom in Judaism. A dedication to his father, Aaron S. Raisin, says the father's life of study and teaching inspired the book, and a verse from Daniel stands on the title page. Only the title page and dedication are present here, so the study itself does not appear.
the-heptalogia: Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote The Heptalogia, shown here from The Collected Poetical Works, Volume V, printed in London by William Heinemann in 1917 after a first printing in 1904. A list of Swinburne's poetical works in six volumes stands at the front, naming Poems and Ballads, Songs Before Sunrise, Tristram of Lyonesse, and A Midsummer Holiday among them. Only the title pages and works list are present here, so the poems themselves do not appear.
the-history-of-louisiana-or-of-the-weste: The History of Louisiana, or of the Western Parts of Virginia and Carolina, is translated from the French of M. Le Page Du Pratz, with notes and observations relating to the colonies. The title page promises a description of the countries on both sides of the river Mississippi, with accounts of settlements, inhabitants, soil, climate, and products. Contents fragments name the first war with the Natchez, French posts at Mobile, and a description of New Orleans. Only the title page and contents fragments are present here.
the-last-west-and-paolo-s-virginia:
G. B. Warren copyrighted his Canadian verse collection in Canada in 1919. The contents list poems on Boundary Bay, the Great Divide, clouds, winter sunset in the Cascade Range, a seal rookery raid, and the coast of British Columbia. A second part holds Paolo Virginia, billed as a spring phantasy.

The opening poem watches daybreak over Boundary Bay below the snowy cone of Mount Baker. Wildfowl call across the water while flooded fields wait for light. Warren writes western scenery in formal stanzas that move from mountain views to coastal towns such as Vancouver and Victoria.
the-life-of-cesare-borgia: Rafael Sabatini wrote his history of Cesare Borgia, first published in 1912 according to the record heading. Only the title page and contents are present here. The books listed cover the house of the Bull and the French invasion. The murder of the Duke of Gandia and Cesare giving up the cardinal purple follow in the list. Later books promise a duchess of Valentinois and the knell of the tyrants. Sabatini history and criticisms themselves cannot be read in this record.
the-little-hunchback-zia:
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote The Little Hunchback Zia, illustrated by Spencer Baird Nichols and W. T. Benda. The story is set roughly nineteen hundred and sixteen years before its telling, in the world of the Bible. Zia, a small hunchback, flees his village by night, keeping to the deepest shadows and hiding behind walls and rocks by day, terrified that anyone will look at him closely.

The old woman who sheltered him has driven him out in fear. She believes a hunchback is born under the blight of Jehovah's wrath and might bring a curse on her house. Starving, footsore, and lost in the dark, Zia wanders on with stolen food and beans dropped from a camel's feeding-bag, giving readers a sorrowful outcast at the center of a religious tale.
the-log-school-house-on-the-columbia:
Hezekiah Butterworth, author of the Zigzag Books, wrote The Log School-House on the Columbia, a tale of the pioneers of the Great Northwest, published by D. Appleton and Company in 1890. His preface explains the book's origin. A librarian in charge of young people's books at the Boston Public Library told him that few popular books described the pioneers of Oregon and Washington. She suggested he write such a story. Soon afterward, Butterworth met an educator fresh from the Columbia River, who told him a legend.

It concerned an old chief said to have died of grief at his son's grave. Butterworth took up the suggestion and the legend together, aiming to give young readers a view of heroic pioneer life in the Northwest.
the-mating-of-lydia:
Mrs. Humphry Ward published The Mating of Lydia in 1913. The novel opens on a wet October evening in a stately Georgian house dating from 1740. Servants Dixon and his wife tend a fire that has no heart for burning. Mrs. Dixon fears the expected guests will never arrive, because floodwater may cover the road by Grier's mill.

Three people with luggage on top of a carriage might have to turn back to Pengarth. Dinner spoils and fires waste while the household waits in deepening gloom. Lamplight picks out a pillared archway, a great double staircase, and carved doorways in the dark hall. Ward notes that the house and its condition seem strangely at war with each other. Readers enter a rich interior where comfort, decay, and expectation hang together in the damp air.
the-mind-in-the-making-the-relation-of-i: James Harvey Robinson's The Mind in the Making, subtitled The Relation of Intelligence to Social Reform, shows only its title page and contents here, so the text itself does not appear. The contents open with a preface on the book's purpose and three disappointed methods of reform. Later sections treat kinds of thinking, rationalizing, and how creative thought transforms the world. Closing sections promise our animal heritage, our savage mind, and the beginnings of critical thinking under Plato and Aristotle.
the-mountains-of-california:
John Muir's The Mountains of California is present here only through its contents and list of illustrations, so Muir's prose does not appear. Sixteen chapters are listed, beginning with The Sierra Nevada, The Glaciers, and The Snow. A Near View of the High Sierra, The Passes, glacier lakes and meadows, and The Forests follow.

Animal and weather chapters come next: the Douglas squirrel, a wind-storm in the forests, river floods, and Sierra thunder-storms. The water-ouzel, the wild sheep, the foothills, and bee-pastures close the list. Illustrations named include Mount Shasta, Mount Rainier, Kolana Rock in Hetch-Hetchy Valley, the General Grant Tree, and maps of the Sierra Nevada and Yosemite Valley.
the-naval-pioneers-of-australia:
Louis Becke and Walter Jeffery's The Naval Pioneers of Australia came out in London in 1899. John Murray published it. Only title page and contents are present here, so the history itself does not appear. The authors are billed for A First Fleet Family and The Mutineer. Twelve chapters are listed, and a list of illustrations is promised.

Introductory chapters cover the earliest Australian voyagers, Portuguese, Spanish, and Dutch. Dampier, the first Englishman in Australia, and Cook, the discoverer, follow. Governor Phillip, founder of New South Wales, Governors Hunter, King, and Bligh, and the explorers Bass and Flinders fill the middle list. Bligh and the mutiny of the Bounty take a chapter of their own.
the-nuttall-encyclop-dia:
The Rev. James Wood edited The Nuttall Encyclopaedia, a one-volume dictionary of general knowledge first sold in many thousands of copies; this printing is the sixty-first thousand, from 1907. Wood also edited Nuttall's Standard Dictionary. The book packs over 16,000 short, original articles into a single handy volume.

Entries cover history, biography, geography, literature, philosophy, religion, science, and art. The A entries begin with A'Ali Pasha, a Turkish reforming statesman, then Aachen, Aalborg in Denmark, and the Aar, a Swiss river about 200 miles long that joins the Rhine. Readers get brief facts fast, with cross references to fuller spellings and names.
the-octopus-a-story-of-california:
Frank Norris wrote The Octopus, subtitled A Story of California. The novel opens with Presley, a young poet staying at the Derrick ranch, cycling on the County Road south from Bonneville. A railroad whistle confuses him about the hour, and errands for Mrs. Derrick have already eaten into his planned ride through the country.

Norris paints a dry, baked San Joaquin Valley at the end of September, after four months without rain. Half the wheat on the Broderson ranch has failed, and dust lies deep on the roads. Presley's small troubles sit inside a larger story of wheat farmers and the railroad that grips their lives.
the-old-franciscan-missions-of-californi:
George Wharton James published The Old Franciscan Missions of California in 1913, with photographs of the missions. James had written books on the Grand Canyon and California heroes. His dedication honors people of all creeds, and none, whose lives show helpful and unselfish humanity. The contents begin with a historical introduction and a chapter on the missions of Lower California in Mexico.

James tells the life and work of the Franciscan friars who built the California missions. Photographs show places such as Mission San Luis Rey, partly restored, with a new monastery behind the old arches. The book serves readers who want the mission story told with sympathy for the friars.
the-one-woman-a-story-of-modern-utopia: Thomas Dixon, Jr. wrote The One Woman, subtitled A Story of Modern Utopia, with illustrations by B. West Clinedinst. Dixon dedicated the novel to his mother, who died in 1902. Here the reader gets front matter and a contents list, and nothing of the story itself. The list runs to twenty-seven chapters. They begin with The Man and the Woman and The Banker and His Fad, and end with A Stolen Kiss and Venus Victrix. The titles promise a tale of love, money, and new social ideals.
the-patagonia:
Henry James wrote The Patagonia, shown here in the 1922 Macmillan edition that bound it with Daisy Miller and Pandora. The story opens on a hot August night in Boston. Beacon Street lies dark and deserted. The narrator looks forward to sailing the next day. He is glad that a slower old ship, the Patagonia, has replaced the Scandinavia, promising ten or twelve days of fresh air.

Passing Mrs. Nettlepoint's house, he sees lights and calls. She is to embark for Liverpool on the same ship, and he offers help. Lone women, he reflects, are grateful for support in taking ship. Her son Jasper, he recalls, is not quite a young man to lean upon. James sets a voyage and a friendship in motion.
the-radio-boys-in-the-thousand-islands-o:
J. W. Duffield sends his Radio Boys on vacation among the Thousand Islands. His 1922 adventure carries a Yankee-Canadian wireless trail as its subtitle. Contents move from vacation plans to a baffling situation. A catwhisker and a radio diagram follow. An island surrounded by islands raises the puzzle.

A deserted camp deepens the mystery. So does a diary kept by a modern Robinson Crusoe. Hal makes a discovery along the way. Shore hook-ups keep wireless at the center of the fun. Only the title pages and contents list are present here. The adventure itself does not appear on these pages.
the-religion-of-babylonia-and-assyria:
Theophilus G. Pinches lectured in Assyrian at University College, London. Archibald Constable first published his account in 1906. A preparer's note warns about special letters in the text. Names such as Hammurabi lose their marks in this version. Greek words appear transliterated inside brackets for readers.

Chapter one defines the subject in broad terms. Two river peoples held this polytheistic faith for ages. Their home was the Tigris and Euphrates valley country. The faith lasted from history's dawn toward Christian times. Pinches writes for readers meeting cuneiform religion fresh. Gods, temples, and records guide his compact survey. Students of the ancient Near East gain a working outline.
the-splendid-idle-forties-stories-of-old: Gertrude Atherton, author of The Conqueror and Senator North, gathered these stories of old California in a 1902 volume illustrated by Harrison Fisher and dedicated to San Francisco's Bohemian Club. The pages present here hold the title pages and Atherton's own note. She explains that the book is a revised and enlarged edition. It grows out of her earlier Before the Gringo Came. The start of a contents list follows. It names The Pearls of Loreto and The Wash-Tub Mail. The stories themselves do not appear.
the-travels-and-adventures-of-monsieur-v:
Captain Marryat's Travels and Adventures of Monsieur Violet, covering California, Sonora, and western Texas, opens with the Revolution of 1830 in France. That upheaval ruined many ancient families attached to the court who would not desert the exiled Charles X. Among the few permitted to share his fortunes was the narrator's father, a noble gentleman of Burgundy who had already proved his faith during a former exile. Holyrood in Scotland was offered as the exiled king's retreat.

There the father bade an eternal adieu to France, setting his son's American wanderings in motion. Marryat, the Royal Navy novelist of Mr Midshipman Easy and Masterman Ready, frames a frontier tale as a French royalist's memoir. Readers get prairie, mission, and mining country through the eyes of a dispossessed aristocrat learning the New World the hard way.
the-waif-of-the-cynthia:
Jules Verne and André Laurie open The Waif of the Cynthia with a celebrity of commerce rather than the sea. Dr. Schwaryencrona of Stockholm, they say, has a face known everywhere, because his portrait appears on millions of green-sealed bottles shipped worldwide. The bottles hold cod liver oil, a useful medicine once made by fishermen and now produced scientifically.

The famous doctor's pointed beard, spectacles, hooked nose, and otter-skin cap make the likeness unmistakable. Chapter one is titled Mr. Malarius's Friend, pointing from the oil king toward the waif's story. Publication details show a cheap Seaside Library pocket edition, copyrighted in 1885 by George Munro, with a finer Rand McNally edition advertised behind it.
the-world-s-great-men-of-music-story-liv: Harriette Brower's The World's Great Men of Music, published in 1922, appears here through its contents list. Brower also wrote Piano Mastery and Vocal Mastery. Fourteen chapters tell story-lives of master musicians. Palestrina opens the line, followed by Bach and Handel. Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven come next. Schubert, Schumann, Chopin, Berlioz, and Liszt close the list shown. The biographies themselves do not appear in the pages present.
through-russia:
Maxim Gorky's Through Russia, translated by C. J. Hogarth, collects stories including The Birth of a Man, The Icebreaker, Gubin, and Nilushka. The first story is set in 1892, a year of leanness, between Sukhum and Otchenchiri on the Kodor river. Sea thunder sounds behind a sparkling rivulet.

Wild laurel leaves spin on white foam like mercury salmon fry, fooling gulls and the narrator alike. Chestnut leaves at his feet resemble amputated human palms. Readers get Russian stories where landscape, hunger, and wandering lives press close together, told in vivid, unsettling images.
tintinnalogia:
Tintinnalogia, or The Art of Ringing, was printed at London in 1671 for F. S., sold by Thomas Archer under the dial of St. Dunstan's Church in Fleet Street. Its anonymous author calls himself a lover of the art. The title promises plain and easy rules for ringing plain changes.

Cross peals, pricking, and hanging bells also fall within its scope. A dedication to the Noble Society of College-Youths explains that a Dutch Latin treatise on little bells inspired a day's labour to save English ringing rules from oral tradition alone. Readers get the founding English manual of change ringing.
town-life-in-australia: R. E. N. Twopeny wrote a series of letters on Australian town life, published by Elliot Stock at London in 1883. An introduction warns the book passed through the press while its author was in New Zealand. Contents promise a walk round Melbourne, then Sydney and Adelaide, followed by houses, servants, food, dress, young Australia, religion, education, politics, and amusements. The introduction and contents are what is shown in this record, so Twopeny's letters themselves do not appear beyond the first chapter heading.
treasure-and-trouble-therewith-a-tale-of: Geraldine Bonner's Treasure and Trouble Therewith, a tale of California printed in 1917, opens with a dedication to her father John Bonner. He was a writer himself, she writes, and trained her in the work he loved. The contents promise chapters named Hands Up, The Tules, Marquis de Lafayette, and The Picaroon. Later chapters bring Michaels the Miner and a marked paragraph. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present here, so the tale itself does not appear.
trivia:
Logan Pearsall Smith's Trivia, dated 1917, collects short pieces of moral prose. A bibliographical note says a few pieces came out privately from the Chiswick Press in 1902. Others ran in the New Statesman and The New Republic.

Smith's preface plays with advice against polishing style too much, lest nothing remain. He jokes that such fastidious polishers sound delightful and that he hopes to meet them. A second address to the reader calls the author a large carnivorous mammal, kin to the orang-outang and the baboon. The contents open Book One with The Author and Happiness, setting the book's dry, self-mocking tone.
un-doc-interim-accord-between-the-hellen:
The Interim Accord between Greece and its northern neighbour was signed at New York on 13 September 1995. The two states had clashed over the young republic's name, flag, and basic law. Greece had shut its ports to the landlocked state in protest. United Nations talks produced this stopgap deal.

Greece accepts the republic as a free state under a stopgap label. Envoys will swap posts in Athens and Skopje. The shared border stands fixed and beyond claim. Skopje drops the disputed sun sign from its flag. It also vows that its basic law grounds no land claims and no meddling abroad. Greece will not block the republic's bids to join world bodies under the stopgap name. Talks on the name itself go on.
venetia:
Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield, wrote the novel Venetia, first published in 1837 and reissued here in 1905. He dedicated it to Lord Lyndhurst, and the dedication says he had hoped to shadow forth two renowned and refined spirits of the age, as in a glass darkly. He kept the letter short, he says, in sadder hours than those when he first planned the book.

Book one opens some ten years before the American revolt, at an ancient hall in a midland county, on the edge of a great forest. The grey stone house, much covered with ivy, belonged to the Herberts, yet no one of the family had lived there since the exile of the Stuarts. The stage is set for a tale of a secluded girl and the poets her life will touch. Disraeli writes romance over real fame, thinly veiled.
who-can-be-happy-and-free-in-russia: The front pages here offer a title page, a short life note, and a partial contents list for Nicholas Nekrassov's poem, with no verses present. Juliet M. Soskice translated Who Can Be Happy and Free in Russia? into English, with an introduction by David Soskice. The World's Classics edition came out in 1917. Nekrassov was born near Vinitza in 1821 and died in St. Petersburg in 1877. The poem first appeared in Russia in 1879. The contents name a prologue, a pope, a village fair, and a drunken night.
with-the-die-hards-in-siberia:
Colonel John Ward wrote With the Die-Hards in Siberia, printed in 1920 with eight plates. He gave the book to his comrades of the Middlesex Regiment, four battalions strong. His foreword says the account began as a private record for his sons, in case he did not return. He wrote events down as they happened, with the reasons men gave at the time.

Later events showed some of those judgments wrong, Ward grants. He refused to fix the text to match the results, since that would kill its value. Russian affairs, he warns, are rarely what they seem. British troops in Siberia after the Great War fill the tale. Candor marks the book from the first page.
with-the-harmony-to-labrador-notes-of-a-: The title pages here are all that is present for With the Harmony to Labrador, by the Reverend B. La Trobe, so his travel notes do not appear. The Harmony was the ship that carried him to the Moravian mission stations on Labrador's north-east coast. The Moravian Church and Mission Agency printed the pamphlet in London. Its price was threepence. A contents heading follows the second title page, with no entries shown. A picture of the Harmony heads the work.
